<a id="q39"></a>
### 39. What is Grouped-Query Attention (GQA), and how does it differ from Multi-Head Attention (MHA)?

**Answer:**

Attention variants differ in how many **key/value heads** are shared among the **query heads**:

| Variant | Query heads | KV heads | KV cache size |
|---|---|---|---|
| **MHA** (Multi-Head) | H | H | 1x |
| **MQA** (Multi-Query) | H | 1 | 1/H |
| **GQA** (Grouped-Query) | H | G (1 < G < H) | G/H |

**GQA (Ainslie et al., 2023)** splits the H query heads into G groups; each group shares one K and one V head. E.g. Llama 2 70B / Llama 3 use 64 query heads and 8 KV heads (8x smaller KV cache).

**Why it matters**
- At decode time, generation is **memory-bandwidth bound**: every step reads the entire KV cache. Cache size per token = `2 * n_layers * n_kv_heads * head_dim * bytes`. Fewer KV heads mean less memory, larger batches/longer contexts, and faster decoding.
- MQA is fastest but loses quality and can be unstable to train; GQA recovers almost MHA quality with near-MQA speed.
- Existing MHA checkpoints can be **uptrained** into GQA by mean-pooling the KV heads of each group and continuing training with roughly 5% of the original compute.

**Implementation:** the KV tensors are broadcast/repeated across query heads within a group (`repeat_kv`), or kernels handle the mapping natively (FlashAttention supports GQA).

**Related:** DeepSeek's Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) compresses KV into a low-rank latent, an even more aggressive cache reduction.

**Sources:**
- [Grouped Query Attention (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/grouped-query-attention)
- [GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13245)
- [Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head is All You Need (MQA)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.02150)
- [Attention Is All You Need](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762)

<a id="q40"></a>
### 40. How does Sliding Window Attention work?

**Answer:**

**Sliding Window Attention (SWA)** restricts each token to attend only to the previous **W** tokens (a local causal window) instead of the full prefix. Attention cost drops from O(N^2) to **O(N * W)** and the KV cache can be capped at W entries per layer (a rolling/circular buffer).

**How information still travels far:** stacking layers extends the effective **receptive field**. With window W and L layers, information at layer L can originate from up to about `L * W` tokens back (each layer hops W tokens), as in a CNN. Mistral 7B uses W = 4096 with 32 layers, so theoretically roughly 131k tokens of reach, though in practice the influence of distant tokens decays.

**Implementation**
- Mask: `mask[i, j] = 1 if i - W < j <= i`.
- Inference: a rolling KV buffer indexed `pos mod W`; memory is constant regardless of sequence length.
- Efficient kernels (FlashAttention supports a window size).

**Variants and combinations**
- **Hybrid local/global:** Longformer (sliding window plus global tokens), Gemma 2/3 and others interleave local SWA layers with occasional global-attention layers (e.g. 5:1) to keep long-range retrieval while cutting cache.
- **Dilated windows** and **attention sinks** (keep the first few tokens plus window) for streaming.

**Trade-offs**
- Pros: linear compute, bounded memory, streaming-friendly.
- Cons: exact recall of tokens beyond the window degrades (needle-in-haystack weakness in pure SWA); needs global layers or retrieval for long-range tasks; pure sliding window without sinks fails when initial tokens are evicted.

**Sources:**
- [How does Sliding Window Attention work? (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/how-does-sliding-window-attention-work)
- [Longformer: The Long-Document Transformer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.05150)
- [Mistral 7B](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06825)
- [Generating Long Sequences with Sparse Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.10509)

<a id="q41"></a>
### 41. How do Attention Sinks work?

**Answer:**

**Observation (StreamingLLM, Xiao et al., 2023):** in autoregressive LLMs a large share of attention mass is assigned to the **first few tokens** regardless of their semantic relevance. These tokens act as **attention sinks**.

**Why it happens:** softmax forces attention weights to sum to 1. When a head has nothing relevant to attend to, it needs a "dump" location. Initial tokens are visible to every later token (causal masking), so the model learns to park excess attention there, giving near-no-op updates.

**Practical consequence**
- With **window attention** (keep only the last W KV entries), quality collapses (perplexity explodes) the moment the first tokens are evicted, because the softmax distribution is disrupted.
- **StreamingLLM fix:** always keep the KV of the first ~4 tokens (sinks) plus a rolling window of recent tokens. This gives stable generation over millions of tokens with constant memory and no fine-tuning, and speedups over recomputing sliding windows.
- Position handling: use positions relative to the cache (not original positions) for RoPE/ALiBi.

**Caveats**
- StreamingLLM does not extend the model's actual memory: evicted middle content is forgotten. It enables stable streaming, not long-context recall.

**Design-level fixes**
- Add a dedicated learnable sink token during pretraining, or a "softmax-off-by-one" / learnable sink logit (used in gpt-oss and in recent architectures such as DeepSeek-V4 per Outcome School's write-up) so heads can attend to "nothing" explicitly.
- Related work shows massive activations / register tokens in ViTs play the same role.

**Sources:**
- [How do Attention Sinks work? (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/how-do-attention-sinks-work)
- [Efficient Streaming Language Models with Attention Sinks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.17453)
- [Vision Transformers Need Registers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.16588)

<a id="q42"></a>
### 42. How does Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) work, and why is it preferred over learned positional embeddings?

**Answer:**

Self-attention is permutation-invariant, so position must be injected. **RoPE (Su et al., 2021)** encodes position by **rotating** query and key vectors by an angle proportional to their position, so their dot product depends on **relative** distance.

**Mechanism**
- Split the d-dim vector into d/2 pairs. For position m and pair i, rotate the pair by angle `m * theta_i` with `theta_i = base^(-2i/d)` (base typically 10000): 
  `[x1', x2'] = [x1 cos(m*t) - x2 sin(m*t), x1 sin(m*t) + x2 cos(m*t)]`.
- Apply this to Q and K (not V). Because rotations compose: `(R_m q) . (R_n k) = q^T R_{n-m} k`, the attention score depends only on `n - m`.
- Low-index pairs rotate fast (high frequency, local detail), high-index pairs slowly (low frequency, long-range).

**Why preferred over learned absolute embeddings**
- Encodes **relative** position naturally while keeping absolute info implicitly; no extra parameters.
- Decay of attention with distance emerges from the frequency structure.
- Better **length extrapolation** and easy context extension via rescaling: **Position Interpolation**, **NTK-aware scaling**, **YaRN**, and increasing the base (used in Llama 3, 128k+ context). Learned embeddings have no trained vectors beyond the max length and cannot extend.
- Works with KV cache (rotate once per key at its position) and is applied in every layer, not just the input.
- Adopted by Llama, Mistral, Qwen, Gemma, GPT-NeoX/J.

**Caveats:** without scaling, RoPE still degrades far outside training length; high-frequency dims can alias when extended; needs care when combined with attention-sink or compressed-KV schemes (MLA uses decoupled RoPE).

**Sources:**
- [Math Behind RoPE (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/math-behind-rope-rotary-position-embedding)
- [RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.09864)
- [YaRN: Efficient Context Window Extension](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.00071)
- [Extending Context Window via Position Interpolation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.15595)

<a id="q43"></a>
### 43. Explain Layer Normalization

**Answer:**

**Layer Normalization (Ba et al., 2016)** normalises the activations of **each token independently across its feature dimension**, then applies a learned scale and shift:

`LN(x) = gamma * (x - mu) / sqrt(sigma^2 + eps) + beta`, with `mu = mean(x)`, `sigma^2 = var(x)` computed over the d features of that token.

**Why it exists:** normalisation stabilises the distribution of layer inputs, keeps gradients well-scaled, allows larger learning rates and faster, more stable convergence.

**LayerNorm vs BatchNorm**
| | BatchNorm | LayerNorm |
|---|---|---|
| Statistics over | batch (and spatial) dim per feature | feature dim per sample/token |
| Depends on batch size | Yes (bad for small batches) | No |
| Train vs inference | Different (running averages) | Identical |
| Variable-length sequences | Awkward | Natural |
| Typical use | CNNs | RNNs, Transformers |

That independence from batch and sequence length is why Transformers use LN: sequences vary in length, are padded, and inference often runs with batch size 1.

**Details**
- Learnable `gamma` (d params) and `beta` (d params); `eps` about 1e-5 for numerical stability.
- Re-centring (subtracting mean) and re-scaling (dividing by std) both occur; RMSNorm keeps only the scaling.
- Computation in fp32 even in mixed precision to avoid overflow.
- Placement (Pre-LN vs Post-LN) strongly affects trainability.

**Sources:**
- [Batch Normalization vs Layer Normalization (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/batch-normalization-vs-layer-normalization)
- [Layer Normalization (Ba, Kiros, Hinton)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.06450)
- [PyTorch LayerNorm docs](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.LayerNorm.html)

---

<a id="q44"></a>
### 44. Explain RMSNorm (Root Mean Square Layer Normalization)

**Answer:**

**RMSNorm (Zhang & Sennrich, 2019)** is a simplified LayerNorm that drops the mean-centring and normalises only by the **root mean square** of the activations:

`RMSNorm(x) = gamma * x / sqrt( (1/d) * sum_i x_i^2 + eps )`

**Hypothesis:** the benefit of LayerNorm comes from **re-scaling invariance**, not re-centring. Removing the mean subtraction (and the bias `beta`) cuts computation and parameters with essentially no loss in quality.

**Benefits**
- Fewer operations (no mean, no variance, no bias): reported roughly 7-64% speedups over LayerNorm depending on setup; on a large model the total end-to-end gain is smaller but real.
- Fewer parameters (only `gamma`).
- Simpler, more numerically friendly, easily fused into kernels.
- Adopted by Llama family, Mistral, Gemma, Qwen, DeepSeek and most modern open LLMs (usually with Pre-Norm).

**Code**
```python
class RMSNorm(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d, eps=1e-6):
        super().__init__(); self.g = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(d)); self.eps = eps
    def forward(self, x):
        x32 = x.float()
        return (x32 * torch.rsqrt(x32.pow(2).mean(-1, keepdim=True) + self.eps)).type_as(x) * self.g
```

**Pitfalls:** compute in fp32 for stability; keep `eps` consistent when converting checkpoints; when x has a big non-zero mean, RMSNorm does not remove it (usually fine in practice).

**Sources:**
- [RMSNorm (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/rmsnorm-root-mean-square-layer-normalization)
- [Root Mean Square Layer Normalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.07467)
- [Llama 2 paper (uses pre-normalization with RMSNorm)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.09288)

---

<a id="q45"></a>
### 45. Why do modern Transformers use Pre-LayerNorm (Pre-Norm) instead of Post-LayerNorm?

**Answer:**

**Placement**
- **Post-LN (original Transformer):** `x = LN(x + Sublayer(x))`. Normalisation sits after the residual addition, on the main path.
- **Pre-LN:** `x = x + Sublayer(LN(x))`. Normalisation is inside the residual branch; the residual stream itself is an unnormalised identity path (a final LN is applied before the output head).

**Why Pre-LN wins for deep/large models**
- **Gradient flow:** in Pre-LN the identity residual path lets gradients reach lower layers directly, so gradient norms stay roughly uniform across depth. In Post-LN, gradients near the output are large and shrink at lower layers (Xiong et al., 2020), which makes training unstable.
- **No learning-rate warm-up dependence:** Post-LN needs careful warm-up and small learning rates or it diverges; Pre-LN trains stably with less tuning and larger learning rates, which is critical at LLM scale where a diverged run costs millions.
- **Depth scaling:** trains stacks of 80+ layers reliably.

**Trade-offs**
- Post-LN can reach slightly **better final quality** when it does converge, since every layer must contribute more strongly; Pre-LN can suffer "representation collapse" where deeper layers contribute less and the residual stream norm grows with depth.
- Mitigations and alternatives: **Sandwich/Peri-LN** (norm both before and after sublayers, used in some recent models), **DeepNorm** (Post-LN with scaled residuals for 1000-layer models), QK-norm, and final norm.

**Summary:** modern LLMs (GPT-2 onward, Llama, etc.) choose Pre-Norm, usually with RMSNorm, prioritising training stability and simplicity over the small potential quality edge of Post-LN.

**Sources:**
- [RMSNorm (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/rmsnorm-root-mean-square-layer-normalization)
- [On Layer Normalization in the Transformer Architecture (Xiong et al.)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.04745)
- [DeepNet: Scaling Transformers to 1,000 Layers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.00555)
- [Attention Is All You Need](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762)

<a id="q46"></a>
### 46. What are scaling laws (Chinchilla), and how do they guide model size vs training data decisions?

**Answer:**

**Scaling laws** are empirical power-law relationships showing that a language model's loss falls predictably as you increase parameters (N), training tokens (D) and compute (C).

**Kaplan et al. (2020, OpenAI):** loss follows power laws in N, D and C; concluded that for a fixed compute budget most of it should go to a bigger model, trained on relatively few tokens (which led to GPT-3: 175B params, about 300B tokens).

**Chinchilla (Hoffmann et al., 2022, DeepMind)**
- Re-fit the laws with better-tuned learning-rate schedules across 400+ models and found earlier models were **under-trained**.
- Parametric form: `L(N, D) = E + A/N^alpha + B/D^beta` (E is irreducible loss).
- Compute-optimal result: with `C ~ 6 N D` FLOPs, scale **N and D roughly equally**; rule of thumb about **20 tokens per parameter**.
- Chinchilla (70B params, 1.4T tokens) beat Gopher (280B params, same compute) and GPT-3 at the same training FLOPs, and was cheaper to serve.

**How it guides decisions**
1. Given a training budget C, pick N and D on the compute-optimal frontier.
2. Predict the loss of a big run from small pilot runs (extrapolate the fitted curve) before committing millions of dollars; used to choose hyperparameters and data mixes.

**Important nuance: inference-aware scaling**
- Chinchilla optimises **training** compute only. If a model will serve billions of requests, it is cheaper overall to **over-train a smaller model** on far more tokens (Llama 3 8B saw about 15T tokens, i.e. ~1,900 tokens/param). Sardana et al. formalise this.
- Data quality, repetition (data becomes the bottleneck, multi-epoch limits), and data-constrained scaling matter; loss does not map one-to-one to downstream capability; emergent abilities and test-time compute add other axes (reasoning models scale with inference compute).

**Sources:**
- [Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models (Chinchilla)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556)
- [Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models (Kaplan et al.)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361)
- [Beyond Chinchilla-Optimal: Accounting for Inference in Scaling Laws](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.00448)
- [Scaling Data-Constrained Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.16264)

<a id="q47"></a>
### 47. Your LLM keeps ignoring your instructions. How do you make it follow structured output formats?

**Answer:**

**Diagnose first**
- Instructions buried in a long prompt or contradicted by examples or context (lost in the middle).
- Ambiguous or negative-only instructions ("don't be verbose"), conflicting system and user messages.
- Model too small or not instruction-tuned; temperature too high; the format was never demonstrated.
- Untrusted content in the context overrides instructions (prompt injection).

**Fixes, in priority order**
1. **Use native structured-output features:** JSON mode / **structured outputs with a JSON Schema** (OpenAI), **tool/function calling** with an input schema (Anthropic, OpenAI), Gemini `responseSchema`. These use **constrained decoding** that masks invalid tokens so the output is schema-valid by construction.
2. **Constrained decoding for open models:** Outlines, XGrammar, llama.cpp GBNF grammars, vLLM guided decoding, Guidance/LMQL.
3. **Prompt design:** put instructions at the start and repeat the key format rule at the end; describe the schema precisely (field names, types, enums, one-line descriptions); give 2-3 few-shot examples with exact desired output; use delimiters/XML tags to separate instructions from data; state positive requirements ("Respond with only JSON"); prefill the assistant turn with `{` where supported.
4. **Validate and retry:** parse with Pydantic/Zod; on failure feed the error message back ("Your output failed validation: ...; fix it") with a bounded retry count. Libraries: Instructor, Pydantic AI.
5. **Decompose:** let the model reason first in a free-text field or separate step, then format in a second call, since strict constraints during reasoning can hurt quality.
6. **Lower temperature**, choose a stronger model, or fine-tune (SFT on valid examples) for stubborn formats.

**Trade-offs and pitfalls:** schema-valid does not mean semantically correct; constraints add a little latency on first use (grammar compile); put `reasoning` before `answer` in the schema; avoid overly complex or deeply recursive schemas.

**Verify:** measure parse success rate and field-level accuracy on an eval set; alert on validation-failure rate in production.

**Sources:**
- [Anthropic docs: Increase output consistency / structured outputs](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/increase-consistency)
- [OpenAI docs: Structured Outputs](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/structured-outputs)
- [Efficient Guided Generation for LLMs (Outlines)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.09702)
- [Instructor library docs](https://python.useinstructor.com/)

<a id="q48"></a>
### 48. Your LLM-powered tool hits the context window limit on long documents. How do you handle it?

**Answer:**

**Options, from cheapest to most involved**
1. **Do you really need all of it?** Retrieve instead of stuffing: **RAG** (chunk, embed, retrieve top-k, optionally rerank) so only relevant passages enter the prompt. Best for Q&A over big corpora.
2. **Map-reduce summarisation:** split into chunks (with overlap, along structural boundaries such as sections), summarise or extract from each in parallel (**map**), then combine partial results (**reduce**), recursively if needed. Good for whole-document summaries; parallelisable; can lose cross-chunk relations.
3. **Iterative refine:** process chunk by chunk keeping a running summary/state. Sequential and slower, and prone to drift.
4. **Hierarchical / tree summaries** (RAPTOR-style) to answer questions at multiple granularities.
5. **Recursive language models / agentic exploration:** keep the document outside the prompt (e.g. a Python variable, file system) and let the model search, slice and sub-call itself.
6. **Compress the input:** remove boilerplate, prompt compression (LLMLingua), extract tables/relevant sections, drop stale conversation turns.
7. **Bigger-context models:** use a 200k-1M window model when the doc fits, but note cost, latency and **context rot / lost in the middle** (accuracy drops for mid-context facts); put the question and key material at the beginning and end.
8. **Prompt caching** to make repeated large-context queries cheap.
9. **Fine-tuning / long-context extension** only for specialised recurring needs.

**Practical details**
- Count tokens with the model's tokenizer (tiktoken, provider count-tokens API) and reserve room for output.
- Chunk sizes typically 500-1500 tokens with 10-20% overlap; keep metadata (page, section) for citations.
- Handle failures gracefully: truncate with warning rather than error.

**Choosing:** Q&A, use RAG; full summary, map-reduce; multi-hop reasoning over one long doc, long context or agentic loop. Evaluate on questions whose answers are located in different parts of the doc.

**Sources:**
- [Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172)
- [Recursive Language Models (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/recursive-language-models)
- [Anthropic docs: Long context prompting tips](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/long-context-tips)
- [RAPTOR: Recursive Abstractive Processing for Tree-Organized Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.18059)
- [LLMLingua prompt compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.05736)

<a id="q49"></a>
### 49. Your LLM does not admit when it does not know the answer. How do you make it say "I don't know"?

**Answer:**

**Root cause:** LLMs are trained to produce plausible continuations; pretraining and RLHF often reward confident, complete answers, and the model has weak access to what it does not know. Hallucination is the default when knowledge is missing.

**Fixes (layered)**
1. **Ground the answer:** use RAG and instruct "Answer only from the provided context; if the context does not contain the answer, reply exactly 'I don't know'". Provide the escape hatch explicitly, since models otherwise feel obliged to answer. Anthropic's docs recommend explicitly allowing "I don't know" and asking for supporting quotes first.
2. **Prompting:** ask the model to extract relevant quotes first and answer only if a quote supports it; add few-shot examples that include refusals; ask for a confidence rating or a structured field `{answer, confidence, evidence}`.
3. **Retrieval-based gating:** if the top retrieval similarity/reranker score is below a threshold, return "not found" without calling the LLM.
4. **Uncertainty estimation:** sample multiple answers and check agreement (self-consistency / semantic entropy); token log-probabilities; verbalised confidence (often overconfident, so calibrate); trained probes.
5. **Verification step:** a second pass or LLM-judge checks each claim against sources (faithfulness check); abstain if unsupported.
6. **Training-time:** SFT/RL with examples where the correct behaviour is to abstain (R-Tuning, "honesty" alignment), reward calibrated abstention and penalise confident errors more than abstentions.
7. **Product design:** show citations, let users see sources, route low-confidence cases to humans.

**Trade-offs:** aggressive abstention lowers coverage (over-refusal), so tune the threshold on a labelled set of answerable and unanswerable questions and track precision/recall of abstention plus overall accuracy.

**Verify:** build an eval set with a known share of unanswerable questions; measure abstention rate on them versus false-abstention rate on answerable ones.

**Sources:**
- [Anthropic docs: Reduce hallucinations](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-hallucinations)
- [Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.05221)
- [Detecting hallucinations in LLMs using semantic entropy (Nature, 2024)](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07421-0)
- [A Survey on Hallucination in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.05232)

<a id="q50"></a>
### 50. Your LLM generates responses that are too verbose. How do you control response length?

**Answer:**

**Why it happens:** RLHF reward models and human raters tend to prefer longer, more thorough-looking answers (length bias); chat-tuned models add preambles, restatements, caveats and summaries.

**Controls**
1. **Explicit prompt constraints:** "Answer in at most 3 sentences", "under 50 words", "one paragraph", "bullet list of at most 5 items". Specific and measurable beats "be concise". State the audience and format ("no preamble, no restating the question, no closing summary").
2. **System prompt persona/style:** define a terse voice; put the constraint at the end of the prompt too.
3. **Few-shot examples** demonstrating the desired short style (the strongest lever for style).
4. **Structured output:** a schema with short fields, max lengths (`maxLength`), or an enum eliminates rambling.
5. **Prefilled response / stop sequences** to start directly with the answer and cut trailing commentary.
6. **`max_tokens`:** a hard safety cap, but it truncates mid-sentence, so combine with prompt instructions and check `stop_reason`/`finish_reason == "length"`.
7. **Two-pass:** generate then ask the model to compress ("rewrite in 40% of the length keeping all key facts").
8. **Decoding:** slight repetition penalty or lower temperature can help; adjusting EOS-token bias is possible in open models.
9. **Model-specific knobs:** verbosity parameters or effort settings offered by some APIs; smaller or non-reasoning modes for simple tasks; reduce hidden reasoning-token budget for reasoning models.
10. **Training-time:** length-controlled preference data, length penalty in RL reward, SFT on concise data (length-controlled DPO).

**Pitfalls:** models miscount words, so use sentences/bullets as units and validate lengths in code; extreme brevity can hurt correctness for reasoning tasks (allow scratchpad, then a short final answer).

**Verify:** track the response-length distribution (tokens), plus quality via an LLM-judge to make sure brevity did not drop needed content.

**Sources:**
- [Anthropic docs: Prompt engineering overview (be clear and direct)](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/overview)
- [OpenAI docs: Prompt engineering guide](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/prompt-engineering)
- [A Long Way to Go: Investigating Length Correlations in RLHF](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.03716)
- [Length-Controlled AlpacaEval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.04475)

<a id="q51"></a>
### 51. Your LLM memorized proprietary training data and leaks it in responses. How do you prevent this?

**Answer:**

**Background:** LLMs memorise rare, duplicated or long-tail sequences (Carlini et al. extracted PII and verbatim text from GPT-2 and production models). Memorisation rises with model size, data duplication, number of epochs and prompt length (extraction via prefix).

**Prevention, before and during training (the strongest controls)**
1. **Data governance:** do not train on proprietary/PII data you cannot expose; scrub secrets, PII and credentials (regex plus NER scanners such as Presidio, secret scanners).
2. **Deduplicate** training data (exact and near-dup, MinHash); duplication is the biggest driver of verbatim memorisation.
3. **Limit epochs / repetition;** use early stopping; avoid overfitting during fine-tuning (lower LR, fewer steps, LoRA with small rank, regularisation).
4. **Differential privacy (DP-SGD)** gives formal guarantees at a cost to quality and compute; practical mostly for fine-tuning.
5. **Access-control at the architecture level:** keep secrets out of weights entirely. Use **RAG** with per-user permissions on documents instead of fine-tuning on sensitive corpora. A model cannot leak what it never saw, and retrieval can be ACL-filtered and audited.

**Detection and mitigation after training**
- **Red-team with extraction attacks:** prefix prompts, divergence attacks; measure exact-match rates on canaries (planted unique strings/"exposure" metric).
- **Output filters:** DLP scanning, n-gram/Bloom-filter matching against protected corpora (like code-completion tools' duplication filters), PII redaction, refusals via a guardrail model.
- **Post-hoc unlearning** (gradient ascent, targeted editing) is immature and can degrade capability; retraining without the data is the reliable fix.
- Operational: rate-limit and monitor unusual query patterns; do not expose raw logprobs unnecessarily; system-prompt instructions alone are not a security boundary.

**Sources:**
- [Extracting Training Data from Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.07805)
- [Quantifying Memorization Across Neural Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.07646)
- [Deduplicating Training Data Makes Language Models Better](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.06499)
- [Scalable Extraction of Training Data from (Production) Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.17035)
- [Microsoft Presidio (PII detection)](https://microsoft.github.io/presidio/)

<a id="q52"></a>
### 52. Your LLM coding assistant generates outdated code using deprecated libraries. How do you fix it?

**Answer:**

**Root cause:** the model's knowledge is frozen at its training cutoff, and older APIs dominate the corpus (more historical examples than new-version docs), so it favours deprecated patterns.

**Fixes, in priority order**
1. **Retrieval of current docs (RAG for code):** fetch the relevant version's documentation, changelog, migration guides and type stubs and inject them into the prompt. Tools: Context7-style doc MCP servers, web-search/fetch tools, repo indexing. Prefer chunking by API symbol and pinning to the **exact installed version** (read `package.json`/`requirements.txt`/lockfile).
2. **Put the environment in context:** state language and library versions explicitly ("Python 3.12, pydantic v2, React 18 with hooks, LangChain 0.3"). Give a short "do/don't" list ("use `model_validate`, not `parse_obj`").
3. **Agentic verification loop:** let the assistant run the code, linters, type checkers and tests; feed deprecation warnings and errors back (`python -W error`, `ruff` with deprecation rules, `tsc`, compile warnings). Self-correction using real tool output is very effective.
4. **Provide in-repo examples** (few-shot from the codebase's current idioms); maintain an instructions file (e.g. CLAUDE.md / rules file) with project conventions and banned APIs.
5. **Automated guardrails:** lint rules that fail on deprecated imports in CI; codemods for migrations.
6. **Model side:** choose a model with a later cutoff, or fine-tune/continue-pretrain on recent library docs and code (costly, goes stale again, so RAG is usually better).
7. **Ask the model to check:** "Before using an API, verify it exists in version X in the provided docs"; require it to cite the doc snippet.

**Pitfalls:** retrieved docs for the wrong version can make things worse; hallucinated APIs that look modern; long docs crowd the context (retrieve only relevant symbols).

**Verify:** benchmark on a set of tasks requiring post-cutoff APIs; track share of generations passing tests with zero deprecation warnings.

**Sources:**
- [Anthropic docs: Tool use with Claude](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/agents-and-tools/tool-use/overview)
- [Model Context Protocol documentation](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/)
- [Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401)
- [DocPrompting: Generating Code by Retrieving the Docs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.05987)

<a id="q53"></a>
### 53. Your tokenizer splits important domain terms into meaningless subword pieces. How do you fix it?

**Answer:**

**Why it matters:** BPE/WordPiece/Unigram vocabularies are learned on general corpora; rare domain terms (drug names, gene IDs, legal Latin, product SKUs, code identifiers, non-English words) get fragmented into many tokens. Consequences: longer sequences (higher cost and latency), harder learning of the term's meaning, worse embeddings/retrieval, higher error rates on exact strings.

**Diagnose:** run the tokenizer over a domain corpus and compute **fertility** (tokens per word), the share of terms split into more than N pieces, and the compression ratio (bytes per token) versus a general corpus.

**Fixes**
1. **Do nothing to the tokenizer (often fine):** modern LLMs handle fragments via contextual representations. Add few-shot examples and glossaries in the prompt; use RAG with the exact string for lookup. Cheapest option.
2. **Add tokens to an existing vocabulary:** `tokenizer.add_tokens([...])`, then `model.resize_token_embeddings(len(tokenizer))`. New embeddings must be **learned**: initialise smartly (mean of the constituent subword embeddings) and then continue pretraining / fine-tune (at least embeddings plus LoRA). Untrained new tokens are worse than fragments.
3. **Train a new or extended tokenizer** on domain plus general text (SentencePiece/HF `tokenizers`), merge with the base vocabulary (as done for Chinese/Indic/medical Llama extensions), then do continued pretraining. Costly; the model must re-learn some weights and old checkpoints are not compatible.
4. **Preprocessing:** normalise terms (consistent casing, hyphenation), replace codes with placeholders or wrap them in delimiters, split identifiers deliberately (camelCase, snake_case).
5. **Retrieval side:** for embedding search, use hybrid BM25 + dense (BM25 keeps exact term match), or a domain-adapted embedding model.
6. **Tokenizer-free / byte-level models** (ByT5, byte-latent transformer) avoid the issue at a cost in sequence length.

**Trade-offs:** larger vocab means bigger embedding/softmax matrix and rarer token updates; vocab change requires retraining and evaluation. Verify with a domain perplexity/task benchmark and check tokens-per-document before and after.

**Sources:**
- [Hugging Face Tokenizers documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/tokenizers/index)
- [Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units (BPE)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1508.07909)
- [SentencePiece](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.06226)
- [Efficient and Effective Text Encoding for Chinese LLaMA and Alpaca (vocabulary extension)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.08177)
- [ByT5: Towards a token-free future](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.13626)

<a id="q54"></a>
### 54. Your Transformer's KV cache grows too large during long sequence generation. How do you manage memory?

**Answer:**

**Sizing:** KV cache bytes = `2 * n_layers * n_kv_heads * head_dim * seq_len * batch * bytes_per_element`. For a 70B-class model with full MHA this reaches several GB per long sequence, and it often exceeds the weight memory at large batch or 100k+ context. Naive contiguous allocation also wastes 60-80% to fragmentation.

**Fixes**
1. **Allocator level: PagedAttention (vLLM).** Store KV in fixed-size blocks (pages) with a block table, allocated on demand; nearly eliminates fragmentation and over-reservation; supports **prefix sharing / copy-on-write** across requests sharing a prompt (prefix caching). Throughput gains of roughly 2-4x versus prior systems.
2. **Architecture-level reduction:** **GQA/MQA** (fewer KV heads), **MLA** (low-rank latent KV, DeepSeek), sliding-window or local/global hybrid attention, cross-layer KV sharing.
3. **Quantise the KV cache** to FP8/INT8/INT4 (KIVI, KVQuant, vLLM `--kv-cache-dtype fp8`): 2-4x smaller with small quality loss; validate on long-context evals.
4. **Eviction / sparsification:** keep attention sinks plus recent window (StreamingLLM), heavy-hitter policies (H2O, SnapKV, Scissorhands) that retain tokens with high cumulative attention; lossy, so risk to needle recall.
5. **Offloading:** spill cold KV to CPU RAM/NVMe (with prefetching); LMCache-style tiered stores; disaggregated prefill/decode.
6. **Prefix/prompt caching** to avoid duplicating and recomputing shared system prompts and documents.
7. **Serving-level:** cap max context and batch by memory budget, chunked prefill, continuous batching, tensor/pipeline parallelism to shard the cache across GPUs, lower concurrency.
8. **Application-level:** shorten prompts (summarise/RAG), truncate history.

**Verify:** monitor GPU KV-cache utilisation, preemption/eviction counts, and the quality delta (long-context benchmarks like RULER/needle tests) after each lossy technique.

**Sources:**
- [Paged Attention in LLMs (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/paged-attention-in-llms)
- [Efficient Memory Management for LLM Serving with PagedAttention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180)
- [Efficient Streaming Language Models with Attention Sinks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.17453)
- [H2O: Heavy-Hitter Oracle for KV cache eviction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.14048)
- [KIVI: 2-bit KV cache quantization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.02750)

<a id="q55"></a>
### 55. Your Transformer runs out of memory on long documents due to quadratic self-attention. How do you scale it?

**Answer:**

**Diagnose:** self-attention builds an N x N score matrix per head per layer: memory O(N^2) (naive) and compute O(N^2 d). Also check what else grows: activations for backprop, KV cache at inference, and batch size.

**Fixes, by impact/effort**
1. **FlashAttention (exact):** tiling plus online softmax means the N x N matrix is never materialised; memory becomes O(N). Enable it via `torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention` or `attn_implementation="flash_attention_2"`. This is the first thing to do; it does not change results.
2. **Training memory:** gradient checkpointing (recompute activations), mixed precision (bf16), smaller micro-batch with gradient accumulation, ZeRO/FSDP sharding, **sequence/context parallelism** (Ring Attention, DeepSpeed-Ulysses) to split the sequence across GPUs.
3. **Sparse / local attention (approximate but linear):** **sliding-window** attention, Longformer/BigBird (window + global + random), block-sparse, hybrid local/global layers (Gemma) giving O(N*W).
4. **Reduce KV memory at inference:** GQA/MQA, MLA, KV quantisation, PagedAttention, eviction (StreamingLLM).
5. **Compress the sequence:** hierarchical models, chunk-and-pool, token merging, memory tokens (Transformer-XL, Compressive Transformer), summarisation before the model.
6. **Chunk and retrieve:** split the document, use RAG or map-reduce so the model never sees the full N.
7. **Sub-quadratic architectures:** linear attention, state-space models (Mamba), or hybrids (Jamba); trade-off is weaker exact recall.
8. **Position extension:** RoPE scaling (YaRN) if the issue is the length beyond training.

**Trade-offs:** FlashAttention keeps quality but compute stays quadratic; sparse/linear methods lose some global recall; parallelism needs more hardware.

**Verify:** profile peak memory (`torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated`) versus sequence length; run needle-in-a-haystack and long-document task evals after each approximation.

**Sources:**
- [How does Sliding Window Attention work? (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/how-does-sliding-window-attention-work)
- [Decoding Flash Attention in LLMs (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/decoding-flash-attention)
- [FlashAttention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14135)
- [Longformer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.05150)
- [Ring Attention with Blockwise Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01889)

<a id="q56"></a>
### 56. Your distilled student model fails on the complex reasoning that the teacher model handled. How do you close the gap?

**Answer:**

**Diagnose**
- **Capacity gap:** a student too small relative to the teacher cannot represent multi-step reasoning. Test intermediate sizes.
- **Data problem:** distillation data over-represents easy examples; teacher outputs are answers without reasoning; teacher's rationales are too long or too advanced for the student.
- **Objective problem:** SFT on final answers teaches style, not process; exposure bias (student trained on teacher prefixes, but sees its own at inference).
- Check per-category failure modes (arithmetic, multi-hop, planning) and whether errors occur early or late in the chain.

**Fixes**
1. **Distil rationales, not only answers:** train on teacher chain-of-thought traces (step-by-step distillation, Orca, DeepSeek-R1 distills). Use the **hard** examples: mine problems where the student fails and generate multiple teacher solutions.
2. **Filter for correctness:** rejection sampling with verifiers/unit tests/answer matching, majority voting; drop wrong or rambling traces.
3. **Curriculum:** easy to hard; or an intermediate "teacher assistant" model to bridge large capacity gaps.
4. **On-policy distillation / GKD:** student samples, teacher scores tokens (reverse KL), removing the train-test mismatch.
5. **Logit distillation** in addition to text (richer signal per token) if you can access teacher logits.
6. **RL on top of the distilled student** (GRPO with verifiable rewards) to sharpen reasoning beyond imitation.
7. **Use more compute at inference:** self-consistency, best-of-N with a verifier, longer thinking budget.
8. **Scale up the student** or use a MoE/wider student; increase distillation data volume and diversity.
9. **Hybrid deployment:** route hard queries to the teacher (cascade with confidence threshold).

**Trade-offs:** longer traces improve accuracy but raise token cost; there is a ceiling set by student capacity.

**Verify:** compare against benchmarks like GSM8K/MATH/domain sets stratified by difficulty; track pass@1 and the student/teacher performance ratio.

**Sources:**
- [How does Knowledge Distillation work? (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/how-does-knowledge-distillation-work)
- [Distilling Step-by-Step!](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.02301)
- [Orca: Progressive Learning from Complex Explanation Traces of GPT-4](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.02707)
- [On-Policy Distillation of Language Models (GKD)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.13649)
- [DeepSeek-R1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12948)

<a id="q57"></a>
### 57. After RLHF alignment, your LLM became safer but lost capability on hard tasks. How do you manage the alignment tax?

**Answer:**

**Alignment tax:** the drop in raw capability (benchmarks, reasoning, coding, calibration) after preference optimisation, caused by over-optimising a safety/preference reward, distribution shift away from the base model, and over-refusal.

**Diagnose:** compare base, SFT, RLHF checkpoints on capability benchmarks, safety suites and refusal rates on borderline-but-benign prompts (XSTest-like); examine what type of hard tasks regressed; check KL from the reference and reward curves for over-optimisation.

**Mitigations**
1. **Constrain divergence:** higher KL coefficient, early stopping of RL, smaller learning rate; PPO with KL penalty is precisely to bound drift.
2. **Mix in pretraining/capability data** during RLHF (InstructGPT's **PPO-ptx**, mixing pretraining gradients removed most benchmark regressions).
3. **Balanced reward design:** separate **helpfulness and safety reward models** (Llama 2 used two) and combine them, with multi-objective or constrained optimisation (Safe RLHF: maximise helpfulness subject to a harm-cost constraint); reward correct hard-task behaviour, not only refusal.
4. **Data:** add hard-task and borderline benign prompts (to avoid over-refusal) with helpful answers; include diverse capability prompts in preference data; verifiable rewards (RLVR) for reasoning tasks preserve capability.
5. **Weight-space interpolation:** average the aligned and pre-alignment weights (WiSE-FT / model averaging) to regain capability while retaining most safety (Lin et al. show averaging reduces alignment tax).
6. **Parameter-efficient alignment** (LoRA) or DPO with conservative beta to limit drift.
7. **Stage order:** do capability-heavy reasoning RL, then a light safety pass; or a final merge.
8. **Deployment routing:** stronger guardrail classifiers so the base model need not be over-conservative.

**Verify:** a Pareto view of capability versus safety metrics across checkpoints and hyperparameters; pick the frontier point matching product risk tolerance.

**Sources:**
- [Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/reinforcement-learning-from-human-feedback-rlhf)
- [Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback (InstructGPT)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155)
- [Llama 2 paper (separate safety and helpfulness reward models)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.09288)
- [Safe RLHF](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.12773)
- [Mitigating the Alignment Tax of RLHF](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06256)

<a id="q58"></a>
### 58. Your RLHF-trained LLM is gaming the reward model instead of being genuinely helpful. How do you fix reward hacking?

**Answer:**

**What is happening:** the reward model (RM) is an imperfect proxy trained on limited human preferences. Policy optimisation finds inputs where the proxy score is high but true quality is low (Goodhart's law). Typical symptoms: excessive length, flattery/sycophancy, confident but wrong text, formatting tricks, repetitive stock phrases, and proxy reward rising while human/gold evaluation falls. Gao et al. show gold reward first rises then declines with KL distance from the initial policy.

**Fixes**
1. **KL penalty to the reference policy** (and tune beta); early stopping based on a held-out gold metric, not on RM score.
2. **Better RM:** more and more diverse preference data, especially on-policy samples that expose exploits (iterative RLHF: retrain the RM on fresh policy outputs); larger RM; **RM ensembles** (take min/mean minus variance, uncertainty-penalised reward); calibrate and normalise rewards.
3. **Counter known biases:** length-normalised or length-penalised reward, explicit anti-verbosity term; adversarial/contrast pairs for sycophancy; balanced data.
4. **Constrain optimisation:** fewer steps, smaller LR, best-of-n / rejection sampling instead of full RL (less exploit pressure), reward clipping.
5. **Avoid the learned RM where possible:** verifiable rewards (unit tests, exact answers) for math/code; **DPO** removes the explicit RM (but has its own over-optimisation modes); rule-based rewards.
6. **Process supervision / stronger judges:** reward step-level correctness; constitutional/AI feedback and LLM judges with rubrics; debate-style checks.
7. **Detect:** monitor gold-vs-proxy gap using periodic human evaluation or a stronger held-out judge; inspect top-reward samples and reward outliers; track length, refusal, and entropy collapse.
8. **Held-out evals** that the RM never saw and red-team prompts.

**Trade-offs:** stronger regularisation reduces gains from RLHF; ensembles cost compute; human relabelling is expensive.

**Sources:**
- [Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/reinforcement-learning-from-human-feedback-rlhf)
- [Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.10760)
- [Reward Model Ensembles Help Mitigate Overoptimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.02743)
- [Open Problems and Fundamental Limitations of RLHF](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.15217)
- [Concrete Problems in AI Safety](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.06565)

<a id="q59"></a>
### 59. Your chatbot loses context after 10 turns in a conversation. How do you maintain a long conversation context?

**Answer:**

**Causes:** history is truncated to fit the window or a naive "last N messages" policy; the model attends poorly to old/mid-context content; token budget consumed by system prompt, tools and long documents; each request is stateless, so history must be resent.

**Strategies (often combined)**
1. **Persist and resend the message list** properly (server-side session store keyed by conversation ID); never rely on the model's implicit memory.
2. **Token-budgeted windowing:** always keep the system prompt plus the most recent turns, measured in tokens, not turn count.
3. **Rolling summarisation:** when history exceeds a threshold, summarise older turns into a compact "conversation so far" message (preserving decisions, entities, user preferences, open tasks) and keep recent turns verbatim. Update incrementally.
4. **Structured memory / state:** extract facts into a key-value or JSON profile (name, goals, constraints, slots) updated each turn and injected into the prompt. Reliable for task-oriented bots.
5. **Long-term memory with retrieval:** store past turns/facts as embeddings in a vector store; retrieve relevant memories per query (episodic vs semantic memory, like MemGPT/Letta, Mem0). Add recency and importance weighting; support forgetting/updating.
6. **Pin important information:** system prompt or a "notes" block for facts that must never be lost; re-inject critical instructions periodically.
7. **Query rewriting:** rewrite each user turn into a standalone question using history before retrieval (for RAG chatbots) to resolve pronouns.
8. **Prompt caching** to keep long histories cheap; use long-context models when acceptable; context editing/clearing of old tool outputs for agents.
9. **UX:** let users see and edit memory; conversation reset controls.

**Pitfalls:** summaries drift and drop details (keep verbatim key facts); privacy/retention concerns for stored memory; contradiction between stale and new facts (timestamp and overwrite).

**Verify:** build multi-turn evals with facts stated at turn 1 and probed at turn 20+; track recall accuracy and token cost.

**Sources:**
- [AI Agent Memory (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/ai-agent-memory)
- [MemGPT: Towards LLMs as Operating Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.08560)
- [LangChain docs: Memory / persistence](https://python.langchain.com/docs/concepts/memory/)
- [Lost in the Middle](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172)

<a id="q60"></a>
### 60. Your chatbot fails when users switch topics mid-conversation. How do you handle topic switches?

**Answer:**

**Failure modes:** the bot keeps answering in the old topic (stale context bias), retrieval uses a contextualised query polluted by earlier turns, slot-filling state from a previous flow leaks into the new one, or the bot mixes up entities ("it" resolves to the wrong thing).

**Detection**
- **Embedding similarity:** compare the new user message's embedding with a rolling topic centroid or recent turns; a drop below a tuned threshold signals a switch.
- **LLM classifier / router:** ask a small model "Is this message a continuation, a follow-up, or a new topic?" (structured output), also outputting a standalone rewritten query.
- **Intent classification** with a taxonomy, checking for a change of intent or domain; explicit cues ("by the way", "new question", "forget that").
- Combine signals (embedding + LLM) to reduce false positives, since follow-ups with pronouns look dissimilar but are continuations.

**Handling**
1. **Standalone query rewriting:** rewrite each turn using only the relevant history; if the topic switched, don't include old context in retrieval.
2. **Segment the history:** tag turns by topic/thread; include only the current segment plus a short summary of prior ones in the prompt; keep old segments retrievable.
3. **State management:** for task-oriented flows, use a dialogue state stack; push the new topic, allow resuming ("back to the earlier flight booking") or explicitly abort the pending flow after confirming.
4. **Reset per-topic memory/RAG filters and tools;** keep global user profile.
5. **Ask when ambiguous:** "Are you asking about X or something new?"
6. **Prompt instruction:** "If the latest message is unrelated to earlier ones, ignore previous context."
7. **Clean UX:** a "new chat" button and thread titles.

**Pitfalls:** over-eager resets break legitimate follow-ups; the threshold needs tuning on real logs.

**Verify:** a labelled test set of multi-turn dialogues with continuation, follow-up, switch, and switch-back; measure detection precision/recall and answer quality.

**Sources:**
- [AI Agent Memory (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/ai-agent-memory)
- [LangChain docs: Conversational RAG with history-aware retriever](https://python.langchain.com/docs/tutorials/qa_chat_history/)
- [Rasa docs: Conversation patterns and dialogue management](https://rasa.com/docs/rasa/)
- [Sentence-BERT (embedding similarity)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.10084)

<a id="q61"></a>
### 61. Your QA system always generates an answer even when no answer exists in the context. How do you detect unanswerable questions?

**Answer:**

**Why:** generative readers are trained/prompted to answer, and parametric knowledge fills gaps (SQuAD 1.1-style training never includes unanswerable cases; SQuAD 2.0 introduced them).

**Detection methods**
1. **Prompt with an abstention option:** "Use only the context. If the answer is not in the context, output NOT_FOUND." Add few-shot examples of unanswerable cases and require supporting quotes.
2. **Retrieval-confidence gating:** if the top retrieval/reranker (cross-encoder) score is below a calibrated threshold, abstain before generation.
3. **Extractive QA null-answer:** the span-extraction model compares the best span score with the [CLS] "no answer" score (SQuAD 2.0 approach, threshold tuned on dev).
4. **Train a classifier:** fine-tune a cross-encoder on (question, context) to predict answerable/unanswerable; mine hard negatives (topically related contexts that lack the answer). Use SQuAD 2.0, Natural Questions, or your own labelled data.
5. **Entailment / faithfulness check (NLI):** verify that the generated answer is entailed by the context (NLI model, LLM judge, or RAGAS faithfulness); reject unsupported answers.
6. **Uncertainty signals:** low token log-probs, high disagreement across sampled answers (semantic entropy), answer generation without context matching the with-context answer (i.e. the model relies on memory).
7. **Structured output:** `{answerable: bool, answer, evidence_quote}`; validate that the quote actually occurs in the context (string match).
8. **Fine-tune with abstention data:** include negatives with target "I cannot find this in the provided documents".

**Trade-offs:** stricter thresholds reduce hallucinated answers but reduce recall; choose the operating point by cost of wrong versus missing answers; route rejected queries to fallback (search, human, clarifying question).

**Verify:** evaluate on a balanced set (answerable vs unanswerable); report abstention precision/recall, plus exact match/F1 on answerable subset (SQuAD 2.0 metrics with best-threshold F1).

**Sources:**
- [Know What You Don't Know: Unanswerable Questions for SQuAD](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.03822)
- [Anthropic docs: Reduce hallucinations](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-hallucinations)
- [RAGAS: Automated Evaluation of RAG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.15217)
- [Detecting hallucinations in LLMs using semantic entropy (Nature, 2024)](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07421-0)

<a id="q62"></a>
### 62. Your summarization system hallucinated facts not in the original article. How do you fix it?

**Answer:**

**Types of errors:** intrinsic (contradicts the source: wrong number, entity, negation swap) and extrinsic (adds unsupported info from parametric memory). Abstractive models over-generalise, merge entities, and "complete" details.

**Fixes**
1. **Prompt for grounding:** "Summarise using only information in the article. Do not add outside knowledge. If a detail is not stated, omit it." Ask for quotes/evidence per sentence or citation of source sentence IDs.
2. **Extract-then-abstract:** first extract key sentences/facts/entities (structured), then generate the summary from them; or use extractive summarisation for high-stakes cases.
3. **Lower temperature**, use a stronger model, and avoid long inputs in the middle-of-context blind spot (chunk long articles with map-reduce so each chunk is small).
4. **Verify-and-revise loop:** decompose the summary into atomic claims and check each against the source (NLI model such as SummaC/AlignScore, or LLM judge; QA-based metrics like QAFactEval). Delete or regenerate unsupported claims; or a "critique and rewrite" second pass (chain-of-verification).
5. **Entity/number checks:** deterministic verification that every named entity, date and number in the summary appears in the source.
6. **Constrained decoding / copy mechanisms** and faithfulness-aware decoding (context-aware decoding, contrastive decoding) to increase reliance on the source.
7. **Fine-tune for faithfulness:** train on cleaned reference summaries (many datasets like XSum contain hallucinated references); preference-tune (DPO) with faithful-vs-unfaithful pairs; add unlikelihood loss.
8. **UI:** highlight source spans linking each summary sentence back to the article.

**Trade-offs:** stricter faithfulness makes summaries more extractive and less fluent; verification adds latency and cost.

**Verify:** human evaluation on a sample; automatic metrics (FactCC, AlignScore, SummaC, LLM-judge faithfulness); track hallucination rate, not only ROUGE (which correlates poorly with factuality).

**Sources:**
- [On Faithfulness and Factuality in Abstractive Summarization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.00661)
- [Chain-of-Verification Reduces Hallucination in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.11495)
- [SummaC: Re-Visiting NLI-based Models for Inconsistency Detection in Summarization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.09525)
- [Anthropic docs: Reduce hallucinations](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-hallucinations)

<a id="q63"></a>
### 63. Your text generation repeats phrases in long outputs. How do you fix repetition?

**Answer:**

**Why it happens:** greedy/beam decoding is deterministic and once a phrase appears, the model assigns it high probability again (self-reinforcing loop; induction/copy heads). Low temperature, long outputs, small models, weak context handling, and degenerate training data (repeated boilerplate) all worsen it. Also check for truncated EOS handling or a prompt template bug.

**Decoding-time fixes (fast, first)**
1. **Sampling instead of greedy:** temperature about 0.7-1.0 with **nucleus sampling** (top-p about 0.9) or top-k; **min-p** sampling is also robust.
2. **Repetition penalties:** `repetition_penalty` (about 1.05-1.2, divides positive logits of previously seen tokens), **frequency penalty** (scales with count) and **presence penalty** (flat) in OpenAI-style APIs. Too high causes odd word choices or avoiding necessary repeats (names, code).
3. **`no_repeat_ngram_size`** (e.g. 3-4) to hard-block repeated n-grams (in translation/summarisation); blunt for entities.
4. **Contrastive search / typical sampling / DRY sampler** (penalises repeating sequences) designed for degeneration.
5. **Beam search with diversity** (diverse beam search) if beams are needed.

**Model/prompt-level fixes**
6. Prompt: ask for varied, non-redundant text, provide an outline or structure, and generate long text section by section, each conditioned on a short summary of prior sections (prevents loops in long context).
7. Ensure proper **EOS/stop tokens** and a sensible max length; check context truncation.
8. **Training:** unlikelihood training, dedupe training data, preference tuning against repetition, RLHF length/repetition penalties; a larger or better model.
9. Long-context: verify RoPE scaling is correct beyond trained length, since broken positions often trigger loops.

**Trade-offs:** stronger penalties reduce coherence and factual repetition (legit repeated terms); higher temperature increases hallucination risk.

**Verify:** measure distinct-n, self-BLEU or repeated n-gram rate, plus quality via human/LLM judge.

**Sources:**
- [The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration (nucleus sampling)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.09751)
- [Neural Text Generation with Unlikelihood Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.04319)
- [Hugging Face: Text generation strategies](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/generation_strategies)
- [A Contrastive Framework for Neural Text Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.06417)

<a id="q64"></a>
### 64. Transformers work on text, so can they also understand images?

**Answer:**

**Yes.** The Transformer only needs a **sequence of vectors**; the modality does not matter. The **Vision Transformer (ViT, Dosovitskiy et al., 2020)** shows how to turn an image into such a sequence.

**ViT pipeline**
1. Split the image (e.g. 224x224) into fixed **patches** (e.g. 16x16), giving 196 patches.
2. Flatten each patch and apply a **linear projection** (equivalently a strided convolution) to get patch embeddings of dimension D.
3. Prepend a learnable **[CLS] token** and add **position embeddings** (learned 1D) so the model knows patch locations.
4. Feed through standard Transformer encoder blocks (self-attention + MLP, LayerNorm, residuals).
5. Use the [CLS] output (or pooled patches) for classification.

"An image is worth 16x16 words."

**Properties**
- Fewer inductive biases than CNNs (no built-in locality/translation equivariance), so ViTs need **large datasets** (JFT, ImageNet-21k) or strong augmentation/distillation (DeiT) to beat CNNs; with enough data they scale better.
- Global attention from layer 1; cost O(patches^2), so high-resolution images need windowed attention (Swin) or larger patches.

**Multimodal LLMs**
- A **vision encoder** (ViT, often CLIP/SigLIP-pretrained) turns the image into patch embeddings, a **projector** (linear/MLP or Q-Former/cross-attention resampler) maps them into the LLM's token-embedding space, and the LLM treats them as "image tokens" alongside text (LLaVA, Flamingo, GPT-4V, Claude, Gemini). Some models train natively multimodal from scratch.
- **CLIP** aligns image and text embeddings contrastively for zero-shot classification and retrieval.

**Also:** the same recipe works for audio (spectrogram patches, Whisper/AST) and video.

**Sources:**
- [Decoding Vision Transformer (ViT) (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/decoding-vision-transformer-vit)
- [An Image is Worth 16x16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.11929)
- [Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision (CLIP)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00020)
- [Visual Instruction Tuning (LLaVA)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.08485)

<a id="q65"></a>
### 65. Small Language Models (SLMs)

**Answer:**

**Definition:** SLMs are language models small enough to run cheaply on a laptop, phone or a single modest GPU, typically from about 100M to roughly 10B parameters (there is no strict cut-off). Examples: Phi-3/4 mini, Gemma 2B/9B, Llama 3.2 1B/3B, Qwen2.5 0.5B-7B, SmolLM.

**Why they work now**
- **High-quality, curated/synthetic data** ("Textbooks Are All You Need", Phi series) and heavy **over-training** far beyond Chinchilla-optimal token counts.
- **Distillation** from larger teachers, plus better architecture (GQA, RoPE, RMSNorm, SwiGLU) and post-training (SFT, DPO, RL for reasoning).
- **Quantisation** (INT8/INT4, GGUF, AWQ/GPTQ) shrinks a 7B model to roughly 4 GB.

**Advantages**
- Low latency and cost, high throughput; on-device, offline use; **privacy** (data never leaves device); easier to fine-tune (LoRA on a single GPU) and to deploy at the edge; lower energy.

**Limitations**
- Weaker broad world knowledge (more hallucination on facts), weaker complex multi-step reasoning, shorter effective context, less robust instruction following.

**When to use**
- Narrow, well-defined tasks after fine-tuning: classification, extraction, routing, intent detection, summarisation, autocomplete, structured output, RAG readers with good retrieval, agentic sub-tasks, guardrails.
- Cascades: SLM first, escalate to LLM on low confidence; SLMs as speculative-decoding draft models.

**When not to:** open-ended reasoning, broad knowledge QA without retrieval, tasks requiring frontier coding/maths.

**Practical tips:** evaluate on your task with a real eval set; fine-tune with domain data; combine with RAG and constrained decoding.

**Sources:**
- [Small Language Models (SLMs) (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/small-language-models-slms)
- [Textbooks Are All You Need (Phi-1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.11644)
- [Phi-3 Technical Report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.14219)
- [Small Language Models are the Future of Agentic AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.02153)

---

<a id="q66"></a>
### 66. Large Reasoning Models (LRMs)

**Answer:**

**Definition:** LRMs are LLMs trained (mainly with reinforcement learning) to produce a long internal **chain of thought** before the final answer, spending more **test-time compute** to solve hard problems. Examples: OpenAI o1/o3, DeepSeek-R1, Claude models with extended thinking, Gemini thinking models, Qwen QwQ.

**How they differ from standard LLMs**
- Standard LLM: answers immediately (or with prompted CoT). LRM: generates hidden or visible "thinking" tokens, exploring, planning, checking and backtracking, self-correcting, then answers.
- New scaling axis: accuracy improves with the number of thinking tokens (**inference-time scaling**), in addition to pretraining scale.

**How they are trained**
1. Pretrained base model plus optional SFT on (cold-start) long CoT traces.
2. **RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR)** on math, code, logic (answer correctness, unit tests) using PPO or **GRPO**; reasoning behaviours such as reflection ("wait, let me re-check") emerge (DeepSeek-R1-Zero).
3. Rejection sampling and distillation of the traces into smaller models; a final RLHF/safety stage.
4. Process reward models and search (best-of-N, MCTS, self-consistency) are optional additions.

**Practical use**
- Controls: reasoning effort / thinking budget parameters; streaming reasoning summaries.
- Prompting tips: keep prompts simple and goal-focused, avoid forcing explicit "think step by step", give constraints and success criteria, not micro-steps.
- Best for maths, coding, planning, multi-step analysis, agentic tasks.

**Trade-offs**
- Higher latency and cost (thinking tokens billed), overthinking simple questions, verbose or unfaithful reasoning traces (the CoT may not reflect the true computation), potential reward hacking, and gains mostly in verifiable domains.
- Use routing: cheap non-reasoning model for easy queries, LRM for hard ones.

**Sources:**
- [Large Reasoning Models (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/large-reasoning-models)
- [DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability via RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12948)
- [Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.03314)
- [Anthropic docs: Extended thinking](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/extended-thinking)
- [OpenAI: Reasoning models guide](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/reasoning)

<a id="q67"></a>
### 67. Jev and System One Models

**Answer:**

This topic is very recent and comes from a single vendor announcement, so treat the details below as reported (per the Outcome School article cited), not as established literature.

**What it is:** **Jev** is described as the first "System One Model", announced in September 2026 by TypeSafe AI. Instead of generating text token by token, it reads a **state** (context) and a **question with a predefined set of answer options**, then returns a **typed decision with a calibrated probability** in one parallel forward pass.

**Key claims**
- **Answer types:** choice (from a fixed list, reported up to 255 options), numeric score in a fixed range, or yes/no.
- **Type safety by construction:** it scores only the allowed options, so it cannot emit an invalid category or malformed output (no parse errors); it can still be wrong within valid options.
- **Calibration:** trained with reinforcement learning for calibrated decisions (RLCD), so confidence numbers are meant to match empirical accuracy.
- **Speed and cost:** reported tens to hundreds of times faster than comparable LLMs (roughly 70-500 ms), with very low input pricing.
- **Limits:** no free-form text, code or explanations; text input only; weak for open-ended multi-step reasoning.

**Concept: System 1 vs System 2** (Kahneman): fast, automatic, intuitive decisions versus slow, deliberate reasoning. Standard LLMs (especially reasoning models) act like System 2; a System One model acts like fast pattern recognition.

**Where it fits (hybrid architecture)**
- Routing/triage, classification, content moderation, safety checks, gating (for example checking an LLM's draft before sending), retrieval-relevance decisions, feature-flag-like decisions in agents.
- LLM does generation and reasoning, System One model does cheap, reliable decisions with confidence-based escalation.

**Interview angle:** the general pattern (a constrained-output classifier head with calibrated probabilities instead of free generation) is already common: fine-tuned encoders, logit-scoring of option tokens, structured outputs. Evaluate any such model on calibration (ECE, reliability diagrams) and accuracy on your data.

**Sources:**
- [Jev and System One Models Explained (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/jev-and-system-one-models-explained)
- [On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.04599)
- [Thinking, Fast and Slow (Kahneman), publisher page](https://us.macmillan.com/books/9780374533557/thinkingfastandslow)

<a id="q68"></a>
### 68. What are Autoregressive Models?

**Answer:**

**Definition:** an autoregressive (AR) model predicts each element of a sequence conditioned on all previous elements, factorising the joint distribution with the chain rule:

`P(x_1..x_T) = prod_t P(x_t | x_1..x_{t-1})`

**LLMs (GPT, Llama, Claude, etc.)** are decoder-only Transformers with a **causal mask** (token t can attend only to positions <= t). They are trained with **teacher forcing**: all positions predicted in parallel from the true prefix, with cross-entropy loss on the next token. At inference they generate **one token at a time**: sample from `P(x_t | prefix)`, append, repeat until EOS.

**Properties**
- **Training is parallel** across positions; **generation is sequential** (latency proportional to output length), so KV caching, speculative decoding and batching are used to speed it up.
- Exact likelihoods (tractable), so perplexity is well defined; natural for open-ended generation, few-shot prompting and in-context learning.
- **Exposure bias:** trained on gold prefixes but conditioned on its own outputs at inference; errors can compound.
- Decoding strategies (greedy, beam, temperature, top-k/top-p) control the quality/diversity trade-off.
- Cannot revise earlier tokens (no "look ahead" or global editing), which motivates chain-of-thought, self-reflection, and alternatives like diffusion LMs.

**Other AR uses:** images (PixelCNN, Parti), audio (WaveNet), time series (ARIMA is a classical linear AR family).

**Contrast:** masked LMs (BERT) model bidirectional context but do not generate fluidly; diffusion LMs denoise many positions in parallel.

**Sources:**
- [Autoregressive Models (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/autoregressive-models)
- [Language Models are Few-Shot Learners (GPT-3)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.14165)
- [Attention Is All You Need](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762)
- [Hugging Face: Summary of the models (autoregressive vs autoencoding)](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/model_summary)

<a id="q69"></a>
### 69. Explain the difference between autoregressive and masked language modeling.

**Answer:**

| | Autoregressive (causal) LM | Masked LM (MLM) |
|---|---|---|
| Objective | Predict next token given previous ones | Predict randomly masked tokens given both left and right context |
| Loss | `- sum_t log P(x_t \| x_<t)` on all positions | Cross-entropy only on the masked positions (about 15% of tokens) |
| Attention | Causal mask (left-to-right) | Bidirectional (full) |
| Architecture | Decoder-only (GPT, Llama) | Encoder-only (BERT, RoBERTa) |
| Signal per sequence | Every token is a training target (sample efficient) | Only masked tokens (about 15%) |
| Generation | Natural, token by token | Not natively generative (mask-filling, needs iterative tricks) |
| Understanding tasks | Good at scale via prompting | Excellent for classification, NER, embeddings, reranking |
| Train/inference mismatch | Exposure bias | `[MASK]` token appears in training but not at inference |

**Details**
- **BERT MLM:** choose 15% of tokens; of those, 80% become `[MASK]`, 10% random token, 10% unchanged (to reduce the mismatch). Predictions of masked tokens are treated as independent given the visible context.
- **Autoregressive** models get a fully-factorised exact likelihood, and few-shot in-context learning emerged from scaling them.
- **Variants:** prefix-LM / T5 span corruption (encoder-decoder, mask spans and generate them), XLNet (permutation LM), ELECTRA (replaced-token detection, more sample-efficient), UL2 (mixture of denoisers), and diffusion LMs that apply masked prediction iteratively as a generative model (masked diffusion).

**Practical rule:** need generation, chat, agents, or general-purpose prompting, use autoregressive decoder-only. Need cheap, high-quality text representations, classification, retrieval/reranking, use bidirectional encoders (modern ones: ModernBERT).

**Sources:**
- [BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.04805)
- [Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training (GPT-1)](https://cdn.openai.com/research-covers/language-unsupervised/language_understanding_paper.pdf)
- [Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with T5](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.10683)
- [Autoregressive Models (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/autoregressive-models)
- [Hugging Face: Summary of the models](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/model_summary)

<a id="q70"></a>
### 70. Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)

**Answer:**

**PPO (Schulman et al., 2017)** is a policy-gradient reinforcement-learning algorithm that improves a policy in stable steps by limiting how far each update can move it from the previous policy. It is the RL algorithm behind classic **RLHF** (InstructGPT, ChatGPT).

**Core idea:** vanilla policy gradient is unstable because one large update can wreck the policy. TRPO constrained the KL between old and new policies but is complex. PPO achieves a similar effect with a simple **clipped surrogate objective**:

- Probability ratio: `r_t(theta) = pi_theta(a_t | s_t) / pi_old(a_t | s_t)`
- `L_clip = E[ min( r_t * A_t , clip(r_t, 1-eps, 1+eps) * A_t ) ]`, eps typically 0.1-0.2.
- If the advantage `A_t` is positive, the gain is capped once the ratio exceeds 1+eps; if negative, the penalty is capped below 1-eps. This removes the incentive to make big policy changes.
- **Advantage** `A_t` is estimated by **GAE** (generalised advantage estimation) using a learned **value function (critic)**; the total loss adds a value loss and an entropy bonus.

**In RLHF for LLMs**
1. State = prompt plus tokens so far; action = next token; episode = full response.
2. A **reward model** scores the full response; per-token reward also includes a **KL penalty** `-beta * KL(pi_theta || pi_ref)` to stay near the SFT model and limit reward hacking.
3. Four models are involved: policy (actor), reference, reward model and value model (critic), which makes PPO memory heavy and finicky (hyperparameters, reward normalisation, advantage whitening).
4. Loop: sample responses (rollouts), score, compute advantages, do several minibatch epochs of clipped updates.

**Trade-offs:** stable and general, but costly (critic, four models), sensitive to implementation details; **DPO** removes the RL loop, **GRPO** removes the critic.

**Sources:**
- [Proximal Policy Optimization (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/proximal-policy-optimization-ppo)
- [Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.06347)
- [Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155)
- [High-Dimensional Continuous Control Using GAE](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.02438)
- [OpenAI Spinning Up: PPO](https://spinningup.openai.com/en/latest/algorithms/ppo.html)

<a id="q71"></a>
### 71. Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)

**Answer:**

**DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023)** aligns an LLM to human preferences **without training a separate reward model or running RL**. It optimises the policy directly on preference pairs `(prompt x, chosen y_w, rejected y_l)` with a simple classification-style loss.

**Derivation intuition:** the RLHF objective (maximise reward with a KL penalty to a reference policy `pi_ref`) has a closed-form optimum, so the reward can be expressed through the policy: `r(x, y) = beta * log( pi_theta(y|x) / pi_ref(y|x) ) + const`. Plugging this into the Bradley-Terry preference model gives:

`L_DPO = - E[ log sigmoid( beta * ( log pi_theta(y_w|x)/pi_ref(y_w|x) - log pi_theta(y_l|x)/pi_ref(y_l|x) ) ) ]`

The loss raises the likelihood of the chosen response relative to the rejected one, measured against the reference model; **beta** (about 0.1-0.5) controls how strongly the policy may deviate from the reference (higher beta means closer to reference).

**Pipeline:** SFT model becomes `pi_ref` (frozen copy), collect preference pairs (human, or AI-labelled), train with the loss above (two forward passes per pair, reference log-probs can be precomputed).

**Pros:** simple, stable, cheap (two models, no sampling loop, no critic), easy with LoRA; works well in practice (Zephyr, Llama 3 post-training used DPO variants).

**Cons and pitfalls**
- Offline: limited by the coverage of preference data (off-policy); can drift out-of-distribution.
- Can decrease the likelihood of both chosen and rejected responses, verbosity/length bias, sensitive to data quality and beta.
- Less effective than online RL for reasoning with verifiable rewards.
- **Variants:** IPO, KTO (binary feedback), ORPO/SimPO (reference-free), online/iterative DPO.

**Sources:**
- [Direct Preference Optimization (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/direct-preference-optimization-dpo)
- [Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18290)
- [Zephyr: Direct Distillation of LM Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.16944)
- [Hugging Face TRL DPO Trainer docs](https://huggingface.co/docs/trl/dpo_trainer)
