<a id="q132"></a>
### 132. Compare RAG vs fine-tuning. When would you use each?

**Answer:**

**Mental model.** RAG changes what the model **knows at inference time** (external, updatable knowledge in context). Fine-tuning changes how the model **behaves** (weights: style, format, skills, domain patterns).

| Dimension | RAG | Fine-tuning |
|---|---|---|
| Best for | Factual, changing, private knowledge | Style, tone, format, task skills, domain language, reliability of a narrow task |
| Knowledge updates | Instant (update index) | Requires retraining; stale |
| Hallucination / attribution | Grounded, can cite sources | Cannot cite; may hallucinate facts |
| Data needs | Documents (unlabelled) | Curated input-output examples (hundreds to thousands+) |
| Upfront cost | Pipeline and infra | Data prep, training compute, evals |
| Inference cost | Longer prompts (retrieval + context tokens), extra latency | Shorter prompts; can distil to a small cheap model |
| Access control / deletion | Easy (filters, delete docs) | Hard (knowledge baked into weights) |
| Risks | Retrieval errors, injection through documents | Catastrophic forgetting, overfitting, poor factual injection |
| Iteration speed | Fast | Slower |

**Evidence.** Ovadia et al. found RAG consistently beat unsupervised fine-tuning for injecting new factual knowledge; fine-tuning struggles to teach new facts reliably.

**Use RAG when** answers depend on proprietary or frequently changing information, you need citations, permissions, and quick iteration.

**Use fine-tuning when** you need consistent output format/tone, specialised task behaviour (classification, extraction, tool-call style), lower latency/cost via a smaller model, or domain vocabulary understanding that prompting cannot deliver.

**Combine them (often best).** RAG for facts + fine-tuning for behaviour: e.g. fine-tune the generator to use retrieved context faithfully and ignore distractors (RAFT), or fine-tune the embedder/reranker on domain pairs. 

**Decision path.** Start with prompting; add RAG if the gap is missing knowledge; add fine-tuning if the gap is behaviour/format/cost after prompting and RAG; evaluate each step.

**Sources:**
- [Fine-Tuning or Retrieval? Comparing Knowledge Injection in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.05934)
- [RAFT: Adapting Language Model to Domain Specific RAG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.10131)
- [Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401)
- [AI Engineering Explained: LLM, RAG, MCP, Agent, Fine-Tuning, Quantization (video)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lnfWvX66FUk)

<a id="q133"></a>
### 133. Long context windows keep getting cheaper. When should you use retrieval (RAG) vs putting everything in the context window?

**Answer:**

**Both approaches have improved, so choose per workload.**

**Prefer long context (stuffing) when:**
- The corpus is **small and stable** (a contract, a codebase module, a few reports) and fits comfortably.
- Questions require **global reasoning** across the whole document (summarise, compare, find contradictions) where top-k retrieval would miss pieces.
- **Prompt caching** makes repeated queries against the same corpus cheap (large discounts on cached prefixes, lower latency).
- You want a quick, simple system with no retrieval infra, or high recall matters more than cost.

**Prefer RAG when:**
- Corpus is **large** (millions of tokens to TBs); exceeds any window.
- **Cost and latency at scale**: cost scales with tokens per query; sending 500k tokens per question is expensive and slow (prefill time), even if per-token price falls.
- Data **changes frequently** or per-user permissions apply (filter before the model sees it).
- You need **citations** and precise grounding with small contexts.
- Accuracy: models degrade with very long inputs (lost in the middle, distractors; effective context often smaller than the advertised one), so focused context can beat brute-force stuffing.
- Security/privacy: minimise what is sent to the model.

**Evidence.** Studies (Li et al. 2024, Self-Route) found long-context models often beat RAG on average when resources are unconstrained, but RAG is far cheaper and retrieval-then-fallback routing recovers most of the quality at a fraction of the tokens; LOFT benchmarks show both have strengths.

**Hybrid patterns.**
- Retrieve broadly (large k, or whole documents) then rerank/compress, using long context for room.
- **Route**: try RAG first; if the model says "cannot answer" or confidence is low, fall back to full-context.
- Retrieve at the **document level**, then give entire documents to the model.
- Cache a stable knowledge prefix and retrieve for the rest.

**Decision factors.** corpus size, query volume (cost), latency SLA, freshness, permissions, need for global reasoning, measured accuracy on your data. Benchmark both on your eval set; the answer often changes with model releases.

**Sources:**
- [The Lost in the Middle Problem in LLMs (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/lost-in-the-middle-problem-in-llms)
- [Retrieval Augmented Generation or Long-Context LLMs? A Comprehensive Study and Hybrid Approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.16833)
- [Can Long-Context Language Models Subsume Retrieval, RAG, SQL, and More? (LOFT)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13121)
- [Anthropic: Prompt caching](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/prompt-caching)

<a id="q134"></a>
### 134. What is query transformation in RAG (HyDE, query decomposition, step-back prompting)?

**Answer:**

**Motivation.** User queries are short, ambiguous, conversational or phrased differently from documents, which hurts retrieval (the query-document vocabulary and style gap). Query transformation rewrites or expands the query before retrieval to raise recall.

**Techniques.**
- **Query rewriting / condensation**: turn a follow-up ("what about its price?") into a standalone query using chat history; fix typos, expand acronyms, add context.
- **HyDE (Hypothetical Document Embeddings)**: the LLM writes a **hypothetical answer passage**; embed *that* and search. The fake document may contain factual errors, but it lies in the "answer space" near real relevant documents, and the encoder's bottleneck filters hallucinated details. Helps zero-shot/domain-mismatch cases; risky if the LLM knows nothing about the topic or when the query is very specific.
- **Query decomposition**: split a complex question into sub-questions, retrieve each, combine (multi-hop, comparison questions).
- **Step-back prompting**: generate a more abstract, higher-level question ("What are the principles of X?") and retrieve for both the original and the step-back query, giving background context (Zheng et al.).
- **Multi-query / RAG-Fusion**: generate several paraphrases, retrieve per variant, merge with Reciprocal Rank Fusion.
- **Reverse HyDE / hypothetical questions**: at indexing time, generate questions each chunk answers and embed those (matches user question style).
- **Routing / self-querying**: pick the data source and derive metadata filters from the query.
- **Sparse expansion**: add synonyms/keywords for BM25.

**Trade-offs.**
- Extra LLM calls add latency and cost; use a small fast model and apply selectively (a router decides whether transformation is needed).
- Drift: rewrites can change intent or drop key terms; retrieve with both the original and transformed queries.
- HyDE hallucination risk; decomposition may over-split.

**Evaluate** by comparing recall@k and end-to-end answer quality with/without each transformation on your query set (segmented by query type).

**Sources:**
- [How does HyDE work in RAG? (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/how-does-hyde-work)
- [Precise Zero-Shot Dense Retrieval without Relevance Labels (HyDE)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.10496)
- [Take a Step Back: Evoking Reasoning via Abstraction in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06117)
- [Query Rewriting for Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14283)

<a id="q135"></a>
### 135. How do you implement citation and source attribution in RAG?

**Answer:**

**Why.** Citations let users verify answers, build trust, support audits/compliance, and give you a mechanism to detect hallucinations.

**Implementation pattern.**
1. **Carry provenance through the pipeline**: each chunk keeps `doc_id`, title, URL, page/section, offsets, version, date.
2. **Label context with stable IDs** in the prompt:
```
<source id="1" title="Refund Policy v3" page="4">...text...</source>
<source id="2" ...>...</source>
Answer using only the sources. After each claim add [id]. If the sources do not
contain the answer, say so. Quote exact supporting text in the "evidence" field.
```
3. **Structured output**: ask for JSON such as `{"answer": ..., "claims": [{"text":..., "source_ids":[1], "quote":"..."}]}`. Some APIs offer native citation features (e.g. Anthropic's Citations, which returns exact cited spans; OpenAI file search annotations).
4. **Post-process**: map IDs back to titles/URLs/pages and render links; deep-link to the page or highlight the passage.

**Verification (do not trust the model's citations blindly).**
- **Programmatic checks**: cited IDs exist in the retrieved set; quoted text is an actual substring (fuzzy match) of the source.
- **Entailment check**: an NLI model or LLM judge tests whether the cited passage supports each claim (citation precision/recall as in ALCE).
- Drop or flag unsupported sentences; regenerate or abstain when support is missing.

**Design choices.**
- **Granularity**: document-level (easy), passage-level, sentence/span-level (best trust, more effort).
- **Inline vs footnote** style; limit to sources actually used, not everything retrieved.
- **Post-hoc attribution** (retrieve support for a finished answer) vs **generation-time** (model cites while writing); the latter is usually better integrated, the former can fix gaps.
- Avoid over-chunking: tiny chunks break citation context.

**Pitfalls.** Fabricated or mismatched citations, citing a source that merely relates, stale or superseded versions, permission leaks through titles/URLs, injection text in sources that gets cited as authoritative.

**Metrics.** Citation precision (cited source supports claim), citation recall (each claim has support), coverage, user click-through/feedback.

**Sources:**
- [Enabling Large Language Models to Generate Text with Citations (ALCE)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14627)
- [Anthropic: Citations](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/citations)
- [Attributed Question Answering: Evaluation and Modeling for Attributed LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.08037)

<a id="q136"></a>
### 136. How do you scale a RAG system to millions of documents?

**Answer:**

**Where scale bites.** Index size and memory, ANN latency and recall, ingestion throughput and cost, retrieval noise (more documents mean more near-duplicates and distractors), operational complexity.

**1. Index and ANN.**
- Use ANN, not brute force: **HNSW** (high recall, memory-heavy), **IVF-PQ / IVF-HNSW** (compressed, billions scale), **DiskANN**-style disk-based indexes.
- **Compress**: product quantisation, scalar int8, binary quantisation, Matryoshka-truncated dimensions; rescore top candidates with full-precision vectors.
- **Shard and replicate**: partition by tenant/collection/time/hash for capacity and QPS; replicas for throughput and availability; use managed/distributed vector DBs (Milvus, Qdrant, Pinecone, Weaviate, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, pgvector for moderate size).
- Tune recall/latency knobs (`ef_search`, `nprobe`) against a recall benchmark.

**2. Reduce the search space.**
- **Metadata pre-filtering/namespaces**, routing queries to relevant shards/collections.
- **Hierarchical retrieval**: retrieve documents (summary embeddings) first, then chunks within them.
- Deduplicate and remove low-value content at ingestion.

**3. Retrieval quality at scale.**
- **Hybrid search** (BM25 + dense) and a **reranker** on the top 50-100: the standard way to keep precision when the candidate pool is huge.
- Query transformation, and evaluation with a large, representative query set; monitor recall vs the brute-force ground truth.

**4. Ingestion pipeline.**
- Distributed, queue-based, idempotent pipeline (Kafka/SQS + workers/Spark/Ray); batch embedding on GPUs; retries and dead-letter queues; incremental updates via content hashes.
- Control embedding cost (choose a smaller/cheaper model, batch, cache).

**5. Serving.**
- Caching (query embeddings, results, semantic cache), async, autoscaling; separate read/write paths; keep the hot index in RAM.
- Multi-stage pipeline with latency budgets and graceful degradation.

**6. Cost and ops.** Estimate memory = N_vectors x dim x bytes (+ graph overhead); track cost per query; backup, versioned re-indexing, observability, per-tenant quotas, ACL enforcement.

**Verify.** Load test QPS and p95/p99, measure recall@k versus exact search, and track answer quality as the corpus grows.

**Sources:**
- [How does Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search work? (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/how-does-approximate-nearest-neighbor-ann-search-work)
- [Efficient and robust approximate nearest neighbor search using Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.09320)
- [The Faiss library](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.08281)
- [Pinecone Learn: Vector database and indexing](https://www.pinecone.io/learn/)

<a id="q137"></a>
### 137. What is parent-child chunking, and how does it improve retrieval?

**Answer:**

**Definition.** Parent-child (small-to-big) chunking indexes **small "child" chunks** for retrieval, but returns their larger **"parent" chunk** (a section, page or big window) to the LLM. Each child stores a reference (`parent_id`) to its parent.

**Why it helps: resolves the precision-vs-context dilemma.**
- **Small chunks** yield sharp embeddings that match specific questions precisely (less dilution of meaning).
- **Large chunks** give the LLM enough surrounding context to answer correctly and coherently (definitions, exceptions, preceding conditions, pronoun antecedents).
- Retrieval matches on precise children; generation sees rich parents.

**Implementation.**
1. Split documents into parents (e.g. 1000-2000 tokens or by section).
2. Split each parent into children (e.g. 128-300 tokens).
3. Embed and index **children**; store parents in a docstore (key-value).
4. Query: retrieve top-k children, map to unique `parent_id`s, **deduplicate**, fetch the parents, (optionally rerank parents), pass to the LLM.

```python
# LangChain-style
retriever = ParentDocumentRetriever(vectorstore=vs, docstore=store,
    child_splitter=RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(chunk_size=300),
    parent_splitter=RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(chunk_size=1500))
```

**Variants.**
- **Sentence-window retrieval**: embed single sentences, return +/- n surrounding sentences.
- **Auto-merging retrieval** (LlamaIndex): hierarchy of chunk levels; if enough sibling children of a parent are retrieved, merge up to the parent.
- **Multi-vector**: index summaries or hypothetical questions per parent, return the full parent.
- **Contextual retrieval**: prepend document context to children.

**Trade-offs.**
- Larger prompts (higher token cost, lost-in-the-middle risk); mitigate with rerank/compress and a parent size limit.
- Extra storage/complexity (docstore, mapping); need dedup when multiple children share a parent.
- Not helpful when documents lack coherent structure, or when questions need only a tiny fact.

**Tune** child size, parent size, k, and the merge threshold with a retrieval eval.

**Sources:**
- [Chunking Strategies for RAG (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/chunking-strategies-for-rag)
- [LangChain: Parent Document Retriever](https://python.langchain.com/docs/how_to/parent_document_retriever/)
- [LlamaIndex: Auto-merging retriever](https://docs.llamaindex.ai/en/stable/examples/retrievers/auto_merging_retriever/)

<a id="q138"></a>
### 138. Your RAG system is hallucinating despite having the right context. How do you fix it?

**Answer:**

**First confirm the premise.** Check whether the right passage was really in the final prompt (not truncated, not buried mid-context, not overridden by a contradictory chunk). Then classify the hallucination: (a) ignores context and uses parametric memory, (b) over-generalises or extrapolates beyond the text, (c) mixes facts from different chunks, (d) misreads numbers/negation, (e) answers when it should abstain.

**Fixes (prioritised).**
1. **Prompt for grounding**: "Answer using only the provided sources; if they don't contain the answer, say 'I don't know'." Provide an explicit abstain option and format; place instructions before and after the context.
2. **Force evidence-first output**: quote the supporting sentences (with source IDs) before writing the answer (extract-then-answer); require a citation per claim.
3. **Clean the context**: rerank and keep fewer, more relevant chunks; dedupe; remove contradictions; reorder to mitigate lost-in-the-middle; compress noisy chunks; use parent context where snippets lack qualifiers.
4. **Lower temperature** (0-0.2), constrain output length and format.
5. **Model choice / tuning**: a stronger instruction-following model; models tuned for faithfulness or "context-faithful prompting"; fine-tune with grounded and unanswerable examples (RAFT / distractor training).
6. **Verification layer**: run a claim-level faithfulness check (NLI or LLM judge, HHEM-style) against the context; if unsupported, regenerate with stricter instructions, drop the claim, or abstain. Optionally self-consistency across samples.
7. **Handle knowledge conflicts**: when the context disagrees with the model's memory, instruct "the documents override your prior knowledge"; models often stick to memory otherwise.
8. **Retrieval sufficiency gate**: if top scores are low or a judge says context insufficient, refuse or ask for clarification rather than generating.
9. **Task decomposition** for complex synthesis (per-document summaries then merge).

**Measure** with faithfulness/groundedness metrics on a labelled set including unanswerable questions; track abstain precision (does it decline when it should?) and answer rate. Sample production traces regularly.

**Sources:**
- [RAGAS: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.15217)
- [Context-faithful Prompting for Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.11315)
- [RAFT: Adapting Language Model to Domain Specific RAG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.10131)
- [Anthropic: Reduce hallucinations](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-hallucinations)

---

<a id="q139"></a>
### 139. Your RAG chunk overlap causes redundant results. How do you reduce redundancy?

**Answer:**

**Why it happens.** Overlap (say 20%) duplicates text at chunk borders, so adjacent chunks are near-identical and both rank high for a query; top-k fills with near-duplicates, wasting context tokens and crowding out diverse evidence.

**Fixes (prioritised).**
1. **Reduce or remove overlap**: often 0-10% is enough when chunks follow natural boundaries (paragraphs/sections). Prefer **structure-aware splitting** so ideas are not cut, making overlap unnecessary.
2. **Merge adjacent hits**: if chunks `i` and `i+1` of the same document are both retrieved, stitch them (removing the overlapping span using stored offsets) into one passage before prompting.
3. **Diversify at retrieval time**: **MMR (maximal marginal relevance)** trades relevance against similarity to already-selected chunks: `argmax [ lambda * sim(q,d) - (1-lambda) * max sim(d, selected) ]`. Also cap chunks per document/section.
4. **Dedupe post-retrieval**: drop candidates with cosine similarity above a threshold (e.g. > 0.95) to a higher-ranked candidate, or with high n-gram/Jaccard overlap, or same `parent_id`.
5. **Parent-child / sentence-window retrieval**: retrieve small non-overlapping children and expand to a parent; deduplicate by `parent_id`.
6. **Overfetch then rerank**: retrieve top 50, dedupe, rerank, keep 5.
7. **Store offsets** (`start_char`, `end_char`, `chunk_index`) in metadata to make merging and overlap removal deterministic.
8. **Context compression** to strip repeated sentences.

**Trade-offs.** Less overlap can lose answers that straddle boundaries, so compensate with adjacent-chunk expansion at query time (fetch `i-1`, `i+1` only for top hits) rather than by duplicating text at index time.

**Verify.** Measure the redundancy rate (average pairwise similarity or duplicate fraction in top-k), distinct-documents-in-top-k, and recall@k/answer quality before and after; ensure no drop in answers that span boundaries.

**Sources:**
- [Chunking Strategies for RAG (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/chunking-strategies-for-rag)
- [LangChain: Text splitters](https://python.langchain.com/docs/concepts/text_splitters/)
- [Qdrant: Maximal marginal relevance and search diversity](https://qdrant.tech/documentation/concepts/search/)
- [Pinecone Learn: Chunking strategies](https://www.pinecone.io/learn/chunking-strategies/)

---

<a id="q140"></a>
### 140. Your RAG retrieval is too slow with a large knowledge base. How do you speed it up?

**Answer:**

**Diagnose.** Measure where time goes: embedding the query (often 10-100 ms, more with remote APIs), ANN search, filtering, network hops, reranking, and payload fetching. Confirm you are not doing exact (brute-force) search or scanning with a heavy metadata filter.

**Fixes (prioritised).**
1. **Use an ANN index** (HNSW, IVF, IVF-PQ, DiskANN) instead of flat search; tune `ef_search`/`nprobe` to the minimum meeting your recall target (measure recall vs exact search).
2. **Shrink the vectors**: quantisation (scalar/product/binary) with rescoring, lower dimensions (Matryoshka), so more fits in RAM and distance computations are faster.
3. **Keep the index in memory / on fast NVMe**; right-size RAM to avoid paging; use HNSW memory tuning (`M`, `ef_construction` at build time).
4. **Shard and replicate**: partition by tenant/time/category; route each query to a subset; replicas for throughput.
5. **Pre-filter efficiently**: index metadata fields, use filtered ANN or partitions/namespaces instead of post-filtering huge result sets.
6. **Reduce candidate counts**: smaller top-k, lightweight first stage, then a rerank only on the top 20-50; smaller/quantised reranker.
7. **Cache**: query embedding cache, result cache for frequent queries, semantic cache for near-duplicates.
8. **Embedding step**: use a small local model or co-locate with the app; batch requests; avoid cross-region API calls.
9. **Parallelise** dense + sparse retrieval and independent sub-queries; use async I/O and connection pooling.
10. **Hierarchical retrieval**: coarse routing (cluster/document summaries) then fine search.
11. **Reduce index size**: dedupe, drop low-value chunks, and use better chunking, so fewer vectors are searched.
12. **Choose a purpose-built vector engine** (or tune pgvector indexes, `maintenance_work_mem`) if the current store is the bottleneck.

**Trade-offs.** Faster ANN settings and compression reduce recall; validate with recall@k and end-to-end answer quality, and set latency SLOs (p95) with load tests.

**Sources:**
- [How does Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search work? (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/how-does-approximate-nearest-neighbor-ann-search-work)
- [Efficient and robust approximate nearest neighbor search using HNSW graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.09320)
- [The Faiss library](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.08281)
- [Qdrant documentation: Optimization and quantization](https://qdrant.tech/documentation/guides/quantization/)

<a id="q141"></a>
### 141. Your RAG system returns duplicate results. How do you deduplicate?

**Answer:**

**Sources of duplication.**
- The **same document ingested multiple times** (re-crawls, copies across drives, versions).
- **Near-duplicates**: boilerplate, templates, reposted content, multiple versions of a policy, quoted email threads.
- **Chunk-level**: overlapping chunks, repeated headers/footers, same paragraph in many docs.
- Multiple retrievers (dense + sparse, multi-query) returning the same chunk.

**Where to dedupe.**

**1. At ingestion (best, prevents pollution).**
- Exact: hash normalised text (SHA-256) at document and chunk level; skip or link existing.
- Near-duplicate: **MinHash/LSH** or SimHash on shingles; embedding-based clustering (SemDeDup: remove points within a cosine threshold of a cluster representative).
- Strip boilerplate (headers, footers, nav, signatures, disclaimers) before chunking.
- Versioning policy: keep the latest version (flag older `is_latest=false`), or store version metadata.
- Canonical IDs from source URL/path so re-ingestion upserts rather than appends.

**2. At retrieval time.**
- Merge results from multiple retrievers by `chunk_id` (RRF handles this naturally).
- Drop candidates with similarity above a threshold (e.g. 0.95) to an already selected one; group by `doc_id`/`parent_id` and cap per group; **MMR** for diversity.
- Collapse near-identical text with n-gram/Jaccard checks.

**3. At context assembly.** Remove repeated sentences, compress, and cite one representative source (listing duplicates as "also found in").

**Considerations.**
- **Threshold tuning**: too aggressive removes legitimate near-similar content (e.g. differing clauses in two contracts), too lenient leaves duplicates. Tune on labelled pairs; prefer keeping the source with the best authority/recency.
- Keep provenance so citations still list all locations if needed.
- Make dedup idempotent and monitored (duplicate rate, index growth).

**Verify** with duplicate-rate metrics in the top-k, distinct-source counts, and regression tests on known duplicate clusters.

**Sources:**
- [SemDeDup: Data-efficient learning at web-scale through semantic deduplication](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.09540)
- [Deduplicating Training Data Makes Language Models Better](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.06499)
- [Datasketch: MinHash LSH documentation](https://ekzhu.com/datasketch/lsh.html)
- [Chunking Strategies for RAG (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/chunking-strategies-for-rag)

<a id="q142"></a>
### 142. Your RAG system needs per-user access control on internal documents. How do you implement it?

**Answer:**

**Principle.** Authorisation must be enforced **at retrieval time, before content reaches the LLM**. Never rely on the prompt ("do not reveal restricted info"), because anything in context can leak. Also enforce the same permissions the source system uses.

**Implementation.**
1. **Capture ACLs at ingestion**: for each document/chunk, store the permission model from the source (users, groups, roles, org units, labels/sensitivity, tenant) in metadata (`allowed_groups`, `allowed_users`, `classification`, `tenant_id`). Inherit folder-level permissions; keep chunks tied to their document's ACL.
2. **Authenticate and resolve identity** at query time (SSO/OIDC token); compute the user's groups/roles (from IdP/directory).
3. **Filter in the retrieval query**: apply a metadata filter (`acl_groups IN user_groups OR user_id IN allowed_users`) as a **pre-filter** in the vector, sparse and graph search, so unauthorised chunks are never candidates. Post-filtering alone can return empty or leak via ranking side effects.
4. **Isolation strategies**:
   - Shared index + ACL metadata filter (flexible, needs efficient filtered search).
   - **Namespaces/partitions/collections per tenant** for strong isolation in multi-tenant SaaS.
   - Separate indexes or clusters for highly sensitive data.
   - Alternative: query the source system's permission API (ReBAC like OpenFGA/Zanzibar, SharePoint) to check candidates at query time (fresher, but latency).
5. **Keep permissions fresh**: sync ACL changes quickly (revocation must propagate; webhooks/CDC plus periodic full reconciliation); fail closed on errors.
6. **Cover all paths**: caches (semantic cache keyed per permission set or user), agent tools, summaries and knowledge graphs derived from restricted docs, logs and citations (titles/URLs can leak).
7. **Defence in depth**: audit logging of retrieved doc IDs per user, output PII/DLP scanning, least-privilege service accounts, prompt-injection defences.
8. **Test**: automated tests with multiple personas verifying restricted content never appears in retrieval, prompts or answers; red-team.

**Pitfalls.** Stale ACLs, group explosion (large membership lists in filters: use group IDs/ReBAC), leaking through aggregate or global summaries, shared semantic cache across users, embedding inversion (treat vectors as sensitive data too).

**Sources:**
- [Pinecone documentation: Namespaces and multitenancy](https://docs.pinecone.io/guides/index-data/implement-multitenancy)
- [Qdrant documentation: Multitenancy](https://qdrant.tech/documentation/guides/multiple-partitions/)
- [OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (Sensitive Information Disclosure)](https://owasp.org/www-project-top-10-for-large-language-model-applications/)
- [How does a Vector Database work? (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/how-does-a-vector-database-work)

<a id="q143"></a>
### 143. Your RAG system fails on domain-specific jargon. How do you fix it?

**Answer:**

**Why it fails.** General embedding models and LLMs saw little of the jargon: abbreviations, product codes, internal names, and specialist terms are split into subwords with weak semantics, so dense retrieval misses them; users also use synonyms that documents do not, or vice versa (vocabulary mismatch).

**Fixes (prioritised).**
1. **Hybrid search**: add BM25/sparse retrieval so exact terms, codes and acronyms match lexically; tune fusion weights (RRF). Often the quickest and highest-impact fix.
2. **Query expansion / normalisation**: a domain **glossary/synonym map** (acronym expansion, aliases), LLM-based query rewriting with glossary in the prompt, HyDE with domain hints. Also expand at index time (append expansions or synonyms to chunks, or index generated hypothetical questions).
3. **Domain-adapted embeddings**: choose a domain-specialised model (biomedical, legal, code) or **fine-tune the embedder** on in-domain query-passage pairs, using synthetic queries from your chunks (generated by an LLM) and hard negatives (GPL-style adaptation, contrastive fine-tuning). Even a few thousand pairs help.
4. **Fine-tune or upgrade the reranker** on domain data (cross-encoders adapt well).
5. **Learned sparse models** (SPLADE, BGE-M3 sparse) that expand terms semantically while keeping lexical precision.
6. **Give the LLM the vocabulary**: include glossary definitions for terms detected in the query/context in the prompt; provide few-shot examples; consider fine-tuning or continued pretraining the generator if jargon understanding is the bottleneck.
7. **Improve chunk context**: include definitions/headings; keep acronym definitions near usage; add contextual retrieval headers.
8. **Tokenisation-aware handling**: preserve identifiers (do not split codes; separate field for IDs with exact match/keyword filters).
9. **Evaluation**: build a jargon-specific query set (acronyms, codes, misspellings) and track recall@k separately; collect failed queries from logs and feed them back into the glossary and training pairs.

**Trade-offs.** Fine-tuning needs data and re-indexing; glossaries need maintenance; synonym expansion can add noise, so validate on the eval set.

**Sources:**
- [How does Hybrid Search work? (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/how-does-hybrid-search-work)
- [GPL: Generative Pseudo Labeling for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation of Dense Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.07577)
- [BEIR: A Heterogeneous Benchmark for Zero-shot Evaluation of IR Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.08663)
- [Sentence Transformers: Training and fine-tuning embedding models](https://www.sbert.net/docs/sentence_transformer/training_overview.html)

<a id="q144"></a>
### 144. Your text-only RAG system now needs to handle images and tables. How do you extend it?

**Answer:**

**Options overview.**

**A. Convert to text (simplest, often good).**
- **Images/figures/charts**: generate captions or detailed descriptions with a vision-language model (VLM); OCR embedded text; for charts, extract underlying data tables. Index the description as text (keep a pointer to the original image); return the image + description to a multimodal LLM at answer time.
- **Tables**: parse to Markdown/HTML/CSV with headers (layout-aware parser); keep each table as one unit with caption and an LLM-generated **summary** for embedding, while passing the full table to the generator; for numeric analysis, load into SQL/dataframes and use a tool.

**B. Multimodal embeddings.**
- Use a joint embedding model (CLIP/SigLIP-style, or multimodal text-image embedders from Cohere/Voyage/Jina) to embed images and text in one space, so a text query can retrieve images directly.
- Answer with a multimodal LLM that receives the retrieved images.

**C. Page-image retrieval (skip parsing).** ColPali-style models embed **whole page screenshots** with multi-vector late interaction, retrieving pages by visual and textual content, layouts, tables and figures included; feed the page images to a VLM. Avoids brittle OCR/layout pipelines, at higher index storage and VLM cost.

**D. Hybrid / multi-vector retriever.** Store summaries for retrieval and raw content (image/table) in a docstore; retrieve via the summary and return the raw item (multi-vector retriever pattern).

**Pipeline changes.**
- Ingestion: layout analysis, element typing (text/table/figure), extraction, association with captions and nearby text; metadata (page, section).
- Retrieval: per-modality indexes or a unified one; routing by query intent; rerank across modalities.
- Generation: a multimodal model or textualised evidence; prompt with element IDs; cite page/figure.
- Evaluation: multimodal test sets (chart/table questions, e.g. ViDoRe), separate metrics per modality.

**Trade-offs.** Captioning loses details (mitigate with high-quality VLM prompts and keeping the original); multimodal embeddings are weaker for fine text; page-level approaches cost storage and compute; more moving parts and higher cost/latency; security (hidden text in images, injection).

**Sources:**
- [ColPali: Efficient Document Retrieval with Vision Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.01449)
- [Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision (CLIP)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00020)
- [LangChain: Multi-vector retriever](https://python.langchain.com/docs/how_to/multi_vector/)
- [Docling Technical Report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.09869)

<a id="q145"></a>
### 145. Your RAG knowledge base gets updated frequently and needs versioning. How do you manage it?

**Answer:**

**Requirements to clarify.** Do users need only the latest version, or also historical answers ("what did the policy say in March?"), audit/reproducibility, rollback, and low-latency updates?

**Design.**
1. **Version metadata on every chunk**: `doc_id`, `version`, `valid_from`, `valid_to`, `is_latest`, `content_hash`, `source_commit/etag`, `ingest_run_id`. Deterministic chunk IDs (`doc_id#version#chunk_no`).
2. **Immutable, append-oriented writes**: a new version inserts new chunks and flips old ones to `is_latest=false` (or sets `valid_to`) in one atomic step (transactional or via an alias/version filter) so queries never see a half-updated document.
3. **Query-time version semantics**:
   - Default filter `is_latest = true`.
   - Time-travel: filter `valid_from <= t < valid_to` for "as of" questions; allow explicit version selection.
   - Surface version/date in citations.
4. **Index-level versioning (bulk changes)**: build a new index/collection (`kb_v42`) offline, evaluate it against the regression set, then **switch an alias** (blue/green); keep the previous index for instant **rollback**. Essential when changing chunking or the embedding model.
5. **Incremental pipeline**: change detection by hash, re-embed only changed chunks, propagate deletes, keep derived artefacts (summaries, graph, caches) in sync and version-tagged.
6. **Retention and cost**: prune old versions per policy (keep N versions or X days); archive to cheap storage; legal requirements may force deletions to propagate to all versions.
7. **Governance and observability**: change log (who/what/when), audit of which version answered each query (store `version` in traces), freshness/lag metrics, canary queries after each publish, automated eval gate before promotion.
8. **Handling contradictions**: avoid retrieving old and new simultaneously unless requested (filter or version-aware rerank).

**Pitfalls.** Mixed versions in one answer, stale caches, orphaned chunks, embedding model change without re-index, ACL changes lagging content changes.

**Sources:**
- [Pinecone documentation: Manage indexes and namespaces](https://docs.pinecone.io/guides/manage-data/manage-namespaces)
- [Qdrant documentation: Collection aliases](https://qdrant.tech/documentation/concepts/collections/)
- [LlamaIndex: Ingestion pipeline with document management](https://docs.llamaindex.ai/en/stable/module_guides/loading/ingestion_pipeline/)
- [FreshLLMs: Refreshing LLMs with Search Engine Augmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.03214)

<a id="q146"></a>
### 146. Your RAG system fails on multi-hop questions that require combining multiple facts. How do you fix it?

**Answer:**

**Diagnose.** For failing questions, check per-hop retrieval: was fact A retrieved? Fact B? Typically the second hop is missing because it is not lexically or semantically close to the original question, or top-k is filled with distractors around hop 1. If both facts were retrieved but the answer is still wrong, the problem is reasoning/synthesis.

**Fixes (prioritised).**
1. **Iterative retrieval (agentic RAG)**: loop of retrieve, reason, generate the next query, retrieve again (IRCoT, ReAct, Self-Ask) with a sufficiency check and step limit. The most direct fix for genuine multi-hop dependencies.
2. **Query decomposition**: LLM splits into sub-questions (parallel where independent, sequential where dependent), retrieves per sub-question, merges evidence.
3. **Improve first-stage retrieval breadth**: hybrid search, higher k plus a reranker, multi-query expansion with RRF, MMR for diversity to cover different documents.
4. **Graph-based retrieval**: build entity/relationship links (GraphRAG, HippoRAG, entity-linked chunk graphs) and traverse to neighbours so that connected facts arrive together; add document links (citations, hyperlinks, hierarchy).
5. **Better context construction**: include parent sections, add neighbouring chunks, order by dependency, deduplicate, and keep only relevant evidence to reduce distraction; ask the model to list the intermediate facts (evidence chain) before answering.
6. **Stronger reasoning at generation**: CoT, reasoning models, or a dedicated "synthesise from evidence" step; verifying that each hop is supported.
7. **Indexing-time enrichment**: propositions, generated questions per chunk, summaries or "bridge" entity annotations, so that relevant chunks are more retrievable.
8. **Fine-tune** retriever/generator on multi-hop data (HotpotQA/MuSiQue-style) if domain-specific.

**Trade-offs.** More latency/cost, error propagation from wrong early hops, risk of loops; mitigate with routing (only use the multi-hop path when a classifier or complexity check says so), caching, and budgets.

**Verify.** Multi-hop eval set with annotated supporting facts: measure supporting-fact recall (per hop), answer EM/F1 and cost; compare single-shot vs iterative.

**Sources:**
- [Agentic RAG (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/agentic-rag)
- [GraphRAG (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/graphrag)
- [Interleaving Retrieval with Chain-of-Thought Reasoning (IRCoT)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.10509)
- [Measuring and Narrowing the Compositionality Gap in Language Models (Self-Ask)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03350)

---

<a id="q147"></a>
### 147. Your enterprise RAG system returns contradictory answers from different source documents. How do you resolve conflicts?

**Answer:**

**Why conflicts arise.** Multiple versions of a policy, drafts vs final, different departments or regions with different rules, outdated documents, errors, or opinion vs fact. LLMs given conflicting passages tend to pick arbitrarily, blend them, or favour whichever appears first/last, and they may prefer their own memory (Adaptive Chameleon or Stubborn Sloth; ClashEval).

**Strategy: resolve upstream where possible, then surface remaining conflicts honestly.**

1. **Source hygiene and governance (root cause)**
   - Deduplicate and retire superseded documents; keep a single source of truth; mark status (`draft/approved/deprecated`), owner, effective dates.
   - Version metadata and `is_latest` filters (see versioning).
2. **Metadata-based disambiguation at retrieval**: filter/boost by authority, status, recency, jurisdiction/business unit matching the user's context (region, role, product). Personalise: the "right" answer often depends on who is asking.
3. **Ranking policy**: rerank with authority and recency signals (official policy > wiki > chat); explicit precedence rules in code, not in the LLM's judgment alone.
4. **Conflict detection**: NLI/LLM check across retrieved chunks for contradictions on the same claim (pairwise entailment/contradiction), or ask the model in a pre-step "do these sources disagree?"
5. **Generation policy in the prompt**:
   - "If sources conflict, prefer the most recent approved source; state the conflict, cite each source with its date/status, and do not merge them."
   - Present both views when authority is unclear; recommend contacting the owner; provide confidence.
6. **Abstain/escalate** when conflicts cannot be resolved by rules (route to human, ticket, or "needs review").
7. **Feedback loop**: log detected conflicts and send them to content owners to fix the source; track a conflict rate metric.
8. **Evaluate** with a test set of seeded contradictions (old vs new policy, regional variants) and measure whether the system picks the right source or flags the conflict.

**Pitfalls.** Silently blending contradictory facts; over-trusting recency (a newer draft is not necessarily approved); leaking restricted documents through conflict explanations (apply ACLs first).

**Sources:**
- [ClashEval: Quantifying the tug-of-war between an LLM's internal prior and external evidence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.10198)
- [Adaptive Chameleon or Stubborn Sloth: Revealing the Behavior of LLMs in Knowledge Conflicts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13300)
- [Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.10997)

---

<a id="q148"></a>
### 148. Your RAG system returns outdated answers from an evolving knowledge base. How do you keep it current?

**Answer:**

**Find the cause first (staleness can enter at many layers).**
- Ingestion lag or failed sync jobs; changes never detected.
- Old versions still in the index (updates appended, not replaced).
- Deleted documents not removed.
- **Caches** (semantic/response cache, CDN) serving old answers.
- Stale derived artefacts (summaries, embeddings of old text, graph nodes).
- Ranking ignores recency, so older, more-linked docs outrank new ones.
- The LLM answering from parametric memory instead of context.

**Fixes (prioritised).**
1. **Reliable change propagation**: webhooks/CDC plus scheduled reconciliation via content hashes/last-modified; incremental upserts and hard deletes; alerts on failed ingestion.
2. **Replace, don't append**: stable document IDs, versioned chunks with `is_latest` (or `valid_to`); atomic swap; remove tombstoned content from vector, sparse and graph indexes.
3. **Freshness-aware retrieval**: store `updated_at`; apply recency filters/boosts for time-sensitive topics (query-type routing: "current price" vs "history"); prefer latest version; display document dates in answers.
4. **Cache invalidation**: key caches by document version or short TTL; invalidate on update; never cache time-sensitive queries long.
5. **Live tools for volatile facts**: call APIs/databases/web search at query time (prices, status, inventory) instead of indexing them; combine with static RAG.
6. **Prompt policy**: "Use only the provided context; note the date of sources; if information may be outdated or missing, say so"; include the current date in the prompt; ensure context overrides model memory.
7. **Monitoring**: end-to-end freshness SLA (time from source change to retrievable), stale-document ratio, canary documents that are updated periodically with tests, drift dashboards; user feedback ("outdated") routing.
8. **Periodic re-embedding/re-crawl** for sources without reliable change signals; full reindex via blue/green when parsing or embedding models change.

**Verify.** Automated test: modify a fact in a source, wait for the SLA, confirm the system answers with the new fact and cites the new version; delete and confirm disappearance; run daily canaries.

**Sources:**
- [FreshLLMs: Refreshing Large Language Models with Search Engine Augmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.03214)
- [Pinecone documentation: Upsert and manage records](https://docs.pinecone.io/guides/index-data/upsert-data)
- [LlamaIndex: Ingestion pipeline and document management](https://docs.llamaindex.ai/en/stable/module_guides/loading/ingestion_pipeline/)
- [Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.10997)

---

<a id="q149"></a>
### 149. Your RAG system struggles with PDF documents containing tables and layouts. How do you fix PDF parsing?

**Answer:**

**Why PDFs are hard.** A PDF is a print format (positioned glyphs), not a semantic structure. Naive text extraction (`pdftotext`, PyPDF) breaks reading order in multi-column layouts, merges table cells into a stream of numbers, mixes headers/footers/footnotes into the text, loses headings, mishandles scanned pages (no text layer), formulas and figures, and often splits tables across pages.

**Fixes (prioritised).**
1. **Use a layout-aware parser**: Docling, Unstructured (hi-res), LlamaParse, Azure Document Intelligence, AWS Textract, Google Document AI, Marker, MinerU, Nougat (academic PDFs), GROBID (scholarly). They detect regions (title, paragraph, list, table, figure, header/footer), reading order, and output structured Markdown/JSON/HTML.
2. **Table handling**: detect tables (Table Transformer, layout models), reconstruct structure (rows, columns, merged cells), and output Markdown/HTML/CSV with headers and caption. Repeat header rows for tables spanning pages. Keep a table as one chunk (or split by row groups with the header repeated), plus an LLM-generated summary for embedding; for analytics, load to a dataframe/SQL.
3. **OCR for scans**: Tesseract, PaddleOCR, cloud OCR, or VLM-based OCR; check quality (confidence, dictionary) and deskew/denoise.
4. **VLM-based parsing**: render pages to images and use a vision-language model to transcribe to Markdown (strong on complex layouts, at higher cost/latency), or skip parsing with page-image retrieval (ColPali) and feed page images to a VLM.
5. **Clean and structure**: remove headers/footers/page numbers, fix hyphenation, dehyphenate, normalise Unicode/ligatures; retain hierarchy (heading path) as metadata; then **structure-aware chunking** by sections, not fixed windows; attach page numbers for citations.
6. **Figures**: caption via VLM, extract chart data, store references.
7. **Routing**: use a cheap parser for simple born-digital PDFs and the heavy pipeline for complex or scanned ones.
8. **Quality assurance**: build a small gold set of tricky PDFs; measure table extraction accuracy (e.g. TEDS), text fidelity, reading order; sample-review ingested chunks; add regression tests when the parser or version changes; track downstream retrieval and answer quality per document type.

**Trade-offs.** Accuracy vs cost/latency (VLM/cloud parsing per page pricing), privacy of sending documents to cloud APIs, and maintenance of the pipeline.

**Sources:**
- [Docling Technical Report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.09869)
- [PubTables-1M: Towards comprehensive table extraction from unstructured documents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.00061)
- [Nougat: Neural Optical Understanding for Academic Documents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.13418)
- [Unstructured documentation](https://docs.unstructured.io/)

## AI Agents and Agentic Systems

<a id="q150"></a>
### 150. What is an AI agent, and how does it differ from a simple LLM call?

**Answer:**

An **AI agent** is a system in which an LLM acts as the decision-making core of a loop: it observes a goal and the current state, decides on an action (usually a tool call), executes it, observes the result, and repeats until the goal is met or a stop condition fires. A **simple LLM call** is a single stateless transformation: prompt in, text out.

**Key differences**

| Aspect | Simple LLM call | Agent |
|---|---|---|
| Control flow | One pass, fixed by the developer | Dynamic, chosen by the model at run time |
| Tools / side effects | None (text only) | Search, code, APIs, files, browsers |
| State | Stateless | Working memory, scratchpad, long-term memory |
| Steps | 1 | N (unbounded without limits) |
| Error handling | Caller retries | Agent observes errors and adapts |
| Cost/latency | Predictable | Variable, often 10-100x higher |

**Anatomy of an agent**
- **Model** (reasoning/planning), **tools** (actions and observations), **memory/state** (context, scratchpad, stores), **loop/orchestrator** (control), **guardrails** (limits, permissions).

```python
messages = [system, user_goal]
for step in range(MAX_STEPS):
    resp = llm(messages, tools=TOOLS)
    if not resp.tool_calls:
        return resp.text            # final answer
    for call in resp.tool_calls:
        result = run_tool(call)     # side effect
        messages += [call, result]  # observation goes back into context
```

**Workflows vs agents** (Anthropic's distinction): workflows orchestrate LLMs through predefined code paths (prompt chaining, routing, parallelisation); agents let the LLM direct its own process. Start with the simplest thing (single call with retrieval), move to workflows, and only use agents when the number of steps cannot be predicted.

**Trade-offs and pitfalls**: higher cost and latency, compounding errors over many steps, harder testing, and larger security surface (tools with side effects). Use an agent for open-ended tasks (coding, research, support triage); avoid it when a deterministic pipeline solves the problem.

**Sources:**
- [AI Agent Explained (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/ai-agent)
- [AI Engineering Explained: LLM, RAG, MCP, Agent, Fine-Tuning, Quantization (video)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lnfWvX66FUk)
- [Building effective agents (Anthropic)](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents)
- [ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629)

---

<a id="q151"></a>
### 151. AI Agent Memory

**Answer:**

LLMs are stateless: everything they "remember" must be in the context window at inference time. **Agent memory** is the set of mechanisms that store, select and re-inject information so an agent can stay coherent within a task and improve across tasks.

**Layers**
- **Short-term / working memory**: the current context window (messages, tool results, scratchpad). Limited by window size and attention quality; managed via trimming, summarisation and compaction.
- **Long-term memory**: persisted outside the model (vector DB, key-value store, files, graph DB) and retrieved on demand.
  - **Semantic**: facts and preferences ("user prefers Python").
  - **Episodic**: records of past interactions/trajectories ("last time this deploy failed because...").
  - **Procedural**: how to do things (system prompts, skills, learned rules).

**Write path**: decide *what* to store (extract salient facts after each turn or at session end, often with an LLM), *how* (embedding + metadata, or structured schema), and *when* (hot path vs background job). Include dedup, conflict resolution (newer overrides older) and timestamps.

**Read path**: retrieve by similarity, recency and importance (Generative Agents scored memories on recency + importance + relevance), then inject a compact selection into the prompt. Alternatively let the agent call memory tools itself (MemGPT-style paging between context and external store).

**Implementation patterns**
- File-based memory (e.g. `CLAUDE.md`, notes files) that the agent reads at start and edits over time.
- Vector store of summaries + metadata filters per user.
- Knowledge graph for entity relations.

**Pitfalls**: stale or wrong memories that persist (poisoning, including via prompt injection), privacy/PII and deletion requirements, memory bloat degrading retrieval, retrieving irrelevant memories that distract the model, and cross-user leakage (always namespace by user/tenant).

**Evaluation**: test recall accuracy, whether memories change behaviour correctly, and contradiction handling over long horizons.

**Sources:**
- [AI Agent Memory (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/ai-agent-memory)
- [Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.03442)
- [MemGPT: Towards LLMs as Operating Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.08560)
- [Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents (CoALA)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.02427)

<a id="q152"></a>
### 152. Harness Engineering in AI

**Answer:**

The **harness** is everything around the model that turns it into a working agent: the loop, system prompt, tool definitions and implementations, context management, permissions, memory, sandbox, hooks, retries, and evaluation glue. **Harness engineering** is the discipline of designing and iterating on that scaffolding so a given model performs reliably.

**Why it matters**: with the same model, differences in tool design, context strategy and feedback loops often change task success dramatically (benchmarks like SWE-bench show large gaps between scaffolds using the same base model). The model provides capability; the harness determines how much of it is usable and how safely.

**Components**
- **Prompting layer**: system prompt, project instructions, few-shot examples.
- **Tool layer**: schemas, descriptions, error messages, output truncation, idempotency.
- **Context management**: retrieval on demand (grep/read rather than preloading), compaction, sub-agents for isolation, scratchpad/todo files.
- **Control loop**: stop conditions, max steps, budgets, retries, planning steps.
- **Safety layer**: permission prompts, allow/deny lists, sandboxing, hooks that block dangerous commands.
- **Feedback loop**: run tests/linters/compilers so the agent verifies its own work.
- **Observability**: traces, replay, evals.

**Principles**
- Give the model verifiable feedback (tests, type checks) - the highest-leverage element in coding agents.
- Keep tools few, clear, and ergonomic to the model ("agent-computer interface").
- Prefer simple, transparent loops over heavy frameworks.
- Re-evaluate the harness when the model changes: scaffolding that compensated for weaker models can become dead weight or even harmful.

**Pitfalls**: over-engineering rigid workflows around a model that could plan itself; brittle prompts; no evals so changes are not measurable.

**Sources:**
- [Harness Engineering in AI (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/harness-engineering-in-ai)
- [Building effective agents (Anthropic)](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents)
- [Writing effective tools for agents (Anthropic)](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents)
- [SWE-agent: Agent-Computer Interfaces Enable Automated Software Engineering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.15793)

<a id="q153"></a>
### 153. What matters more for an agentic coding tool like Claude Code: the model or the harness?

**Answer:**

Both are necessary, and the honest answer is that they are multiplicative: `success ≈ model capability × harness quality`. A weak model cannot be rescued by any scaffold, and a strong model in a poor harness wastes most of its ability.

**Case for the model**
- Reasoning, code quality, long-horizon planning, tool-use reliability and instruction following are model properties.
- Each model generation has removed the need for elaborate scaffolding (fewer forced plans, less prompt hand-holding).
- Ceiling on hard tasks is set by the model.

**Case for the harness**
- Same model, different scaffold can swing SWE-bench-style scores substantially.
- Harness supplies what the model lacks: **grounding** (read files, run tests), **context management** (search instead of stuffing, compaction, sub-agents), **safe execution** (sandbox, permissions, hooks), **persistence** (project memory files, todo lists), and **verification loops**.
- Latency, cost and UX (streaming, diffs, undo/checkpoints) are harness concerns.

**Practical framing**
- Early in a project or when the model is the bottleneck, model upgrades give the biggest jump.
- Once the model is "good enough", most marginal gains come from the harness: better tools, faster feedback, tighter context.
- Because models improve quickly, keep the harness thin and revisit assumptions on each model release; co-design is best (Claude Code is tuned to Claude's tool-use behaviour).

**How to answer in an interview**: state it's multiplicative, give an example (same model with and without test-running feedback), and describe how you would measure each factor: hold the model fixed and vary the harness (ablate tools, context strategy), then hold the harness fixed and swap models, on a representative eval set.

**Sources:**
- [Harness Engineering in AI (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/harness-engineering-in-ai)
- [How does Claude Code work? (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/how-does-claude-code-work)
- [Claude Code overview (Anthropic docs)](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/claude-code/overview)
- [SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06770)

<a id="q154"></a>
### 154. Explain the ReAct (Reasoning + Acting) agent architecture.

**Answer:**

**ReAct** (Yao et al., 2022) interleaves natural-language **reasoning traces** ("Thought") with **actions** ("Action") and their **observations**. Reasoning helps the model plan, track state and handle exceptions; actions ground it in external information, reducing hallucination.

**Loop**
```
Thought:  I need the population of the capital of France.
Action:   search["capital of France"]
Observation: Paris
Thought:  Now I need Paris population.
Action:   search["Paris population"]
Observation: ~2.1M
Thought:  I have the answer.
Action:   finish["about 2.1 million"]
```
Each iteration appends Thought/Action/Observation to the context and re-prompts the model until it emits a final answer or hits a step limit.

**Why it works**: chain-of-thought alone hallucinates facts; action-only agents lack planning. ReAct combines both, improving results on HotpotQA/FEVER (fewer hallucinations) and on interactive tasks like ALFWorld and WebShop versus imitation/RL baselines, per the paper.

**Modern form**: native tool calling replaces text parsing; the "thought" may be an extended-thinking block or hidden reasoning. The core loop is the same.

**Strengths**: simple, adaptive to unexpected observations, interpretable traces, works with any tool.

**Weaknesses**
- Greedy, one step at a time: no global plan, can wander or loop.
- Token cost grows every step (context re-sent).
- Sequential latency (no parallelism unless the model emits parallel calls).
- Error compounding; brittle parsing if using text format.

**Mitigations**: max steps, loop detection, planning steps (Plan-and-Execute), reflection, tool-result truncation.

**Sources:**
- [ReAct Agent (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/react-agent)
- [ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629)
- [Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.11903)
- [LangGraph documentation (prebuilt ReAct agent)](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/)

<a id="q155"></a>
### 155. What is the Plan-and-Execute agent pattern?

**Answer:**

**Plan-and-Execute** separates an agent into a **planner** that produces a multi-step plan up front and an **executor** that carries out each step (possibly with its own ReAct loop or tools). An optional **re-planner** updates the plan after results arrive.

**Flow**
1. Planner LLM: goal -> ordered list of steps (`["find X", "compute Y", "write summary"]`).
2. Executor: runs step i with tools, returns result.
3. Re-planner (optional): given the original goal, plan, and results so far, either finalize or revise the remaining plan.

**Benefits**
- **Cost**: a large model plans once; a smaller/cheaper model executes steps.
- **Global coherence**: less wandering than step-by-step ReAct; easier to audit and approve a plan (human-in-the-loop).
- **Parallelism**: independent steps can run concurrently (ReWOO / LLMCompiler variants use variable references between steps to avoid re-prompting the planner).
- **Fewer LLM calls** on the planner side, shorter contexts for executors.

**Drawbacks**
- Plans go stale when early steps reveal surprises; needs re-planning.
- Upfront planning is poor for highly exploratory tasks where next step depends on observations.
- Planner errors propagate to every step.

**When to use**: well-decomposable tasks (report generation, data pipelines, multi-file refactors). **When not**: exploratory debugging, chat-like short tasks - use ReAct.

**Related**: Plan-and-Solve prompting, ReWOO, LLMCompiler, todo-list tools in coding agents (the model plans and updates a checklist as it works).

**Sources:**
- [Plan-and-Execute Agent (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/plan-and-execute-agent)
- [Plan-and-Solve Prompting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.04091)
- [ReWOO: Decoupling Reasoning from Observations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18323)
- [LangGraph documentation](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/)

<a id="q156"></a>
### 156. What is tool use (function calling) in LLMs, and how does it enable agents?

**Answer:**

**Tool use / function calling** lets a model emit a *structured request* to run an external function instead of (or before) a text answer. The model never executes anything itself: your application runs the function and returns the result.

**Mechanism**
1. You send messages plus **tool definitions**: name, description, JSON Schema for parameters.
2. The model decides to answer or emit one or more `tool_call`s (`name` + JSON arguments). Models are fine-tuned to produce this format reliably.
3. Your code validates arguments, executes the tool, and appends a `tool_result` message.
4. You call the model again; it uses the result to continue or answer.

```json
{"name": "get_weather",
 "description": "Current weather for a city",
 "input_schema": {"type":"object",
   "properties":{"city":{"type":"string"}}, "required":["city"]}}
```
Model output: `{"type":"tool_use","name":"get_weather","input":{"city":"Warsaw"}}`.

**How it enables agents**: tools give the model *perception* (search, read files, query DBs) and *action* (write, send, deploy). Wrapped in a loop, tool calls + results become the observe-act cycle. Features like parallel tool calls, forced tool choice (`tool_choice`), and streaming arguments support efficient loops.

**Best practices**
- Clear names and descriptions (they are prompts); enums and constraints in schemas.
- Validate arguments server-side; never trust model output.
- Return concise, informative results and actionable errors.
- Apply least privilege and confirmation for destructive tools.

**Pitfalls**: hallucinated tools/params, wrong tool choice with many tools, prompt injection via tool results, large outputs eating context.

**Sources:**
- [How does Function Calling work in LLMs? (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/how-does-function-calling-work-in-llms)
- [AI Engineering Explained (video)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lnfWvX66FUk)
- [Tool use with Claude (Anthropic docs)](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/tool-use/overview)
- [Function calling guide (OpenAI docs)](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/function-calling)
- [Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.04761)

<a id="q157"></a>
### 157. What is the difference between structured output and function calling?

**Answer:**

Both use JSON Schema, but they serve different purposes.

| | Structured output | Function calling |
|---|---|---|
| Goal | The *final response* conforms to a schema | The model *requests an action* to be executed |
| Who acts next | Your code just parses/uses the JSON | Your code runs a tool and feeds back the result |
| Turn pattern | Usually single call | Multi-turn loop |
| Side effects | None by itself | Typically yes |
| Typical use | Extraction, classification, API responses, UI data | Agents, retrieval, actions |

**Structured output** enforces a format via constrained decoding (grammar/JSON-schema masking of logits, e.g. OpenAI Structured Outputs, `strict` mode) or via JSON mode + validation and retry. Guarantees syntactic validity (and schema conformance when strict), not semantic correctness.

**Function calling** yields structured arguments too, but the semantics is "call this function with these args". Many providers implement structured output using the same machinery, and you can emulate structured output by defining a single "respond" tool and forcing `tool_choice` to it.

**Choosing**
- Need the answer to the user in a fixed shape -> structured output.
- Need the model to fetch data or act in the world -> function calling.
- Agents commonly use both: tool calls during the loop, structured output for the final answer.

**Pitfalls**: schemas too complex or deeply nested reduce quality; first-request latency for grammar compilation; validity is not truth, so still validate business rules (Pydantic) and handle refusals/truncation (`max_tokens`).

**Sources:**
- [How does Function Calling work in LLMs? (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/how-does-function-calling-work-in-llms)
- [Structured Outputs guide (OpenAI docs)](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/structured-outputs)
- [Function calling guide (OpenAI docs)](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/function-calling)
- [Tool use with Claude (Anthropic docs)](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/tool-use/overview)

<a id="q158"></a>
### 158. How do you design and define tools for an AI agent?

**Answer:**

Treat tools as an **interface designed for a non-deterministic user** (the model). Good tool design often moves agent quality more than prompt tweaking.

**Principles**
1. **Right granularity**: not a thin wrapper of every API endpoint, and not one mega-tool. Consolidate multi-step workflows into task-level tools (`schedule_meeting` rather than `list_users` + `list_slots` + `create_event`), but keep each tool single-purpose.
2. **Clear naming and namespacing**: `github_create_issue`, `jira_search` help selection.
3. **Descriptions as prompts**: say what it does, when to use / not use it, parameter semantics, formats, examples, side effects.
4. **Strict schemas**: types, enums, required fields, defaults, constraints; use unambiguous parameter names (`user_email` not `user`).
5. **Model-friendly outputs**: return the relevant fields in readable form (names rather than opaque UUIDs where possible), pagination, filtering, truncation with hints ("showing 20 of 340, refine your query"), and a `response_format` (concise/detailed) option to save tokens.
6. **Actionable errors**: "date must be YYYY-MM-DD, got 12/03" instead of a stack trace.
7. **Safety**: least privilege, read vs write separation, confirmation for destructive actions, idempotency keys, dry-run modes.
8. **Few tools**: each extra tool raises selection confusion and prompt tokens; load tools dynamically if there are many.

**Process**: prototype, write evals of realistic tasks, run the agent, read transcripts to find confusion, then iterate on descriptions/schemas (even let an LLM propose improvements).

**Pitfalls**: overlapping tools, ambiguous parameters, huge outputs, hidden required ordering between tools, missing side-effect documentation.

**Sources:**
- [AI Engineering Explained (video)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lnfWvX66FUk)
- [Writing effective tools for agents (Anthropic)](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents)
- [Building effective agents, Appendix 2: Prompt engineering your tools (Anthropic)](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents)
- [Function calling guide (OpenAI docs)](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/function-calling)

<a id="q159"></a>
### 159. How does an agent decide when to call a tool versus answering from its own knowledge?

**Answer:**

The decision is made by the model itself at every step, conditioned on the system prompt, tool descriptions and conversation so far. Under the hood the model produces either a tool-call token sequence or a text answer; fine-tuning on tool-use data taught it when each is appropriate.

**Signals that drive the choice**
- **Tool descriptions and system prompt** ("use search for anything after 2024 or any factual claim you cannot verify").
- **Knowledge confidence / uncertainty** about the query (imperfectly calibrated).
- **Task type**: needs fresh data, private data, exact computation, or side effects -> tool; general reasoning, style, well-known facts -> answer.
- **Cost cues** if specified (tool calls are expensive; prefer answering when sure).

**Controlling it**
- `tool_choice`: `auto` (model decides), `required/any` (must call some tool), specific tool (forced), `none` (no tools).
- Prompt rules: explicit policies ("always calculate with the calculator tool", "never guess order status").
- Routers: a cheap classifier or first LLM call decides whether retrieval/tool is needed (adaptive RAG, Self-RAG's retrieve tokens).
- Tool design: descriptions that state when *not* to use it.

**Failure modes**
- *Under-calling*: hallucinated answers, stale facts, mental arithmetic.
- *Over-calling*: needless latency/cost, tool called for trivia, redundant repeated searches.

**Improving**: build evals with cases labelled "should call tool X" / "should not call"; measure precision/recall of tool invocation; add few-shot examples; tune descriptions; use a forced tool for high-stakes domains; add verification (cite sources from tool output).

**Sources:**
- [Tool use with Claude: controlling tool choice (Anthropic docs)](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/tool-use/overview)
- [Function calling guide, tool_choice (OpenAI docs)](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/function-calling)
- [Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.04761)
- [Self-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.11511)

<a id="q160"></a>
### 160. What is the difference between single-agent and multi-agent systems?

**Answer:**

A **single-agent** system uses one LLM loop with one context and a set of tools. A **multi-agent system (MAS)** uses several LLM-driven agents, each with its own role, prompt, tools and context, coordinating to solve a task.

**Multi-agent topologies**
- **Orchestrator-worker (supervisor)**: a lead agent decomposes tasks and delegates to sub-agents, then synthesises.
- **Pipeline / hand-off**: agents pass work along a chain (planner -> coder -> reviewer).
- **Debate / critic**: agents argue or review each other.
- **Peer network / swarm**: agents route to each other dynamically.

| | Single agent | Multi-agent |
|---|---|---|
| Complexity | Low | High (coordination, protocols) |
| Context | One shared window (can overflow) | Separate windows, compressed hand-offs |
| Parallelism | Limited | Natural for breadth-first tasks |
| Cost | Lower | Often several times more tokens |
| Debuggability | Simple trace | Distributed traces, emergent behaviour |
| Specialisation | One prompt, many tools | Focused prompts and tool sets per role |

**Benefits of MAS**: parallel exploration (research), context isolation (each worker keeps a clean window), specialisation, independent verification, security separation (untrusted-content agent has no dangerous tools).

**Costs**: token overhead, coordination errors, information loss between agents, harder evaluation.

**Rule of thumb**: start with a single agent plus good tools; add agents when there is clear need (context limits, parallelisable subtasks, separation of privileges). Anthropic reported their multi-agent research system beating single-agent on breadth-heavy research but at far higher token use.

**Sources:**
- [Multi-Agent Systems (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/multi-agent-systems)
- [How we built our multi-agent research system (Anthropic)](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system)
- [AutoGen: Enabling Next-Gen LLM Applications via Multi-Agent Conversation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.08155)
- [MetaGPT: Meta Programming for Multi-Agent Collaborative Framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.00352)

---

<a id="q161"></a>
### 161. When do multi-agent systems break down, and when is a single agent the better choice?

**Answer:**

**Breakdown modes**
- **Context fragmentation**: sub-agents lack the shared context; decisions made in isolation conflict (Cognition's argument: "share full traces, actions carry implicit decisions"). Coding tasks with tightly coupled edits suffer most.
- **Lossy hand-offs**: summaries drop crucial details; telephone-game degradation.
- **Coordination overhead**: orchestrators mis-delegate, duplicate work, or spawn too many workers for simple queries.
- **Cost blow-up**: each agent re-reads shared context; multi-agent runs can consume several times the tokens of a single agent.
- **Error propagation and cascading failures**: one hallucinated intermediate result is trusted by others.
- **Emergent loops**: agents endlessly delegate, agree sycophantically, or argue.
- **Debugging difficulty**: non-deterministic interactions across many traces.
- **Latency**: sequential delegation adds round trips.
- The MAST failure taxonomy of multi-agent LLM systems highlights specification, inter-agent misalignment, and verification failures as common categories.

**Prefer a single agent when**
- The task is sequential and interdependent (most code edits, single-document reasoning).
- The whole context fits in a window (or compaction suffices).
- Low latency / cost matters.
- You are still learning the task; simpler is easier to eval and iterate.

**Prefer multi-agent when**
- The task is breadth-first and parallelisable (research over many sources).
- Subtasks need very different tools/prompts or privilege separation.
- Context would overflow a single window and sub-results compress well.
- Independent verification (reviewer with fresh context) adds value.

**Mitigations**: pass full relevant context or use shared state/file system, structured hand-off schemas, effort-scaling rules in orchestrator prompts, hard limits on spawn count and depth, and strong tracing. Consider sub-agents purely as read-only "researchers" that return distilled findings while one agent owns writes.

**Sources:**
- [Multi-Agent Systems (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/multi-agent-systems)
- [Don't Build Multi-Agents (Cognition)](https://cognition.ai/blog/dont-build-multi-agents)
- [How we built our multi-agent research system (Anthropic)](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system)
- [Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.13657)
