<a id="q162"></a>
### 162. What is Model Context Protocol (MCP), and how does it standardize tool integration?

**Answer:**

**MCP** is an open protocol (introduced by Anthropic, late 2024) that standardises how LLM applications connect to external tools, data and prompts. It is often described as "USB-C for AI": one protocol instead of N x M custom integrations between N apps and M services.

**Architecture**
- **Host**: the AI application (Claude Desktop, IDE, agent runtime).
- **Client**: a connector inside the host that maintains a 1:1 session with a server.
- **Server**: a program exposing capabilities. Communication uses JSON-RPC 2.0 over **stdio** (local subprocess) or **Streamable HTTP** (remote; earlier SSE transport).

**Server primitives**
- **Tools**: model-controlled functions with JSON Schema (`tools/list`, `tools/call`).
- **Resources**: application-controlled data (files, DB rows, URIs) for context.
- **Prompts**: user-controlled templates/workflows.

**Client primitives**: **sampling** (server asks the host's model for a completion), **roots** (filesystem scope), **elicitation** (ask the user for input).

**Lifecycle**: initialize with capability negotiation -> discover (`tools/list`) -> invoke -> notifications (e.g. `tools/list_changed`). Remote servers commonly use OAuth-based authorization.

**How it standardises integration**: a service writes one MCP server; any MCP-capable client can use it with no bespoke glue. Tool discovery is dynamic and self-describing, so agents pick up new tools at runtime.

**Benefits**: ecosystem reuse, decoupling, consistent auth/transport, dynamic discovery.

**Risks/pitfalls**: untrusted servers (tool poisoning, malicious descriptions, prompt injection via results), over-broad permissions, "confused deputy" issues, token bloat from many tool schemas, and supply-chain risk. Mitigate with allowlists, user consent, scoped credentials, sandboxing and reviewing tool descriptions.

**Sources:**
- [What is MCP (Model Context Protocol)? (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/what-is-mcp-model-context-protocol)
- [AI Engineering Explained (video)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lnfWvX66FUk)
- [Model Context Protocol introduction](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/introduction)
- [MCP specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification)

---

<a id="q163"></a>
### 163. How does MCP differ from traditional function calling?

**Answer:**

They operate at different layers and are complementary.

- **Function calling** is a *model-level capability*: the model emits a structured request to call a function you defined in the API request. Definitions and execution live inside your application, per provider format (OpenAI, Anthropic, etc. differ slightly).
- **MCP** is a *protocol between application and tool servers*: it defines how tools (plus resources and prompts) are discovered, described and invoked across process/network boundaries, independent of the model vendor.

| | Function calling | MCP |
|---|---|---|
| Layer | Model API feature | Client-server integration protocol |
| Tool definition | Hard-coded in each app's request | Discovered dynamically from servers |
| Execution | Your code, bespoke per tool | Server executes; client forwards via JSON-RPC |
| Portability | Per-provider schema, per-app glue | Write once, use in any MCP client |
| Beyond tools | No | Resources, prompts, sampling, elicitation |
| State/auth | You build it | Transport, session, OAuth conventions |

**How they fit together**: an MCP client fetches tool lists from servers, converts them into the model's function-calling format, passes them to the model; when the model emits a tool call, the client routes it to the correct MCP server and returns the result. So MCP *uses* function calling; it does not replace it.

**When to use which**
- Few tools private to one app: plain function calling is simpler and faster.
- Reusable integrations, third-party tools, many clients/agents, dynamic tool sets: MCP.

**Trade-offs of MCP**: extra moving parts (process/network, latency), security surface from third-party servers, tool-schema token overhead (mitigated by lazy loading/tool search).

**Sources:**
- [What is MCP (Model Context Protocol)? (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/what-is-mcp-model-context-protocol)
- [How does Function Calling work in LLMs? (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/how-does-function-calling-work-in-llms)
- [Model Context Protocol documentation](https://modelcontextprotocol.io)
- [Tool use with Claude (Anthropic docs)](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/tool-use/overview)

<a id="q164"></a>
### 164. What are AI SubAgents?

**Answer:**

A **subagent** is a specialised agent spawned by a parent (main/orchestrator) agent to handle a delegated subtask in its **own isolated context window**, with its own system prompt, tool set and (optionally) model. It returns only a condensed result to the parent.

**Why use them**
- **Context isolation**: exploratory work (reading 50 files, searching) stays out of the main window; the parent receives a summary. This fights context rot and saves tokens in the main thread.
- **Specialisation**: focused prompts and restricted tools (a read-only code reviewer, a test runner, a security auditor).
- **Parallelism**: several subagents work concurrently on independent questions.
- **Cost control**: run cheaper/faster models for simple subtasks.
- **Safety**: least-privilege tool sets per subagent.

**Example (Claude Code)**: subagents are defined as Markdown files with frontmatter (name, description, tools, model) and a prompt body; the main agent delegates automatically based on the description or when asked.

**Design guidelines**
- Give the subagent a *self-contained* task brief (goal, constraints, output format); it does not see the parent's history.
- Ask for a compact, structured return (findings plus file references), not raw dumps.
- Limit depth/number of spawns; prevent recursive runaway.
- Prefer read-only subagents for research; keep write actions with one owner to avoid conflicting edits.

**Pitfalls**: lost context between parent and child, duplicated work, token cost multiplication (each subagent has its own loop), hard-to-debug traces, over-delegation for trivial tasks.

**Sources:**
- [AI SubAgents (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/ai-subagents)
- [Subagents in Claude Code (Anthropic docs)](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/claude-code/sub-agents)
- [How we built our multi-agent research system (Anthropic)](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system)

---

<a id="q165"></a>
### 165. What are the different types of agent memory (short-term, long-term, episodic)?

**Answer:**

The taxonomy borrows from cognitive science (see CoALA).

**Short-term (working) memory**
- Contents: current conversation, tool results, scratchpad, plan.
- Storage: the context window (and state objects/checkpoints in frameworks).
- Limits: window size, attention degradation over long context ("lost in the middle").
- Management: sliding window, summarisation, compaction, trimming old tool outputs.

**Long-term memory** (persists across sessions, stored externally)
- **Semantic memory**: facts and knowledge about the user/world/domain ("the user's stack is Django + Postgres"). Stored as records, profile documents, or vector/graph entries.
- **Episodic memory**: specific past experiences/trajectories with context and outcome ("on 3 March the migration failed because of X; fix was Y"). Used for few-shot recall, learning from mistakes (Reflexion), case-based reasoning.
- **Procedural memory**: skills, instructions, rules on how to act; stored in system prompts, skill files, learned tool-use routines (Voyager's skill library).

**Also mentioned**: *entity memory* (tracked entities and attributes), *knowledge-graph memory*, *shared memory* between agents (blackboard).

| Type | What | Typical store | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Working | Current task state | Context/state | Messages, plan |
| Semantic | Facts | Vector DB/profile | User preferences |
| Episodic | Events | Log + embeddings | Past failed runs |
| Procedural | How-to | Prompts/skill files | Coding conventions |

**Operational concerns**: what to write and when, retrieval relevance, forgetting/TTL, contradiction handling, privacy and deletion, per-user isolation.

**Sources:**
- [AI Agent Memory (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/ai-agent-memory)
- [Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents (CoALA)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.02427)
- [Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.11366)
- [Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.16291)

<a id="q166"></a>
### 166. How do you handle agent failures and implement error recovery?

**Answer:**

Agents fail in many ways: tool errors, malformed calls, bad plans, hallucinated results, timeouts, rate limits, context overflow, and silent wrong answers. Design for failure at each layer.

**1. Classify failures**
- *Transient* (network, 429/5xx): retry with exponential backoff plus jitter, respect `Retry-After`.
- *Deterministic tool errors* (validation, not found): return a clear error to the model so it can self-correct.
- *Model errors* (invalid JSON, wrong tool): validate, re-prompt with the error, or repair.
- *Strategic errors* (wrong approach): reflection, re-planning, backtracking.
- *Systemic* (provider outage, budget exceeded): fallback model/provider, graceful degradation, escalate.

**2. Tools layer**
- Idempotent operations plus idempotency keys so retries are safe.
- Timeouts on every call; circuit breakers for flaky dependencies.
- Actionable error messages ("`start_date` must be before `end_date`").

**3. Agent layer**
- Feed errors back as observations with a bounded retry count (e.g. 2-3 same-call attempts), then change strategy.
- Loop/stall detection and max-step limits.
- Checkpoint state after each step (LangGraph checkpointers, durable execution such as Temporal) so runs resume rather than restart.
- Compensating actions/rollback for multi-step side effects (saga pattern).
- Verification steps (tests, schema checks, second-model critique) to catch silent failures.

**4. Escalation**: hand off to a human with full context when confidence is low, retries are exhausted, or the action is high risk.

**5. Observability**: trace every step, log inputs/outputs and error taxonomy; build regression evals from real failures.

**Pitfalls**: infinite retry loops, swallowing errors (agent claims success), retrying non-idempotent writes, error text that leaks secrets.

**Sources:**
- [Building effective agents (Anthropic)](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents)
- [Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.11366)
- [LangGraph persistence and durable execution docs](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/)
- [Writing effective tools for agents (Anthropic)](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents)

<a id="q167"></a>
### 167. What is an agent loop, and how does it decide when to stop?

**Answer:**

The **agent loop** is the repeated cycle: build context -> call the model -> if it requests tools, execute them and append results -> call the model again -> ... -> return a final answer.

```python
def run(goal, max_steps=25, budget_usd=1.0):
    msgs = [system, goal]; spent = 0
    for step in range(max_steps):
        r = llm(msgs, tools)
        spent += r.cost
        if r.stop_reason != "tool_use":       # natural stop
            return r.text
        if spent > budget_usd: break          # hard stop
        msgs += [r.message] + execute(r.tool_calls)
    return escalate_or_partial(msgs)
```

**Stop conditions**
1. **Natural termination**: the model produces a response without tool calls (or calls an explicit `finish`/`submit` tool). This is the normal, model-decided end.
2. **Goal check**: an external verifier (tests pass, schema valid, acceptance criteria met by an LLM judge or code).
3. **Hard limits**: max iterations, wall-clock timeout, token/cost budget, max tool calls per tool.
4. **Stall/loop detection**: repeated identical calls or no progress across N steps.
5. **Human/system interrupts**: user cancel, approval denied, guardrail violation, error threshold.
6. **Context exhaustion**: compact or stop.

**Design tips**
- Always combine the model's own decision with hard external caps; never rely only on the model saying "done".
- Make the final step explicit (a `final_answer` tool with structured output) to remove ambiguity.
- On hitting a limit, return partial results plus status rather than silently failing.
- Log stop reason for analysis.

**Pitfalls**: premature stopping (model declares victory without verifying), never stopping (loops), "done" without evidence. Mitigate with verification tools and completion criteria in the prompt.

**Sources:**
- [AI Agent Loop (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/ai-agent-loop)
- [Building effective agents (Anthropic)](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents)
- [ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629)

<a id="q168"></a>
### 168. Context Engineering

**Answer:**

**Context engineering** is the discipline of deciding *what goes into the model's context window at each step*: the smallest set of high-signal tokens that maximises the likelihood of the desired behaviour. It generalises prompt engineering from "write a good instruction" to "curate an entire, evolving information state" (system prompt, tools, retrieved data, history, memory, state).

**Why it matters**: context is finite and attention degrades with length ("context rot", lost-in-the-middle); more tokens also mean higher cost and latency. Agents accumulate context every step, so curation is continuous.

**Components**
- **Instructions**: system prompt at the right "altitude" (specific enough to guide, not brittle if-else lists).
- **Tools**: concise, non-overlapping definitions.
- **Knowledge**: RAG, just-in-time retrieval (agents hold lightweight references such as file paths/URLs and load on demand).
- **Memory**: persistent notes, user profile.
- **History**: recent turns, summaries.
- **Output format / examples**: a few canonical few-shot examples.

**Core techniques** (write, select, compress, isolate)
- **Write**: scratchpads, notes files, external memory.
- **Select**: retrieval, reranking, tool search/dynamic tool loading.
- **Compress**: compaction/summarisation, trimming old tool results, clearing stale outputs.
- **Isolate**: sub-agents with clean windows, structured state schemas exposing only needed fields per step.
- Cache-friendly ordering (stable prefix first) for prompt caching.

**Pitfalls**: context poisoning (a hallucination persists), distraction (irrelevant data), confusion (too many tools), clash (contradictory instructions/data).

**Practice**: measure with evals, inspect full prompts at each step, and treat token budget as a design constraint.

**Sources:**
- [Context Engineering (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/context-engineering)
- [Effective context engineering for AI agents (Anthropic)](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents)
- [Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172)

<a id="q169"></a>
### 169. How does context compaction work?

**Answer:**

**Context compaction** shrinks a long-running conversation/trajectory so the agent can continue within its window without losing what matters. Typically the history is summarised into a compact digest, and the run continues with `system prompt + summary + recent turns`.

**Typical procedure**
1. **Trigger**: token usage crosses a threshold (e.g. ~80-90% of the window), or at task/phase boundaries, or on user command.
2. **Summarise**: an LLM call condenses the history, preserving: the goal and constraints, decisions made and why, current state/progress, unresolved issues and next steps, key identifiers (file paths, IDs, error messages), user preferences.
3. **Replace**: old messages are dropped; the summary becomes the new first message; the latest few turns stay verbatim.
4. **Continue**: the agent works from the compacted context (optionally re-reading files as needed).

**Complementary techniques**
- **Tool-result clearing/truncation**: raw outputs of old tool calls are the cheapest tokens to discard.
- **Structured note-taking**: the agent writes progress files or memory outside the context and re-reads them.
- **Sub-agents**: offload verbose exploration and return summaries.
- **Rolling/hierarchical summaries** for very long runs.
- **Server-side compaction/context editing** features in some provider APIs.

**Trade-offs**
- Summaries are lossy: dropped details (exact error text, subtle constraints) can cause regressions; the most important design question is *what to keep*.
- Summarising costs an extra call and can invalidate the prompt cache.
- Compact too late and quality already degraded; too early and you lose useful detail.

**Tips**: tune the summarisation prompt for recall first, then prune; keep identifiers verbatim; test with evals that need facts from early in the session; save originals externally so they can be re-retrieved.

**Sources:**
- [How does context compaction work? (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/how-does-context-compaction-work)
- [Effective context engineering for AI agents (Anthropic)](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents)
- [MemGPT: Towards LLMs as Operating Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.08560)

<a id="q170"></a>
### 170. Loop Engineering

**Answer:**

**Loop engineering** is the practice of designing the *control loop* around an LLM: how each iteration is structured, what feedback the model receives, how progress is verified, and when the loop continues, retries, branches, or stops. The premise is that reliability in agentic systems comes less from a single perfect prompt and more from a well-designed loop with strong feedback signals.

**Design questions**
- **What is one iteration?** Plan -> act -> observe -> verify -> update state.
- **What feedback closes the loop?** Best signals are objective and cheap: unit tests, compilers, linters, type checkers, schema validators, retrieval hits, simulators. LLM-as-judge is a weaker fallback.
- **How is progress measured?** Explicit success criteria, checklists, todo files, metrics per step.
- **What state carries over?** Curated state or notes, not raw growing history.
- **Termination and safety**: max iterations, budgets, stall detection, escalation.
- **Variants**: generate-then-verify, evaluator-optimizer (generator + critic), best-of-N with a verifier, reflection loops, outer "Ralph-style" loops that restart a fresh-context agent repeatedly against a spec/checklist until done.

**Principles**
1. Make success verifiable before you build the loop.
2. Keep each iteration small so failures are attributable.
3. Feed back precise, structured errors.
4. Prevent regressions (run the full test suite, not just the last change).
5. Cap everything (steps, cost, time) and log every iteration for replay.

**Pitfalls**: reward-hacking the verifier (deleting failing tests), oscillation between fixes, context bloat across iterations, ambiguous completion criteria.

**Sources:**
- [Loop Engineering (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/what-is-loop-engineering)
- [Building effective agents: evaluator-optimizer workflow (Anthropic)](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents)
- [Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.17651)
- [Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.11366)

<a id="q171"></a>
### 171. Graph Engineering

**Answer:**

**Graph engineering** is designing agentic systems as an explicit **graph**: nodes are units of work (LLM calls, tools, sub-agents, human checkpoints, validators) and edges define control flow (fixed, conditional, or model-chosen), with shared **state** flowing through it. It sits between rigid linear chains and fully free-form agent loops.

**Building blocks (as in LangGraph)**
- **State**: typed schema (e.g. TypedDict/Pydantic) with reducers defining how updates merge (append messages, overwrite field).
- **Nodes**: functions that read state and return updates.
- **Edges**: static transitions, **conditional edges** (router function picks next node), fan-out/fan-in for parallelism.
- **Cycles**: enable loops (agent -> tools -> agent).
- **Checkpointing**: state persisted per step for resume, time travel and human-in-the-loop interrupts.

**Why graphs**
- Predictability and control: constrain where autonomy is allowed.
- Observability: each node is a traceable unit.
- Reliability: insert validation, retry and approval nodes at known points.
- Composability: subgraphs, reusable nodes; multi-agent topologies map to graphs (supervisor, hierarchical, network).
- Parallel branches with joins for speed.

**Design guidelines**
- Put deterministic logic in code nodes, LLM only where judgment is needed.
- Keep the state small and explicit.
- Model failure paths (error edges, fallback nodes).
- Start with the simplest graph; add nodes only for observed failures.

**Trade-offs**: more upfront design, rigidity if the task varies, risk of over-engineering when a single tool-calling loop suffices. Also graph "explosion" reduces maintainability.

**Sources:**
- [Graph Engineering (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/what-is-graph-engineering)
- [LangGraph documentation: concepts](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/)
- [How does LangGraph work? (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/how-does-langgraph-work)

<a id="q172"></a>
### 172. How AI Agents Communicate?

**Answer:**

Agents communicate at several layers.

**1. Agent <-> tools/data**: function calling and **MCP** (JSON-RPC over stdio/HTTP) - vertical integration.

**2. Agent <-> agent (horizontal)**
- **Shared message history / conversation** (AutoGen group chats, hand-offs): agents append messages to a common thread.
- **Structured hand-offs**: parent passes a task brief, child returns a typed result (orchestrator-worker, subagents).
- **Shared state / blackboard**: agents read/write a common state object (LangGraph state) or a shared store or file system.
- **Message passing / queues**: asynchronous events, pub/sub across services.
- **Protocols for cross-vendor/cross-process agents**: **A2A (Agent2Agent)** - agent cards for capability discovery, tasks with lifecycle states, messages and artifacts over HTTP/JSON-RPC and streaming; **ACP** and others have been proposed. MCP focuses on tools, A2A on peer agents; they are complementary.

**3. Agent <-> human**: chat UI, approval requests, interrupts/resume, notifications.

**Design considerations**
- **Schemas**: use structured messages (JSON with typed fields) rather than free text for reliable parsing.
- **Context transfer**: decide how much history to share; too little loses decisions, too much wastes tokens.
- **Identity, auth and trust**: authenticate agents, scope permissions, treat messages from other agents as untrusted input (prompt injection can propagate).
- **Discovery**: registries or agent cards.
- **Reliability**: acks, timeouts, idempotency, tracing IDs across agents.
- **Sync vs async**: long tasks need task IDs, status polling/streaming and push notifications.

**Pitfalls**: telephone-game information loss, endless ping-pong between agents, unbounded cost, security via message injection.

**Sources:**
- [How AI Agents Communicate (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/how-ai-agents-communicate)
- [Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol](https://a2a-protocol.org)
- [Model Context Protocol documentation](https://modelcontextprotocol.io)
- [AutoGen: Enabling Next-Gen LLM Applications via Multi-Agent Conversation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.08155)

<a id="q173"></a>
### 173. What are Agent Skills?

**Answer:**

**Agent Skills** are portable, folder-based packages of instructions, scripts and resources that teach an agent how to perform a specific task or workflow (e.g. "create a PPTX", "run our release checklist", "analyse this data format"). Introduced by Anthropic for Claude, and adopted as an open format by other tools.

**Structure**
```
my-skill/
  SKILL.md        # YAML frontmatter (name, description) + instructions
  reference.md    # optional extra docs
  scripts/        # optional executable helpers
```

**Progressive disclosure** (the key idea)
1. At startup only each skill's **name and description** (~dozens of tokens) go into the system prompt.
2. When a task matches, the agent reads the full `SKILL.md` into context.
3. If needed, it reads further referenced files or runs bundled scripts (code executes without loading its source into context).

So you can install many skills without bloating the context; the amount of knowledge is effectively unbounded because it lives on the file system.

**Skills vs related concepts**
- **vs tools/MCP**: tools give *capabilities* (actions); skills give *procedural knowledge* about how to do a task, often using existing tools. Skills are cheap to write (Markdown), no server needed.
- **vs system prompt**: skills are loaded on demand, not always.
- **vs subagents**: skills inject instructions into the same context; subagents run in isolated contexts.

**Best practices**: write a precise description (it drives triggering, say what and when), keep SKILL.md focused and split into referenced files, include tested scripts for deterministic steps, version-control skills, and evaluate that they trigger correctly.

**Risks**: skills can contain executable code and instructions, so only install trusted ones and review them (supply chain and injection risk).

**Sources:**
- [What are Agent Skills? (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/what-are-agent-skills)
- [Introducing Agent Skills (Anthropic)](https://www.anthropic.com/news/skills)
- [Claude Code documentation](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/claude-code/overview)

<a id="q174"></a>
### 174. How do you evaluate and test AI agents?

**Answer:**

Agents are non-deterministic, multi-step and side-effectful, so evaluate the **outcome** and the **trajectory**, at multiple levels, repeatedly.

**Levels**
1. **Unit/component**: tool schemas and implementations (deterministic tests), prompt parsing, retrievers.
2. **Step-level**: is the right tool chosen with correct arguments (tool-call precision/recall, argument accuracy)?
3. **Trajectory-level**: efficiency (steps, tokens, redundant calls), adherence to policy, recovery from errors.
4. **End-to-end task success**: did the final state/answer meet the goal?

**Graders**
- **Code-based / state checks** (best): run tests, inspect the DB or file system state after the run (SWE-bench, tau-bench check final DB state).
- **LLM-as-judge** with rubrics for open-ended output; calibrate against human labels; use pairwise or reference-based scoring.
- **Human review** for high-stakes sampling.

**Handling non-determinism**: run k trials per task; report pass@k (any success) and pass^k (all k succeed - reliability), plus confidence intervals. tau-bench highlights that agents' consistency drops sharply with repeated trials.

**Datasets**: start with 20-50 real tasks from production traces and failures; include edge cases, adversarial/injection cases and negative cases (should refuse or not call a tool); grow with every bug.

**Environment**: sandboxed, resettable, mocked or simulated tools and users (user simulators for conversational agents) for reproducibility.

**Metrics**: success rate, cost per task, latency, steps, tool error rate, escalation rate, safety violations.

**Practice**: trace everything (LangSmith, Langfuse, OpenTelemetry), run evals in CI on every prompt/model/tool change, monitor online with sampled grading, and read transcripts - they reveal failures metrics hide.

**Benchmarks**: SWE-bench, tau-bench, WebArena, OSWorld, AgentBench, GAIA.

**Sources:**
- [AI Agent Evaluation (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/ai-agent-evaluation)
- [tau-bench: A Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.12045)
- [AgentBench: Evaluating LLMs as Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.03688)
- [SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06770)

<a id="q175"></a>
### 175. What are the security risks of agentic systems, and how do you mitigate them?

**Answer:**

Agents combine an LLM that follows instructions in any text it reads with tools that have real permissions. That makes the attack surface much larger than for a chatbot.

**Main risks**
- **Prompt injection** (direct and *indirect* via web pages, emails, docs, tool results, MCP descriptions): attacker text hijacks the agent's behaviour. Unsolved in general; no model reliably distinguishes instructions from data.
- **Data exfiltration**: leaking secrets/private data via tool calls, URLs, rendered markdown images, emails.
- **Excessive agency / privilege**: tools with broad permissions (OWASP "Excessive Agency").
- **Insecure tool/output handling**: model output passed to shell, SQL, or eval.
- **Tool/supply-chain compromise**: malicious MCP servers, poisoned tool descriptions ("tool poisoning"), rug-pull updates, compromised skills/packages.
- **Memory poisoning**: malicious content persisted and reused later.
- **Confused deputy / privilege escalation** across agents or users.
- **Denial of wallet**: loops and cost blow-up; **resource abuse**.
- **Sensitive data disclosure** and cross-tenant leakage.
- **Multi-agent propagation**: injection travelling between agents.

**Mitigations (defence in depth)**
1. **Least privilege**: scoped, short-lived credentials; read-only where possible; per-task permissions.
2. **Break the "lethal trifecta"**: avoid combining private data access + untrusted content + external communication in one agent.
3. **Human approval** for irreversible/sensitive actions.
4. **Sandboxing**: containers/VMs, network egress allowlists, filesystem scoping.
5. **Input/output filtering and guardrails** (classifiers, allowlisted URLs, output schema validation); treat them as speed bumps, not guarantees.
6. **Isolation patterns**: quarantined LLM handles untrusted data with no tools; privileged LLM sees only sanitised/structured results (dual-LLM, plan-then-execute, CaMeL).
7. **Validate all tool arguments** in code; parameterised queries.
8. **Vet MCP servers/skills**, pin versions, review descriptions.
9. **Logging, monitoring, rate and cost limits, kill switch.**
10. **Red-team** continuously.

**Sources:**
- [Prompt Injection in LLMs (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/prompt-injection-in-llms)
- [OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications](https://genai.owasp.org/llm-top-10/)
- [Not what you've signed up for: Indirect Prompt Injection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.12173)
- [The lethal trifecta for AI agents (Simon Willison)](https://simonw.substack.com/p/the-lethal-trifecta-for-ai-agents)

---

<a id="q176"></a>
### 176. Your agent reads untrusted content (emails, web pages, documents) and can call tools. How do you prevent indirect prompt injection and data exfiltration?

**Answer:**

**Diagnosis**: the model cannot reliably separate instructions from data; any text it reads can steer it. Damage requires three ingredients (the "lethal trifecta"): access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and a way to communicate externally. Remove or constrain at least one. Filters alone will not solve it.

**Prioritised fixes**

1. **Architectural isolation (strongest)**
   - *Quarantined/privileged split*: an LLM with no tools reads untrusted content and outputs constrained, typed data (e.g. `{"sender": ..., "intent": "meeting"}`); the privileged agent with tools never sees raw text. (Dual-LLM pattern, CaMeL-style control/data-flow separation.)
   - *Plan-then-execute*: fix the tool plan from the trusted user request before reading untrusted data; injected text cannot add new actions.
   - Separate agents per trust level; do not let a browsing agent hold write/send tools.
2. **Least privilege and scoping**: minimal tools per task, read-only tokens, per-user credentials (never a shared admin key), short-lived tokens.
3. **Block exfiltration channels**: egress network allowlist; disable automatic rendering of remote images/links in markdown; strip or allowlist URLs; no arbitrary HTTP tool; restrict email recipients to known domains.
4. **Human-in-the-loop** for actions that send data out, change permissions, spend money or delete; show exactly what will be sent.
5. **Taint tracking**: mark data derived from untrusted sources and require approval/deny when tainted data flows into sensitive tool arguments.
6. **Content handling**: delimiter/"spotlighting" (mark untrusted content, encode it), instruction hierarchy prompts, injection classifiers on inputs and tool results, output checks for secrets (DLP).
7. **Detection and response**: logging of tool calls, anomaly alerts, kill switch.
8. **Testing**: red-team suites with known injection payloads (hidden text, HTML comments, markdown image exfiltration), track attack success rate as a regression metric.

**Verification**: run adversarial evals before each release; confirm that with an injected payload the agent's tool calls stay inside the allowed plan and no egress occurs.

**Trade-off**: isolation reduces flexibility and autonomy; choose the level by data sensitivity.

**Sources:**
- [Prompt Injection in LLMs (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/prompt-injection-in-llms)
- [Defeating Prompt Injections by Design (CaMeL)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.18813)
- [Design Patterns for Securing LLM Agents against Prompt Injections](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08837)
- [Not what you've signed up for: Indirect Prompt Injection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.12173)
- [The lethal trifecta for AI agents (Simon Willison)](https://simonw.substack.com/p/the-lethal-trifecta-for-ai-agents)

<a id="q177"></a>
### 177. What is the difference between reactive and proactive agents?

**Answer:**

**Reactive agents** act only in response to an external trigger, typically a user message or a specific event: the classic chat assistant or a tool-calling agent invoked per request. They have no initiative between requests.

**Proactive agents** initiate behaviour themselves: monitoring signals, anticipating needs, pursuing goals over time, and acting or notifying without being asked (e.g. an agent that watches CI and opens fix PRs, a monitoring agent that investigates alerts, a personal assistant that flags a conflicting meeting).

| | Reactive | Proactive |
|---|---|---|
| Trigger | User request/event | Schedule, event streams, internal goals, anticipated needs |
| Autonomy | Low-medium | Medium-high |
| Lifetime | Per-request | Long-running/persistent |
| State | Session | Persistent memory, goal state |
| Risk | Bounded by user prompt | Higher: acting unasked, noise, unintended actions |
| Cost | Pay per request | Continuous background cost |

Classic AI terminology also places *deliberative/goal-based* agents (proactive) against *reflex* agents (reactive), and hybrid architectures combine both layers.

**Implementing proactivity**
- Triggers: cron/schedules, webhooks, message queues, file/DB change events, alert feeds.
- Goal/task management: backlog, priorities, persistent state and memory.
- Policies for *when to act vs ask* (confidence thresholds, notify-only vs act, approval for side effects).
- Rate limits, budgets, and quiet hours to avoid spam.

**Design cautions**: proactive agents need stronger guardrails, audit logs, easy opt-out, and clear scopes since actions occur without a human watching. Evaluate false-positive rate (unhelpful interruptions) as well as usefulness.

**Practical stance**: start reactive, add proactivity for narrow, well-understood, low-risk triggers, and keep humans in the loop for consequential actions.

**Sources:**
- [Building effective agents (Anthropic)](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents)
- [Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents (CoALA)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.02427)
- [LangGraph documentation (long-running, human-in-the-loop agents)](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/)

<a id="q178"></a>
### 178. How do you manage token consumption and cost in long-running agent workflows?

**Answer:**

Cost in agents is roughly `steps x (context length) x price`, and context is re-sent every step, so spending grows superlinearly with run length. Attack every factor.

**Reduce context per step**
- **Compaction/summarisation** at thresholds; clear stale tool results.
- **Truncate and paginate tool outputs**; return concise fields, offer detail on request.
- **Just-in-time retrieval** (grep/read ranges) instead of preloading whole files.
- **Sub-agents** to isolate verbose exploration.
- **Lean prompts and tool schemas**; load tools dynamically/tool search when there are many.
- Use **notes/scratchpad files** instead of carrying everything in history.

**Reduce cost per token**
- **Prompt caching**: keep a stable prefix (system prompt, tools, earlier turns) so cached input tokens are billed at a steep discount; avoid mutating early context.
- **Model routing/cascades**: small model for simple steps (classification, extraction, summarisation), large model for planning and hard reasoning (FrugalGPT idea).
- Batch APIs for non-interactive work.

**Reduce steps**
- Plan-and-execute, parallel tool calls, combined task-level tools, better tool descriptions to avoid retries, loop detection.
- Cache deterministic tool results and dedupe repeated calls.

**Controls**
- Per-task token/cost/step budgets with hard stops and graceful partial results.
- Cost attribution per trace, per user, per tool; dashboards and alerts.
- Right-size reasoning effort/thinking budgets by task difficulty.

**Verify**: track cost per successful task (not per call) alongside success rate, so optimisations do not silently lower quality; A/B test changes on the eval set.

**Pitfalls**: aggressive compaction losing key facts, cache-busting timestamps in the prompt prefix, cheap models causing more retries that cost more overall.

**Sources:**
- [How does context compaction work? (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/how-does-context-compaction-work)
- [How would you reduce the token consumption? (LinkedIn, Pallavi Shekhar)](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/pallavi-shekhar_ai-aiagents-machinelearning-activity-7439550125015994368-LTmE)
- [Effective context engineering for AI agents (Anthropic)](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents)
- [FrugalGPT: How to Use LLMs While Reducing Cost and Improving Performance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.05176)

<a id="q179"></a>
### 179. What is the human-in-the-loop pattern for agents, and when is it needed?

**Answer:**

**Human-in-the-loop (HITL)** inserts human review, approval, input or correction at defined points in an agent's workflow. The agent pauses, presents context and a proposed action, and resumes based on the human's response (approve, reject, edit, answer a question).

**When it is needed**
- **Irreversible or high-impact actions**: deleting data, payments, deployments, sending external emails, changing permissions.
- **Low confidence or ambiguity**: missing information, conflicting sources, multiple valid interpretations.
- **Regulated/high-stakes domains** (medical, legal, finance) with compliance requirements.
- **Untrusted content in play** (prompt injection risk): approval before exfiltration-capable actions.
- **Early in deployment** to build trust and collect labelled corrections.
- **Subjective judgment** (brand tone, design choices).

**Patterns**
- **Approval gate**: agent proposes action -> human approves/rejects/edits.
- **Plan approval**: human reviews the plan before execution (plan mode).
- **Clarification request**: agent asks questions when underspecified.
- **Escalation/hand-off**: to a human agent with full context transcript.
- **Review of output** (draft-then-send), and **on-the-loop** supervision (monitoring with the ability to interrupt) for lower-risk tasks.
- **Feedback capture**: corrections logged as eval data or memory.

**Implementation**: framework support for interrupts and persistent checkpoints (LangGraph `interrupt` + checkpointer, resume with the human's input), permission systems (allow/deny/ask rules in coding agents), async approval via Slack/email with timeouts and defaults.

**Trade-offs**: safety and quality vs latency and human effort. **Approval fatigue** makes humans rubber-stamp; mitigate by gating only risky actions, batching, showing clear diffs and risk context, and auto-approving safe classes.

**Sources:**
- [Building effective agents (Anthropic)](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents)
- [LangGraph human-in-the-loop documentation](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/)
- [Claude Code documentation (permissions)](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/claude-code/overview)
- [OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (Excessive Agency)](https://genai.owasp.org/llm-top-10/)

<a id="q180"></a>
### 180. How do you implement guardrails for AI agents to prevent harmful actions?

**Answer:**

Guardrails are layered controls that constrain what an agent can perceive, decide and do. No single layer is sufficient; combine them.

**Layers**
1. **Input guardrails**: prompt-injection/jailbreak classifiers, PII detection/redaction, topic and scope checks, rate limiting.
2. **Model-level**: system prompt policies, instruction hierarchy, safety-tuned models, moderation endpoints (e.g. Llama Guard-style classifiers).
3. **Tool/action guardrails (most important for agents)**
   - **Least privilege** and allowlists of tools per task; deny-by-default.
   - **Argument validation in code**: schemas, ranges, allowed domains/paths/tables, SQL parameterisation; block dangerous shell patterns.
   - **Permission tiers**: read-only auto; write requires approval; destructive blocked or two-person.
   - **Pre-/post-tool hooks** that inspect and veto calls deterministically.
   - **Spend/rate/step limits** and kill switch.
4. **Execution environment**: sandbox, read-only mounts, network allowlist, ephemeral credentials.
5. **Output guardrails**: schema validation, secret/PII scanning, groundedness/citation checks, toxicity/policy classifiers.
6. **Dynamic/programmable rails**: dialogue flows and policies (NeMo Guardrails), rule engines.
7. **Human oversight** for sensitive actions; audit logs.

**Principles**
- Prefer **deterministic enforcement** (code, permissions) over asking the LLM to behave.
- Use an LLM judge only for fuzzy policies, and measure its false positive/negative rates.
- Fail closed for high-risk paths, fail open with logging for low-risk ones.
- Keep latency in mind: run cheap checks first, run some in parallel.

**Test**: red-team suites, regression evals of blocked and allowed cases, monitor guardrail trigger rates in production.

**Pitfalls**: bypasses through paraphrase/encoding, over-blocking hurting UX, guardrails that only cover chat text but not tool calls.

**Sources:**
- [How do LLM guardrails work? (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/how-do-llm-guardrails-work)
- [NeMo Guardrails: A Toolkit for Controllable and Safe LLM Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.10501)
- [Llama Guard: LLM-based Input-Output Safeguard](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.06674)
- [OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications](https://genai.owasp.org/llm-top-10/)

<a id="q181"></a>
### 181. What is agent reflection, and how does it improve agent performance?

**Answer:**

**Reflection** is a pattern where an agent critiques its own output or trajectory and uses the critique to improve, either within the same task (iterate on a draft) or across attempts (learn from failure).

**Variants**
- **Self-Refine**: generate -> the same model gives feedback -> refine, loop for a few rounds; no training needed.
- **Reflexion**: after a failed attempt, the agent writes a *verbal reflection* ("I searched the wrong entity; next time verify X first") stored in episodic memory and included in the next attempt; showed gains on coding (HumanEval), ALFWorld and HotpotQA per the paper.
- **Generator-critic / evaluator-optimizer**: separate agents or prompts; the critic can use tools (run tests, check sources).
- **Reflection tokens / self-critique** (Self-RAG) and **process reflection** on plans.

**Why it helps**: catches errors the first pass missed, converts sparse failure signals into actionable guidance, and allows trial-and-error improvement without gradient updates.

**Key finding**: reflection works best with **external, grounded feedback** (unit tests, tool errors, retrieval evidence, compiler output). Pure intrinsic self-correction without external signal can fail or even degrade answers, because models often cannot reliably find their own errors.

**Implementation sketch**
```
draft = agent(task)
for i in range(N):
    fb = critic(task, draft, tool_feedback)   # tests, checks, rubric
    if fb.ok: break
    draft = agent(task, draft, fb.text)
```

**Trade-offs**: extra tokens and latency (multiple passes), diminishing returns after 1-3 rounds, risk of sycophantic self-approval or oscillation. Use a stronger or different model as critic, explicit rubrics, and a hard round cap.

**When to use**: tasks with verifiable quality criteria (code, SQL, structured extraction, writing with a rubric). Skip for simple latency-sensitive calls.

**Sources:**
- [Reflection Agent (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/reflection-agent)
- [Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.11366)
- [Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.17651)
- [Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01798)

<a id="q182"></a>
### 182. What is the difference between code-generating agents and tool-calling agents?

**Answer:**

**Tool-calling agents** emit structured calls (JSON) to predefined tools, one or a few per step; the runtime executes them. **Code-generating (code-as-action) agents** write executable code (usually Python) as their action; the runtime executes it in a sandbox and returns output. CodeAct and Hugging Face smolagents popularised this.

| | Tool-calling | Code-generating |
|---|---|---|
| Action format | JSON tool call | Program (loops, conditionals, variables) |
| Composition | One call per step (or parallel) | Many operations, control flow and intermediate variables in one step |
| Flexibility | Limited to defined tools | Can use any library, compute, transform data |
| Steps/tokens | More steps and round trips | Fewer steps; intermediate data stays in the interpreter, not the context |
| Reliability | Validated schemas, predictable | Runtime errors, harder to constrain |
| Safety | Permissions per tool | Needs strong sandboxing (arbitrary code) |
| Auditability | Easy to approve each call | Must review or restrict code |

**Advantages of code actions**: expressiveness (loops over 100 items in one step), data handling without flooding context, reuse of libraries, self-debugging from tracebacks; CodeAct reports higher success with fewer actions than JSON/text actions on tool-use benchmarks.

**Advantages of tool calling**: safer, simple to validate/approve, model APIs natively optimised for it, better for well-defined business operations and compliance.

**Hybrid**: expose tools as functions inside the code sandbox (tools become APIs); programmatic tool calling lets the model orchestrate many tool calls in code and only return the final result to context.

**Choose**: code agents for data analysis, math, multi-step transformations, coding tasks; tool-calling for constrained, auditable, side-effect-heavy operations. Always sandbox code execution (containers/microVMs, no ambient credentials, network limits, timeouts).

**Sources:**
- [Executable Code Actions Elicit Better LLM Agents (CodeAct)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.01030)
- [Hugging Face smolagents documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/smolagents/index)
- [Tool use with Claude (Anthropic docs)](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/tool-use/overview)

<a id="q183"></a>
### 183. How do you handle multi-modal inputs and outputs in agentic systems?

**Answer:**

**Inputs**
- Use a **natively multimodal model** (image, PDF, audio, sometimes video) so the agent can reason over screenshots, charts, scanned documents, diagrams or speech directly. Images are passed as base64/URL content blocks alongside text, in both user messages and **tool results** (e.g. a screenshot tool returning an image).
- **Pipelines** for non-native modalities: speech-to-text (Whisper-class ASR) for audio, OCR/layout parsers for scans, frame sampling plus captions/ASR for video. Trade-off: cheaper and inspectable but loses information (layout, tone, visual detail).
- **Decide per modality** whether to pass raw or preprocessed: e.g. render PDF pages as images for chart-heavy documents, extract text for text-heavy ones.

**Outputs**
- Text plus structured data as usual; **generated media** via tools (image generation, TTS, chart code executed in a sandbox producing PNG files).
- Agents typically *call* generators as tools rather than emitting pixels themselves; files are returned as artifacts (paths/URLs), with the model verifying them (e.g. viewing the rendered chart).
- Voice agents: streaming ASR -> LLM -> TTS pipeline, or end-to-end speech-to-speech models; handle barge-in and low latency (<~1 s response).

**Design considerations**
- **Cost/tokens**: images consume many tokens; resize/crop, use detail levels, and avoid re-sending images each step (drop or replace old images with text descriptions during compaction).
- **Grounding & verification**: agent looks at outputs (render, screenshot) in the loop to check its work.
- **Storage**: keep binaries out of context; pass references/IDs.
- **Safety**: images and audio can carry hidden prompt injection (text in images); apply the same trust rules; PII in images/faces; content moderation.
- **Evaluation**: modality-specific metrics (OCR accuracy, WER, chart QA) plus end-to-end task success.

**Pitfalls**: OCR errors cascading, hallucinated details in images, small text unreadable at low resolution, context bloat from images.

**Sources:**
- [Vision with Claude (Anthropic docs)](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/vision)
- [Computer use tool (Anthropic docs)](https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/agents-and-tools/tool-use/computer-use-tool)
- [Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision (Whisper)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.04356)
- [OpenAI Vision guide](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/images-vision)

<a id="q184"></a>
### 184. How do you implement state management in complex agent workflows?

**Answer:**

**State** is everything the workflow must remember between steps: messages, plan, intermediate results, retrieved docs, counters, user/session data, pending approvals.

**Core design**
- **Explicit, typed state schema** (TypedDict/Pydantic/dataclass) instead of an ever-growing chat log. Each node reads the fields it needs and returns partial updates.
- **Reducers/merge rules** define how concurrent or successive updates combine (append messages, overwrite score, union sets); essential for parallel branches.
- **Separate concerns**: *conversation* state (messages), *task* state (plan, artifacts), *control* state (step count, budget, status), *long-term* memory (cross-thread store).
- **Keep state lean**: hold references (IDs, file paths) to large artifacts, not raw blobs; expose only relevant fields to each LLM call (context engineering).

**Persistence**
- **Checkpointing** after every step (LangGraph checkpointers backed by SQLite/Postgres/Redis) keyed by `thread_id`, enabling: resume after crashes, human-in-the-loop interrupts, "time travel" and replay/debugging, branching.
- **Durable execution** engines (Temporal, Restate, Inngest) for long-running, retryable workflows with exactly-once semantics for side effects.
- **Cross-session memory** in a store namespaced by user.

**Reliability practices**
- Idempotent nodes and idempotency keys since steps can replay after failures.
- Versioned state schemas with migrations for in-flight runs.
- Concurrency control: one writer per thread, optimistic locking.
- Immutable event log (event sourcing) for audit and replay.
- TTL and cleanup; encryption and PII handling for stored state.

**Pitfalls**: state bloat (token and storage cost), untyped dict sprawl, non-serialisable objects in state, schema changes breaking resumes, hidden global variables.

**Sources:**
- [How does LangGraph work? (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/how-does-langgraph-work)
- [LangGraph documentation: state, checkpointers, persistence](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/)
- [Temporal documentation: durable execution](https://docs.temporal.io/)

<a id="q185"></a>
### 185. How do you build a customer support agent with escalation logic?

**Answer:**

**Architecture**
1. **Intake and routing**: classify intent (billing, technical, account, complaint), language, sentiment, customer tier; identify the customer via authenticated session.
2. **Knowledge**: RAG over help center, policies, past resolved tickets, with citations; product/status data.
3. **Tools**: read tools (order status, account info) and write tools (refund, address change, ticket update) with scoped auth, limits (e.g. refund < $X) and audit logs.
4. **Agent core**: tool-calling loop with a policy-laden system prompt; structured state (customer, issue, actions taken, confidence).
5. **Escalation module** and **handoff**.
6. **Guardrails**: PII masking, no unauthorised promises, tone, prompt injection defences (customer text is untrusted).

**Escalation triggers (combine rules and model signals)**
- **Explicit request** ("agent please").
- **Sentiment/frustration** thresholds or repeated failed resolution attempts (e.g. 2-3 loops without progress).
- **Low confidence / no grounded answer** (retrieval score low, model uncertainty, guardrail flag).
- **Policy/risk**: legal threats, safety, fraud, chargebacks, VIP or enterprise customers, high monetary value, regulated topics.
- **Capability gap**: needed tool missing or tool errors.
- **Loop/time limits**: turn count or session duration exceeded.

**Handoff quality**: pass a summary (issue, steps tried, customer data verified, sentiment, suggested next action) and the full transcript so the customer never repeats themselves; route to the right queue/skill group; tell the customer what happens next and expected wait; handle off-hours (ticket plus callback).

**Metrics**: containment/resolution rate, CSAT, escalation rate and precision (were escalations necessary?), false-negative escalations (should have escalated), average handle time, cost per resolution, policy violations.

**Improve**: mine escalated conversations to add knowledge/tools, and run offline evals with simulated customers (tau-bench style) including adversarial and angry personas.

**Sources:**
- [Building effective agents: customer support example (Anthropic)](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents)
- [tau-bench: A Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.12045)
- [LangGraph human-in-the-loop documentation](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/)

<a id="q186"></a>
### 186. What is agent orchestration, and how do you implement it?

**Answer:**

**Agent orchestration** is the coordination layer that decides which agent/model/tool runs when, with what context, how results are combined, and how failures, budgets and approvals are handled. It is the "control plane" of an agentic system.

**Patterns** (Anthropic's taxonomy plus multi-agent topologies)
- **Prompt chaining**: fixed sequence with gates.
- **Routing**: classify input, dispatch to a specialised handler/model.
- **Parallelisation**: sectioning (independent subtasks) or voting.
- **Orchestrator-workers**: an LLM plans subtasks dynamically and delegates.
- **Evaluator-optimizer**: generate/critique loop.
- **Hierarchical / supervisor** teams, **hand-off/swarm** (agents transfer control), **graph-based** flows.

**Implementation**
- **Code-first** (plain Python with async, explicit control): maximum transparency, good for simple flows.
- **Frameworks**: LangGraph (graph + state + checkpoints), OpenAI Agents SDK (hand-offs, guardrails), AutoGen, CrewAI, Claude Agent SDK (subagents), LlamaIndex workflows.
- **Durable workflow engines** (Temporal etc.) for reliability at scale.

**Core responsibilities**
- **Task decomposition and routing** logic (rules, classifier, LLM planner).
- **Context passing**: structured hand-off briefs, shared state.
- **Concurrency**: fan-out/fan-in with timeouts.
- **State and persistence**, retries, fallbacks and circuit breakers.
- **Budgets and limits** (steps, spend, spawn depth).
- **HITL gates** and permissions.
- **Observability**: end-to-end tracing across agents, per-step cost and latency.
- **Evaluation** of the orchestration itself (routing accuracy, end-to-end success).

**Guidance**: use the simplest pattern that works; deterministic routing when categories are known; model-driven orchestration when subtasks are unpredictable; avoid framework abstractions that hide prompts and make debugging hard.

**Sources:**
- [AI Orchestration (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/ai-orchestration)
- [Building effective agents (Anthropic)](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents)
- [LangGraph documentation](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/)
- [AutoGen: Enabling Next-Gen LLM Applications via Multi-Agent Conversation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.08155)

<a id="q187"></a>
### 187. What is Sakana Fugu, and how does it orchestrate a team of AI models?

**Answer:**

Note: this is a recent, niche topic. The details below follow the general design idea of multi-model orchestration as I understand it; consult the Sakana technical report (linked in the sources) for exact architecture, training details and benchmark numbers.

**Idea**: rather than relying on one frontier model, a **conductor/orchestrator** model coordinates a *team of diverse AI models* (different vendors, sizes, strengths), deciding which model handles which sub-problem, how to combine or refine their answers, and when to stop. It follows Sakana AI's broader research line on collective intelligence and evolutionary/inference-time approaches (for example adaptive branching tree search that lets multiple LLMs cooperate at inference time, AB-MCTS / TreeQuest).

**Typical mechanics of such systems**
- **Routing/assignment**: the orchestrator sees the task and (possibly partial) outputs, and selects the model that is likely best for the next step (coding, math, retrieval, critique).
- **Iterative refinement**: outputs from one model become inputs for another (draft -> critique -> repair), like mixture-of-agents.
- **Search over solution space**: explore many candidate solutions, re-allocate budget to promising branches (deeper) or fresh ideas (wider), using verifiers or scores.
- **Aggregation**: pick, vote or synthesise the final answer.
- **Cost/latency awareness**: cheap models for easy parts, expensive ones only when needed.

**Why it can beat any single model**: models have complementary strengths and errors; diversity plus verification yields better coverage (ensemble effect) - at higher inference cost.

**Trade-offs**: complexity, latency, cost, dependency on several providers, and evaluation difficulty; benefits depend on task verifiability and model diversity.

**Interview tip**: relate it to known ideas - mixture-of-agents, LLM routers/cascades, ensembles, and inference-time scaling - and stress trade-offs.

**Sources:**
- [Sakana Fugu - The Technical Report Explained (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/decoding-sakana-fugu)
- [Sakana AI research and blog](https://sakana.ai/)
- [Wider or Deeper? Scaling LLM Inference-Time Compute with Adaptive Branching Tree Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.04412)
- [Mixture-of-Agents Enhances Large Language Model Capabilities](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.04692)

<a id="q188"></a>
### 188. How do you build a code execution agent safely using sandboxed environments?

**Answer:**

Assume the model-generated code is **untrusted and possibly adversarial** (prompt injection, hallucination, or user intent). Safety comes from isolation and least privilege, not from asking the model to be careful.

**Isolation options (increasing strength)**
- Restricted interpreters / subprocess with limits: weak; not for untrusted code.
- **Containers** (Docker with seccomp, AppArmor, dropped capabilities, non-root, read-only rootfs): common but share the host kernel.
- **User-space kernels / microVMs** (gVisor, Firecracker, Kata): stronger isolation; used by hosted sandboxes (E2B, Modal, Daytona, cloud code-interpreter tools).
- **Serverless/WASM** runtimes for narrow workloads.

**Controls**
1. **No ambient credentials**: no cloud metadata endpoint, no host env secrets; inject short-lived, scoped tokens only if needed.
2. **Network**: default deny; allowlist egress (package mirror, specific APIs) to prevent exfiltration and abuse.
3. **Filesystem**: ephemeral workspace, minimal mounts, read-only where possible, no host paths.
4. **Resource limits**: CPU, memory, disk, process count, wall-clock timeout, output size caps (stop fork bombs, miners).
5. **Per-session/per-task fresh sandboxes**, destroyed afterwards; no state leaks between users.
6. **Dependency control**: pinned images, curated package mirror.
7. **Human approval** for actions with external effects; run dangerous commands only in sandbox.
8. **Logging and audit**: record code, stdout/stderr, network attempts; alert on anomalies.
9. **Output handling**: treat sandbox output as untrusted data returned to the model (injection) and cap size.

**Agent-side design**: return truncated stdout/stderr and tracebacks so the agent can self-debug; snapshot/restore for checkpoints; persistent workspace volume only if isolated per user; expose tools inside the sandbox via a narrow API rather than host access.

**Verification**: red-team the sandbox (escape attempts, egress tests, resource exhaustion) and monitor.

**Pitfalls**: mounting the Docker socket, running as root, sharing a kernel with multi-tenant untrusted code, leaving internet open, forgetting timeouts.

**Sources:**
- [Executable Code Actions Elicit Better LLM Agents (CodeAct)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.01030)
- [Firecracker: Lightweight Virtualization for Serverless Applications (NSDI '20)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/nsdi20/presentation/agache)
- [gVisor documentation](https://gvisor.dev/docs/)
- [OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications](https://genai.owasp.org/llm-top-10/)

<a id="q189"></a>
### 189. Your AI agent is stuck in an infinite loop. How do you detect and break the cycle?

**Answer:**

**Root causes**
- Tool returns the same unhelpful result or error and the model retries identically.
- No progress signal; the model cannot tell it failed (silent tool errors, empty results).
- Ambiguous or unreachable goal, missing stop criteria.
- Context truncation/compaction dropped the memory of previous attempts.
- Two agents delegating to each other or agreeing endlessly.
- Oscillating fixes (fix A breaks B, fix B breaks A).

**Detection**
- **Hard caps**: max iterations, wall-clock time, token/cost budget (the guaranteed backstop).
- **Repetition detection**: hash `(tool_name, normalised_args)`; flag when the same call occurs N times, or when the last K observations are identical/near-identical (embedding similarity).
- **Progress metrics**: no new files changed, no new information gained, plan checklist not advancing for N steps.
- **Cycle detection in state graphs** (repeated node/state sequences); recursion limits (e.g. LangGraph `recursion_limit`).
- Monitoring/alerts on step count and cost outliers.

**Breaking the cycle (escalating responses)**
1. Inject a corrective message: "You already tried X three times with the same result. Try a different approach or explain what is blocking you."
2. Change something: raise temperature slightly, remove/replace the failing tool, offer alternative tools, force a re-plan or reflection step.
3. Cache-and-refuse duplicate calls: return "duplicate call, result unchanged" instead of executing again.
4. Delegate to a stronger model or a fresh-context sub-agent with a summary.
5. Stop gracefully: return partial result plus status, or escalate to a human.

**Prevent**
- Clear success/failure criteria and an explicit `give_up`/`ask_for_help` tool.
- Informative tool errors and explicit "no results found" messages.
- Keep attempt history in state that survives compaction.
- Evals with looping scenarios as regression tests.

**Sources:**
- [Fix an infinite loop in an AI agent (LinkedIn, Pallavi Shekhar)](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/pallavi-shekhar_ai-aiagents-machinelearning-share-7440257380707364864-5Ycc)
- [AI Agent Loop (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/ai-agent-loop)
- [LangGraph documentation (recursion limit, persistence)](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/)
- [Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.13657)

<a id="q190"></a>
### 190. Your AI agent gets conflicting answers from different tools. How does it reconcile them?

**Answer:**

**Diagnose first**: why do sources disagree?
- Different **freshness** (cache vs live), **scope/definitions** (revenue net vs gross, time zones), **quality/reliability**, **bugs**, unit or format mismatches, partial data, or an injected/poisoned source.

**Reconciliation strategy (prioritised)**
1. **Source-of-truth hierarchy**: define authority per data type in the system prompt/config (billing DB > CRM cache > web search; official docs > forum). Prefer primary over secondary, authoritative over aggregated.
2. **Recency and provenance**: compare timestamps, versions, and "as of" dates; require tools to return metadata (source, updated_at, confidence).
3. **Normalise before comparing**: units, currencies, date formats, entity resolution (same customer?).
4. **Verify with a tiebreaker**: call a third independent tool, re-query, or run a deterministic check (recompute from raw data, run the code/test).
5. **Corroboration/voting** across independent sources, weighted by reliability (not just majority: correlated sources can share the same error).
6. **Explain and surface the conflict** when unresolved: present both values with sources and uncertainty rather than silently choosing; ask the user or escalate for high-stakes decisions.
7. **Fail safe**: for actions (refunds, deployments) do not act on unresolved conflicts.

**Implementation**
- Tools return structured results with provenance fields.
- A dedicated "reconcile" step (LLM or code) that outputs `{value, sources, confidence, conflict_notes}`.
- Log disagreements as data-quality issues to fix upstream (fix the root cause, e.g. cache invalidation).

**Pitfalls**: LLM picks the more fluent/confident-sounding answer, averages incompatible values, ignores timestamps, or treats an injected tool result as authoritative.

**Verify**: build evals with deliberately conflicting tool outputs and check the agent applies the hierarchy and flags uncertainty.

**Sources:**
- [Building effective agents (Anthropic)](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents)
- [Writing effective tools for agents (Anthropic)](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents)
- [Survey of hallucination in natural language generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.03629)

---

<a id="q191"></a>
### 191. Your AI agent burns too many tokens per task. How do you reduce token consumption?

**Answer:**

**First measure**: trace token usage per step and per component (system prompt, tool schemas, history, tool outputs, reasoning). Usually a few things dominate, typically **tool outputs** and the **re-sent history**.

**Prioritised fixes**
1. **Trim tool outputs** (often biggest win): truncate, paginate, return selected fields, summarise large results (e.g. via a cheap model), write big outputs to files and return a path plus preview.
2. **Compaction and clearing**: drop or summarise stale tool results and old turns; set a compaction threshold.
3. **Prompt caching**: stable prefix (system prompt, tools, docs) to cut input cost and latency; avoid volatile content (timestamps) early in the prompt.
4. **Just-in-time retrieval**: read targeted line ranges/grep instead of whole files; retrieve top-k chunks.
5. **Slim prompts and tools**: remove redundant instructions, merge overlapping tools, load tools dynamically/search (many-tool schemas can cost tens of thousands of tokens).
6. **Model routing**: cheap model for classification, extraction, summarisation and simple steps; big model for planning.
7. **Fewer steps**: better tool descriptions (fewer retries), parallel tool calls, batch operations, plan first, code execution to process data outside the context.
8. **Sub-agents** to keep verbose exploration out of the main context (but watch multi-agent overhead).
9. **Control reasoning budget**: lower thinking effort for easy tasks; cap output length; concise-answer instructions.
10. **Dedupe/caching of repeated tool calls** and memoisation of deterministic results.

**Verify**: track cost per *successful* task, and run the eval set before/after to ensure quality holds. Set budgets and alerts.

**Trade-offs and pitfalls**: over-aggressive truncation removes crucial detail causing retries (net cost up); compaction invalidates cache; cheap model errors increase loops.

**Sources:**
- [How would you reduce the token consumption? (LinkedIn, Pallavi Shekhar)](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/pallavi-shekhar_ai-aiagents-machinelearning-activity-7439550125015994368-LTmE)
- [How does context compaction work? (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/how-does-context-compaction-work)
- [Effective context engineering for AI agents (Anthropic)](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents)
- [Prompt caching (Anthropic docs)](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/prompt-caching)

<a id="q192"></a>
### 192. Your AI agent keeps exceeding its budget per task. How do you enforce budget limits?

**Answer:**

**Diagnose**: budget overruns come from unbounded loops, long contexts re-sent each step, expensive models used everywhere, retries, over-eager sub-agent spawning, tool costs (paid APIs), and no metering at all.

**Enforcement design: budgets must be enforced in code, outside the model**
1. **Define budgets** per task/user/tenant: max steps, max tokens (input+output), max dollars, wall-clock time, max tool calls per tool, max sub-agents/depth.
2. **Meter every call**: compute cost from provider usage fields after each LLM/tool call (`spent += tokens * price + tool_cost`), stored in run state.
3. **Check before each step** (pre-flight estimate) and after:
   ```python
   if state.spent + est_next_step > budget: return finalize_partial(state)
   ```
4. **Graduated response**: at 50-80% inform the model ("30% budget remaining, prioritise finishing"), switch to cheaper model/lower reasoning effort, compact context, disable expensive tools; at 100% hard-stop with a partial answer or escalation.
5. **Gateway-level limits**: enforce quotas/rate limits in an LLM gateway/proxy (per API key, per user) so bugs in agent code cannot bypass them.
6. **Reservations for multi-agent/parallel work**: allocate sub-budgets to children; parent tracks aggregate.
7. **Durable accounting**: persist spend in the checkpointed state so resumes do not reset counters.

**Reduce spend at the source**: prompt caching, compaction, trimmed tool outputs, model routing, plan-first, dedupe calls.

**Observability**: dashboards for cost per task percentile (p95/p99 outliers), alerts, per-tool cost attribution, kill switch for runaway runs.

**Verify**: chaos tests that induce loops or huge outputs and confirm the stop; check the agent returns useful partial output when cut off.

**Pitfalls**: relying on the prompt ("stay under budget") alone, counting only output tokens, ignoring cached-token pricing and tool fees, hard stop mid-side-effect leaving inconsistent state (finish or roll back cleanly).

**Sources:**
- [AI Agent Loop (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/ai-agent-loop)
- [How would you reduce the token consumption? (LinkedIn, Pallavi Shekhar)](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/pallavi-shekhar_ai-aiagents-machinelearning-activity-7439550125015994368-LTmE)
- [FrugalGPT: How to Use LLMs While Reducing Cost and Improving Performance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.05176)
- [Building effective agents (Anthropic)](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents)

<a id="q193"></a>
### 193. Your AI agent hallucinates tool capabilities and passes wrong inputs. How do you fix it?

**Answer:**

**Symptoms**: calls non-existent tools or parameters, assumes a tool can do something it cannot, invents IDs, wrong types/formats, claims to have performed an action it did not.

**Root causes**
- Vague or overlapping tool descriptions; missing parameter documentation/formats.
- Too many tools, or names similar to well-known APIs.
- No validation, so bad calls silently "work" or return unhelpful errors.
- Missing information (the model fills gaps by guessing, e.g. UUIDs).
- Stale prompt/tool list, weak model, or overly long context.

**Fixes (prioritised)**
1. **Strict schemas**: JSON Schema with types, enums, required fields, patterns, min/max; use provider strict/structured mode (constrained decoding) so calls are syntactically valid and only known tools are callable.
2. **Better descriptions**: what it does, what it does *not* do, when to use it, parameter formats with examples, side effects.
3. **Validate in code, return teaching errors**: reject unknown tools/params; respond "`order_id` must match `ORD-\d{6}`; use `search_orders` to find it". Allow a bounded self-correction retry.
4. **Remove ambiguity**: fewer, non-overlapping tools; replace opaque IDs with lookup tools or names that the tool resolves internally.
5. **Grounding**: give the agent a way to *discover* facts (`list_*`, `search_*`) rather than guess; instruct "never invent identifiers; ask or look up".
6. **Verification of claims**: confirm action results from tool outputs; final answers must cite tool results; check state after write actions.
7. **Few-shot examples** of correct calls, including a negative example.
8. **Model choice**: stronger tool-use models or fine-tuning on tool traces (Gorilla-style) if failures persist.
9. **Dynamic tool exposure**: present only relevant tools per step.

**Measure**: eval set for tool-call accuracy (tool selection, argument exact/semantic match, hallucinated-call rate); review failing transcripts; track error rates in production.

**Sources:**
- [How does Function Calling work in LLMs? (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/how-does-function-calling-work-in-llms)
- [Writing effective tools for agents (Anthropic)](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents)
- [Gorilla: Large Language Model Connected with Massive APIs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.15334)
- [Structured Outputs guide (OpenAI docs)](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/structured-outputs)

<a id="q194"></a>
### 194. Your AI agent deleted a production database. How do you prevent irreversible actions?

**Answer:**

**Root cause analysis**: the agent had credentials and permission to perform a destructive action, no approval gate, no environment separation (prod reachable from a dev/agent context), and no backups or recovery path. The LLM's mistake (or an injection) was the trigger; the design flaw was excessive agency.

**Prevention (defence in depth)**
1. **Least privilege**: agent credentials are read-only by default; separate write roles; no DDL/DROP rights ever for the agent; scoped per task; short-lived tokens. Separate prod from dev/staging credentials and networks so the agent cannot even reach prod unless required.
2. **Action classification**: tag tools as read / reversible write / irreversible. Irreversible ones require **human approval** (showing exact command and target), or are simply not exposed (route via a ticket/runbook).
3. **Deterministic guards, not prompts**: policy layer or hooks that block patterns (`DROP`, `DELETE` without `WHERE`, `rm -rf`, `TRUNCATE`) and enforce row-count limits; require a `dry_run` first and show the impact; run against a transaction/preview.
4. **Reversibility by design**: soft deletes, versioned records, snapshots/backups before destructive operations, point-in-time recovery, object-store versioning; test restores regularly.
5. **Sandbox first**: execute plans against a clone/staging; promote after verification.
6. **Two-person/two-key rule** for prod changes; change windows; rate limits on destructive calls.
7. **Idempotency, audit logs, alerting, kill switch**; anomaly detection on mass deletes.
8. **Prompt-level**: explicit rules ("never run destructive commands without confirmation") help but are the weakest layer.
9. **Injection defences**, since hostile content may induce destructive calls.

**Incident response**: stop the agent, restore from backup/PITR, post-mortem, add regression eval and new controls.

**Verify**: red-team scenarios ("clean up old data" ambiguous request), confirm blocks and approvals work; test backup restore times.

**Sources:**
- [How do LLM guardrails work? (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/how-do-llm-guardrails-work)
- [OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (Excessive Agency)](https://genai.owasp.org/llm-top-10/)
- [Claude Code documentation (permissions and hooks)](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/claude-code/overview)
- [Building effective agents (Anthropic)](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents)
