<a id="q459"></a>
### 459. How do you handle video understanding with AI?

**Answer:**

Video = images over time, so the challenge is capturing temporal information within a limited token budget.

**Pipeline**
1. **Sample frames**: uniform (e.g. 1 fps or N=8-64 frames), or adaptive (scene-change/shot detection, keyframes, query-aware selection). Long videos are the main pain point.
2. **Encode**: per-frame ViT/CLIP/SigLIP features, or a video encoder with spatio-temporal patches (VideoMAE, InternVideo, ViViT).
3. **Reduce tokens**: pooling over space/time, Q-Former/resampler per frame, token merging, so 64 frames do not become 40k tokens.
4. **Temporal modelling**: add temporal position embeddings (or timestamps in text), then feed to an LLM (Video-LLaVA, Video-ChatGPT, Qwen2-VL with multimodal RoPE, Gemini 1.5 with a very long context).
5. **Add audio**: ASR transcript with timestamps (Whisper) plus optional audio-event tags. Transcripts often carry most semantics.
6. **Task heads**: captioning, QA, temporal grounding ("when does X happen?"), action recognition, summarisation, event detection.

**Long video strategies**
- Hierarchical: caption clips -> summarise summaries.
- **RAG over video**: index clip captions/transcripts/frame embeddings, retrieve relevant segments for a question.
- Streaming with memory banks for live feeds.

**Pitfalls**: missing fast events with sparse sampling, hallucinated temporal order, cost explosion, language-prior shortcuts; evaluate with Video-MME, MVBench, EgoSchema and needle-in-a-video tests.

**Practical**: start with frame sampling + transcript + a hosted long-context VLM; move to retrieval or fine-tuned models when scale or accuracy demands.

**Sources:**
- [Video-LLaVA: Learning United Visual Representation by Alignment Before Projection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.10122)
- [Video-ChatGPT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05424)
- [Gemini 1.5 technical report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.05530)
- [Video-MME benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.21075)

<a id="q460"></a>
### 460. What is visual question answering (VQA)?

**Answer:**

**VQA** is the task: given an image (or video) and a natural-language question, produce an answer ("What colour is the bus?" -> "red"). It requires perception, language understanding, and often reasoning or world knowledge.

**Variants**: open-ended vs multiple choice; knowledge-based (OK-VQA); text-in-image (TextVQA, DocVQA); chart/diagram (ChartQA, AI2D); visual commonsense (VCR); video QA; medical VQA.

**Approaches over time**
- *Classic*: CNN image features + LSTM question encoding, fused (concatenation, attention) and classified over a fixed answer vocabulary.
- *Pretrained VL transformers*: ViLBERT, LXMERT, UNITER, OSCAR - joint encoders fine-tuned on VQA.
- *Generative VLMs*: BLIP-2, LLaVA, Qwen-VL, GPT-4o, Claude - treat VQA as image-conditioned text generation, zero-shot or instruction-tuned; can explain their answers.

**Evaluation**: VQA accuracy (answer agrees with at least 3 of 10 human annotators), exact match, ANLS for text answers, LLM-as-judge for open-ended.

**Known issues**
- **Language priors**: answering "yes" or "2" without looking. VQAv2 was built with complementary image pairs to counter this.
- Weakness at counting, spatial relations, small text, negation.
- Hallucination: confident wrong answers; mitigate with grounding (ask for boxes/evidence), higher resolution, abstention training.

**Practical**: use structured prompts, ask for concise answers or JSON, and evaluate on your domain's images.

**Sources:**
- [VQA: Visual Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/1505.00468)
- [Making the V in VQA Matter (VQAv2)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1612.00837)
- [BLIP-2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.12597)
- [Multimodal AI - Outcome School](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/multimodal-ai)

<a id="q461"></a>
### 461. What is document understanding, and how do models parse documents with layouts?

**Answer:**

**Document understanding** (Document AI) extracts structured information and answers questions from documents such as PDFs, scans, invoices, forms, contracts, slides, where meaning depends on **text + layout + visuals** (tables, headers, columns, figures, stamps).

**Approaches**
1. **OCR + layout pipeline**: OCR (Tesseract, PaddleOCR, cloud OCR) -> layout detection (headers, paragraphs, tables, figures) -> table structure recognition -> reading-order reconstruction -> text/Markdown -> LLM. Modular, cheap, debuggable, but error-propagating.
2. **Layout-aware transformers**: LayoutLM/LayoutLMv3 take tokens + their 2D bounding boxes (+ image patches) so attention can use spatial position; fine-tuned for key-value extraction, classification.
3. **OCR-free end-to-end**: Donut, Pix2Struct, Nougat (academic PDF to Markdown/LaTeX) map the page image directly to structured text.
4. **General VLMs**: GPT-4o, Claude, Gemini, Qwen2-VL read pages as images and answer or output JSON; strongest flexibility, higher cost, page-length limits.
5. **Retrieval over page images**: ColPali for RAG on visually rich documents.

**Design choices**
- Native digital PDFs: extract text/coordinates directly (PyMuPDF, pdfplumber) - more accurate than OCR.
- Tables: output as HTML/Markdown; verify totals.
- Output constrained to JSON schema, with field-level confidence and validation rules (sums, dates, IDs).
- Human-in-the-loop for low-confidence fields.

**Metrics**: ANLS, field-level F1, table TEDS, edit distance. **Pitfalls**: multi-column reading order, rotated pages, handwriting, low-DPI scans, and multi-page context.

**Sources:**
- [LayoutLMv3: Pre-training for Document AI with Unified Text and Image Masking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.08387)
- [OCR-free Document Understanding Transformer (Donut)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.15664)
- [Nougat: Neural Optical Understanding for Academic Documents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.13418)
- [ColPali](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.01449)

<a id="q462"></a>
### 462. How do you fine-tune a vision-language model?

**Answer:**

**When**: prompting/RAG fails on domain-specific visuals (medical, industrial, forms), need a strict output format, or want a smaller cheaper model matching a large one.

**Steps**
1. **Data**: (image, instruction, response) triples. Quality over quantity: hundreds to tens of thousands of clean examples often suffice for LoRA. Sources: human labels, distillation from a stronger VLM (verify!), synthetic augmentation. Include diverse prompts, negative/unanswerable cases, and keep a general-data mix to avoid forgetting.
2. **Pick the base**: Qwen2-VL, InternVL, Llama 3.2 Vision, PaliGemma, Idefics, LLaVA - match licence and resolution needs.
3. **What to train**
   - Projector only (alignment) - cheapest, for new visual domains with a good LLM.
   - **LoRA/QLoRA on the LLM** (plus projector) - the standard, memory-friendly choice.
   - Unfreeze the vision encoder (lower LR, e.g. 10x smaller) when domain images differ greatly (X-ray, satellite).
   - Full fine-tuning only with large data and compute.
4. **Training setup**: loss on response tokens only (mask prompt/image tokens), bf16, gradient checkpointing, low LR (1e-5 to 2e-4 for LoRA), packing, correct image preprocessing and chat template (Hugging Face TRL, LLaMA-Factory, Axolotl, Unsloth).
5. **Preference tuning (optional)**: DPO with hallucination-focused pairs (RLHF-V, LLaVA-RLHF) to improve faithfulness.
6. **Evaluate**: held-out domain set + general benchmarks (MMMU, POPE) to check regression.

**Pitfalls**: catastrophic forgetting, resolution mismatch between training and serving, label noise, overfitting to templates, leaking test images.

**Sources:**
- [LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685)
- [QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14314)
- [Hugging Face TRL: fine-tuning vision-language models](https://huggingface.co/docs/trl/index)
- [Aligning Large Multimodal Models with Factually Augmented RLHF (LLaVA-RLHF)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.14525)

<a id="q463"></a>
### 463. What are the latency and cost considerations for multi-modal AI in production?

**Answer:**

**Cost drivers**
- **Image tokens**: an image costs hundreds to thousands of input tokens depending on resolution/tiling (APIs typically bill by tile or pixel area). Video multiplies by frame count.
- **Audio**: billed per minute/second or audio tokens; real-time S2S is usually pricier than text.
- **Generation**: images/video priced per output; diffusion GPU-seconds scale with steps and resolution.
- Egress/storage of media, OCR/pre-processing compute.

**Latency drivers**
- Vision encoder forward pass (per image, possibly per tile).
- **Prefill** of many visual tokens dominates TTFT; decode speed is unaffected by images except through a larger KV cache.
- Upload/download time of large images; fetching by URL adds hops.
- Diffusion: steps x network call time.

**Optimisation levers**
- **Right-size resolution**: downscale where detail is unnecessary; crop regions of interest; use "low detail" modes for classification.
- **Cascade/routing**: cheap classifier, OCR or small VLM first; escalate to a frontier VLM only when needed.
- **Cache**: content-hash images to cache embeddings/answers; use prompt caching when the same image/document is queried repeatedly.
- **Token compression**: pooling, resamplers, fewer frames with smart selection.
- **Batching and serving stack**: vLLM with multimodal support and continuous batching, prefix caching for the shared image prefix, quantisation (FP8/INT4), encoder batching.
- **Async/offload**: process non-interactive jobs in batch APIs at discounts.
- Compress images (JPEG quality), avoid resending base64 every turn in multi-turn chats.
- Diffusion: fewer steps (LCM, distillation), lower res + upscaler, smaller model.

**Practice**: track cost per successful task, p95 latency by stage, tokens per image, and set budgets/alerts.

**Sources:**
- [Anthropic vision documentation (image token cost and sizing)](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/vision)
- [OpenAI Images and vision guide](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/images-vision)
- [vLLM documentation](https://docs.vllm.ai/)
- [Multimodal AI - Outcome School](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/multimodal-ai)

<a id="q464"></a>
### 464. How do you handle multi-modal content moderation?

**Answer:**

**Goal**: detect policy-violating content (sexual content, violence, hate, self-harm, CSAM, weapons, PII, misinformation, copyright) across text, images, audio and video, including combinations where each alone is benign (e.g. a meme: innocuous image + innocuous caption = hateful).

**Layered architecture**
1. **Hash matching** for known illegal content (PhotoDNA, PDQ, NCMEC hashes) - mandatory and cheap; CSAM has legal reporting duties.
2. **Fast classifiers per modality**: NSFW/violence image classifiers, toxicity text classifiers, audio ASR + text moderation, OCR of text within images.
3. **Multimodal models**: VLM or dedicated safety models (Llama Guard 3 Vision, OpenAI omni-moderation, Google Cloud Vision SafeSearch, Azure Content Safety) to judge combined context and memes; policy given in the prompt with structured output (category, severity, rationale).
4. **Video**: sample frames + audio transcript, shot detection; escalate suspicious segments.
5. **Routing and thresholds**: auto-allow, auto-block, or human review for the grey band; per-category thresholds and regional policy variants.
6. **Human review** with tooling, wellbeing support, appeals and feedback into training data.

**Challenges**
- Context and culture dependence (see cross-cultural moderation), satire, news vs glorification.
- **Adversarial evasion**: text in images, noise perturbations, cropping, emoji substitution, jailbreak text inside images (visual prompt injection).
- Scale/latency: cascade cheap-to-expensive; real-time streaming moderation.
- False positives on medical/art content; false negatives on new harms.

**Metrics**: precision/recall per category, review-queue rate, time-to-action, appeal overturn rate.

**Sources:**
- [Llama Guard: LLM-based Input-Output Safeguard for Human-AI Conversations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.06674)
- [OpenAI Moderation guide](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/moderation)
- [The Hateful Memes Challenge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.04790)
- [Multimodal AI - Outcome School](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/multimodal-ai)

---

<a id="q465"></a>
### 465. What is text-to-video generation, and what are the current state-of-the-art approaches?

**Answer:**

**Text-to-video (T2V)** generates a video clip from a text prompt (and optionally an image or video for conditioning).

**Core techniques**
- **Video diffusion**: extend image diffusion with temporal modelling. Early: Make-A-Video, Imagen Video (cascaded spatial and temporal super-resolution), Video LDM / Stable Video Diffusion (temporal layers inserted into a pretrained image U-Net).
- **Diffusion Transformers (DiT) on spatio-temporal patches**: encode video with a 3D VAE into a compressed latent, cut into "spacetime patches", and denoise with a transformer. This is the design described for OpenAI's Sora and used in open models such as CogVideoX, HunyuanVideo, Wan and Mochi; Veo and Kling are strong proprietary systems (their internals are not fully public).
- **Autoregressive / token-based**: VideoPoet, CogVideo - predict discrete video tokens with an LLM-style transformer.
- **Flow matching / rectified flow** replacing classic diffusion for faster, more stable training.

**Conditioning**: text via T5/CLIP/LLM encoders; image-to-video, first/last-frame, camera control, motion/pose/depth control (ControlNet-style), audio-synchronised generation in newer systems.

**Challenges**: temporal consistency, physics and object permanence, long durations, compute (video training and sampling are extremely expensive), prompt adherence for multi-step actions, evaluation (VBench, FVD, human preference), and safety (deepfakes, provenance watermarking/C2PA).

**Efficiency**: latent 3D VAEs, step distillation, cascaded generation (low-res, then upsample and frame-interpolate), sparse/windowed attention.

The state of the art changes month to month; describe categories and verify current leaders before quoting.

**Sources:**
- [Video generation models as world simulators (OpenAI Sora technical report)](https://openai.com/index/video-generation-models-as-world-simulators/)
- [Stable Video Diffusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.15127)
- [Imagen Video: High Definition Video Generation with Diffusion Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.02303)
- [Scalable Diffusion Models with Transformers (DiT)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.09748)
- [CogVideoX: Text-to-Video Diffusion Models with an Expert Transformer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.06072)

<a id="q466"></a>
### 466. Explain Multimodal Fusion Techniques: Early Fusion vs Late Fusion.

**Answer:**

**Fusion** = combining information from several modalities. The key question is *when* in the network.

**Early fusion**
- Combine modalities at the input or low-level feature stage (concatenate raw features/tokens, or feed all modality tokens into one shared transformer from the first layer).
- Pros: model learns fine cross-modal interactions (lip movement + sound, text referring to image regions); best joint reasoning.
- Cons: needs aligned, large paired data; modalities have different sampling rates/scales; a missing modality breaks the input; expensive; one noisy modality can hurt.
- Examples: Chameleon, Gemini-style native models, LLaVA concatenating image tokens with text tokens (fusion in the LLM's self-attention).

**Late fusion**
- Each modality processed by its own model to a prediction or high-level embedding; results combined at the end (averaging, weighted voting, concatenation + small MLP, stacking).
- Pros: modular, can use best unimodal pretrained models, handles missing modalities gracefully, easy to train and debug, parallelisable.
- Cons: misses low-level cross-modal correlations; interaction only at decision level.
- Examples: CLIP dual encoders (similarity at the end), ensembling ASR and video classifiers, hybrid search score fusion.

**Intermediate / hybrid fusion**: modality-specific encoders followed by cross-attention or bottleneck layers (Flamingo gated cross-attention, BLIP-2 Q-Former, Perceiver, "attention bottlenecks").

**Choosing**: small data, missing modalities, or need for interpretability -> late fusion; strong cross-modal reasoning and large data -> early/intermediate fusion. Tips: modality dropout during training for robustness, balance losses to avoid one modality dominating.

**Sources:**
- [Multimodal AI - Outcome School](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/multimodal-ai)
- [Multimodal Machine Learning: A Survey and Taxonomy](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.09406)
- [Flamingo](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.14198)
- [Chameleon](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.09818)

<a id="q467"></a>
### 467. Your vision-language model generates factually incorrect image descriptions. How do you fix it?

**Answer:**

**Diagnose first**: measure the hallucination type and rate. Categories: object (nonexistent items), attribute (wrong colour/count), relation (spatial/action), and OCR errors. Use POPE, CHAIR, HallusionBench plus a domain golden set; check whether errors correlate with resolution, image type, or long outputs.

**Root causes**
- Strong **language priors** in the LLM overriding visual evidence; co-occurrence bias ("kitchen -> microwave").
- Low resolution or a lossy connector (Q-Former compression, 336px encoder).
- Noisy or hallucinated training captions (synthetic captions from other models).
- Instruction data that rewards long, detailed captions (encourages inventing detail).
- Decoding that drifts as text length grows (visual attention decays).

**Fixes, in priority order**
1. **Prompting and output constraints**: ask for only what is visible, allow "cannot tell", shorter answers, structured output; lower temperature.
2. **Increase visual fidelity**: higher resolution/tiling, better encoder (SigLIP, fine-tuned), OCR tool for text.
3. **Decoding-time mitigation**: visual contrastive decoding (VCD), OPERA (over-trust penalty) - no retraining, some cost.
4. **Grounding**: have the model output boxes/regions or evidence and verify with an object detector; a verifier VLM/second pass checks each claim (self-consistency, CoVe-style).
5. **Data**: clean captions, add negative/unanswerable samples, remove hallucination-prone synthetic data.
6. **Preference tuning**: DPO/RLHF on hallucinated vs faithful pairs (RLHF-V, LLaVA-RLHF, LURE post-hoc correction).
7. **Retrieval/tool use**: external detectors, OCR, metadata for facts not derivable from pixels.

**Verify**: re-run POPE/CHAIR and domain eval, check for regression in helpfulness/detail, monitor in production with sampled human review.

**Sources:**
- [Evaluating Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models (POPE)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.10355)
- [Mitigating Object Hallucinations via Visual Contrastive Decoding (VCD)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.16922)
- [OPERA: Alleviating Hallucination in Multi-Modal LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.17911)
- [RLHF-V: Towards Trustworthy MLLMs via Behavior Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.00849)
- [Hallucination of Multimodal Large Language Models: A Survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.18930)

---

<a id="q468"></a>
### 468. Your VLM answers single-image questions but fails on multi-page documents. How do you fix it?

**Answer:**

**Root causes**
- **Context/token budget**: N pages x thousands of tokens exceeds the window, or the pipeline silently downsamples pages, killing legibility.
- **Training distribution**: most VLM data is single-image; the model was never taught cross-page reasoning or page references.
- **Attention dilution / lost in the middle**: the answer page is buried among many pages.
- Missing page boundaries or ordering, no page indices in the prompt.
- Cross-page structures (tables spanning pages, references "see page 12") are not resolved.

**Fixes**
1. **Retrieve, do not stuff**: index pages (OCR text + page-image embeddings, e.g. ColPali) and send only the top-k relevant pages (k = 2-5) to the VLM, with page numbers. Usually the biggest win.
2. **Hierarchical/map-reduce**: per-page extraction or summary (parallelisable), then a reasoning pass over structured page outputs with citations; multi-hop questions via iterative retrieval.
3. **Structured preprocessing**: parse to Markdown with layout, keep page markers ("[Page 7]"), stitch tables across page breaks, build a table of contents/section map.
4. **Prompting**: label pages, ask the model to first identify relevant pages then answer, and require page citations.
5. **Model choice**: long-context VLMs (Gemini 1.5+, Qwen2-VL with dynamic res) or fine-tune on multi-page datasets (MP-DocVQA, SlideVQA) with LoRA.
6. **Resolution management**: adaptive per-page resolution; crop to regions of interest after page-level localisation.
7. **Fallback tools**: text-layer extraction for digital PDFs to avoid image tokens.

**Verify**: measure page-level retrieval recall, answer accuracy stratified by document length and answer-page position, plus citation correctness; check cost/latency.

**Sources:**
- [Hierarchical multimodal pre-training for Document VQA on multi-page documents (MP-DocVQA)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.05935)
- [ColPali](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.01449)
- [Lost in the Middle](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172)
- [SlideVQA: A Dataset for Document Visual Question Answering on Multiple Images](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.04883)

---

<a id="q469"></a>
### 469. Your multimodal LLM ignores the image and generates descriptions from text alone. How do you fix it?

**Answer:**

This is **modality/visual-neglect** (language-prior dominance): the model finds text cues sufficient (or easier) and under-uses visual tokens.

**Diagnose**
- **Blank/shuffled image test**: if answers barely change when the image is replaced by a blank or another image, the image is ignored.
- Inspect attention/gradient contribution of image tokens; check if image embeddings have very different norm/scale from text embeddings.
- Verify the plumbing: is the image actually passed, are `<image>` placeholders correct, correct preprocessing (normalisation, RGB, resolution), correct chat template, image tokens not truncated by max length, batching order bug?

**Root causes**
- Bug or truncation of image tokens (most common in practice).
- Alignment stage too short or projector undertrained.
- Training data where text alone predicts the answer (captions leak information in the prompt; language shortcuts).
- LLM overwhelms weak vision signal; long text history.
- Vision encoder frozen and mismatched to the domain.

**Fixes**
1. Fix pipeline bugs; log token counts per sample.
2. **Data**: add samples requiring the image (counterfactual/complementary pairs, questions whose answer flips with the image), remove text-leaking prompts, add hard negatives.
3. **Training**: longer/better alignment stage, unfreeze the projector (and encoder with low LR), modality dropout of text hints, contrastive image-text auxiliary loss, higher-res encoder.
4. **Architecture**: more visual tokens or place image tokens close to the query, cross-attention layers that force reliance.
5. **Decoding**: visual contrastive decoding to penalise outputs that persist without the image.
6. **Prompting**: instruct the model to describe first what is visible, then answer.

**Verify** with blank-image ablation gap and POPE/MMBench.

**Sources:**
- [Eyes Wide Shut? Exploring the Visual Shortcomings of Multimodal LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.06209)
- [Cambrian-1: A Fully Open, Vision-Centric Exploration of Multimodal LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.16860)
- [Mitigating Object Hallucinations via Visual Contrastive Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.16922)
- [Improved Baselines with Visual Instruction Tuning (LLaVA-1.5)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.03744)

---

<a id="q470"></a>
### 470. Your diffusion model ignores precise control requirements in text prompts. How do you improve controllability?

**Answer:**

**Why it happens**: text encoders (CLIP) give a coarse, bag-of-concepts embedding; cross-attention binds attributes poorly ("red cube left of blue sphere"); counts, positions, and exact layouts are hard to express in language; training captions are vague.

**Solutions from lightest to heaviest**
1. **Prompt engineering / better text encoders**: detailed prompts, use models with T5 or LLM text encoders (SD3, Flux), or LLM-based prompt rewriting; prompt weighting; DALL-E 3-style long synthetic captions in training.
2. **Guidance tuning**: raise CFG scale moderately, negative prompts, separate guidance for attributes.
3. **Spatial conditioning adapters**: **ControlNet** (edges, depth, pose, segmentation, scribbles) or **T2I-Adapter** copy/attach a trainable branch to give pixel-level structure control; **GLIGEN** and layout-to-image for bounding-box grounding; regional prompting.
4. **Subject/style conditioning**: **IP-Adapter** (image prompt), DreamBooth/LoRA for specific identity or style, textual inversion.
5. **Attention manipulation (training-free)**: Attend-and-Excite (ensures each object token gets attention), Prompt-to-Prompt for edits, attention masks per region.
6. **Image-to-image / inpainting** for iterative editing (SDEdit, InstructPix2Pix), multi-pass composition: layout first, then refine.
7. **Fine-tune** on your domain with precise captions, or on compositional data with counts/positions; RL/reward tuning (DPO for diffusion, reward models for prompt adherence).
8. **Planning with an LLM**: LLM produces layout boxes, then a layout-conditioned diffusion generates.

**Verify**: GenEval / T2I-CompBench, detector-based checks (count, position), CLIPScore, and human eval.

**Sources:**
- [Adding Conditional Control to Text-to-Image Diffusion Models (ControlNet)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.05543)
- [IP-Adapter: Text Compatible Image Prompt Adapter](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.06721)
- [GLIGEN: Open-Set Grounded Text-to-Image Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.07093)
- [Attend-and-Excite: Attention-Based Semantic Guidance for T2I Diffusion Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.13826)
- [Diffusion Models - Outcome School](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/diffusion-models)

<a id="q471"></a>
### 471. Your diffusion model generates sharp but repetitive images. How do you balance quality vs diversity?

**Answer:**

**Diagnosis**: sharp but repetitive = **mode collapse-like low diversity**, typically from over-strong guidance or distilled/over-tuned models trading diversity for fidelity.

**Common causes**
- **CFG scale too high** (e.g. >10): pushes samples towards high-likelihood modes; saturation and near-identical compositions.
- Distillation (LCM, Turbo, few-step models) and adversarial objectives reduce diversity.
- Aggressive aesthetic fine-tuning or LoRA/DreamBooth overfitting, small fine-tuning set, too many steps.
- Deterministic samplers (DDIM, eta=0) with the same seed/initial noise; low-entropy prompts.
- Reward/RL tuning that over-optimises a narrow reward.
- Duplicated training data (memorisation).

**Fixes**
1. **Lower CFG** (4-7), or use guidance schedules (strong mid-steps, weaker early/late), guidance intervals, dynamic thresholding; CFG++/APG variants reduce oversaturation.
2. **Sampler**: use stochastic samplers (ancestral, DDPM, SDE, eta > 0) that inject noise; more steps if a few-step model.
3. **Vary the input**: different seeds, noise perturbations, prompt variation/LLM rewriting, wildcards in prompts, random style tokens.
4. **Training**: dedupe data, broader captions, regularisation/prior-preservation loss for DreamBooth, fewer fine-tuning steps/lower LoRA rank, early stopping by diversity metric, diverse-reward or diversity-aware RL objectives, larger/shuffled batches.
5. **Model averaging**: interpolate LoRA weights or mix base and fine-tuned models.
6. **Diversity-promoting sampling**: particle guidance / repulsion between batch samples.

**Measure the trade-off**: FID and precision (quality) vs recall / Vendi score / LPIPS pairwise diversity, plus CLIPScore for adherence; plot a Pareto curve over CFG scales.

**Sources:**
- [Classifier-Free Diffusion Guidance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.12598)
- [Diffusion Models Beat GANs on Image Synthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.05233)
- [Adversarial Diffusion Distillation (SDXL-Turbo)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.17042)
- [Diffusion Models - Outcome School](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/diffusion-models)

<a id="q472"></a>
### 472. Your diffusion model takes too long per image. How do you speed up sampling?

**Answer:**

Latency ~ (number of steps) x (cost per network evaluation), doubled by CFG (two passes per step). Attack both terms.

**1. Fewer steps**
- **Better solvers**: DDIM, DPM-Solver++, UniPC, Euler/Heun: 15-25 steps with little quality loss versus 50-1000 for DDPM.
- **Flow-matching / rectified-flow models** (SD3, Flux) have straighter trajectories.
- **Distillation**: progressive distillation, Consistency Models and **Latent Consistency Models (LCM)** (2-8 steps), Adversarial Diffusion Distillation (SDXL-Turbo, 1-4 steps), DMD, Lightning/Hyper-SD. Trade-off: less diversity, sometimes lower fidelity or weaker negative prompts.

**2. Cheaper steps**
- Work in **latent space** (already), lower resolution + upscaler, smaller model (distilled U-Net, pruned/"tiny" VAE decoder).
- **Guidance distillation** (remove second CFG pass) or apply CFG only in part of the steps.
- **Caching** (DeepCache, block/feature caching reuse activations across adjacent steps).
- **Attention efficiency**: FlashAttention / SDPA, token merging (ToMe), xformers.
- **Precision and compilation**: fp16/bf16, FP8/INT8 quantisation, `torch.compile`, TensorRT, CUDA graphs, channels-last.
- **Batching** and multi-GPU (patch/pipeline parallel like DistriFusion) for throughput or latency.

**3. System-level**: keep models warm on GPU, avoid reload of LoRAs, async queues, autoscaling, cache repeated prompts/seeds, preview at low res then refine.

**Order of attack**: pick a good solver + tuned step count -> fp16 + compile/TensorRT -> distilled/turbo variant if quality is acceptable -> feature caching/quantisation.

**Verify** with FID/CLIPScore and human A/B at the new step count; report latency at p50/p95.

**Sources:**
- [DPM-Solver: A Fast ODE Solver for Diffusion Probabilistic Model Sampling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.00927)
- [Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models (DDIM)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.02502)
- [Latent Consistency Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.04378)
- [Progressive Distillation for Fast Sampling of Diffusion Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.00512)
- [Diffusion Models - Outcome School](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/diffusion-models)

## AI Infrastructure and Scalability

<a id="q473"></a>
### 473. How do you improve inference speed in production LLM deployments?

**Answer:**

First understand the phases: **prefill** (compute-bound, processes the whole prompt in parallel, determines TTFT) and **decode** (memory-bandwidth-bound, one token at a time, determines inter-token latency). Then optimise in layers, measuring after each.

**Model level**
- **Quantisation** (FP8, INT8, INT4 AWQ/GPTQ): fewer bytes moved per token, so faster decode and more KV-cache room.
- Smaller/distilled model, or **routing** easy requests to a small model.
- Efficient architectures: GQA/MQA (smaller KV cache), MoE (fewer active params).

**Algorithmic decoding**
- **Speculative decoding** (draft model, Medusa, EAGLE, n-gram/prompt lookup): 1.5-3x decode speedup typically with identical output distribution.
- Constrained/structured decoding compiled efficiently; limit `max_tokens`; shorter outputs.

**Serving system**
- **Continuous batching** and **PagedAttention** (vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, TGI) to keep the GPU saturated.
- **FlashAttention** kernels, CUDA graphs, fused kernels, `torch.compile`.
- **Prefix/prompt caching** for shared system prompts and RAG context.
- **Chunked prefill** and prefill/decode disaggregation to protect inter-token latency from long prompts.
- KV-cache quantisation/eviction for long contexts.

**Parallelism and hardware**
- Tensor parallelism across GPUs to cut per-request latency; right GPU (H100/H200 with high HBM bandwidth) - see GPU selection.
- Co-locate with retrieval/tools; keep model warm; reduce network hops; streaming responses improve perceived latency.

**Prompt-side**: shorter prompts, fewer few-shot examples, cache-friendly prompt layout (static prefix first).

**Process**: benchmark with realistic traffic, track TTFT/TPOT/throughput and p95, pick the SLO-critical metric (interactive: TTFT + TPOT; batch: throughput per dollar).

**Sources:**
- [LLM Inference Optimization - video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jV2sCj4lHYk)
- [Efficient Memory Management for LLM Serving with PagedAttention (vLLM)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180)
- [Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.17192)
- [LLM Inference Performance Engineering: Best Practices (Databricks)](https://www.databricks.com/blog/llm-inference-performance-engineering-best-practices)

<a id="q474"></a>
### 474. LLM optimization techniques

**Answer:**

Optimisation targets three axes: **latency**, **throughput/cost**, and **memory**. Main technique families:

| Family | Techniques | Main benefit |
|---|---|---|
| Compression | Quantisation (INT8/INT4/FP8), pruning, distillation | Memory, bandwidth, cost |
| Attention/KV | FlashAttention, MQA/GQA/MLA, KV-cache quantisation/eviction, PagedAttention, sliding window | Memory, long context speed |
| Decoding | Speculative decoding (draft, Medusa, EAGLE, n-gram), multi-token prediction, lookahead | Lower per-token latency |
| Scheduling | Continuous batching, chunked prefill, prefill/decode disaggregation, priority queues | Throughput and tail latency |
| Caching | Prefix/prompt caching, semantic caching | Skip recomputation |
| Parallelism | Tensor, pipeline, expert, sequence parallelism | Fit and scale large models |
| Compilation/kernels | CUDA graphs, fused kernels, TensorRT-LLM, torch.compile | Lower overhead |
| Architecture | MoE, state-space/hybrid models | Fewer FLOPs per token |
| Application level | Shorter prompts, model routing/cascades, output length limits, batch APIs | Cost |

**How to apply**
1. Profile: is the workload prefill- or decode-bound? Memory-bound or compute-bound? Which metric matters (TTFT, TPOT, throughput)?
2. Take the cheap, low-risk wins first: an optimised server (vLLM/SGLang/TRT-LLM), FP8/INT8 quantisation, prefix caching, continuous batching.
3. Add speculative decoding and parallelism where latency demands.
4. Only then consider distillation/fine-tuning of a smaller model.
5. Evaluate quality after each change on your own eval set - quantisation and KV compression can silently degrade long-context or reasoning tasks.

**Pitfalls**: optimising average instead of p95, benchmarking with unrealistic prompt lengths, and stacking techniques that interact (e.g. speculative decoding gains shrink at large batch sizes because the GPU is already compute-saturated).

**Sources:**
- [5 LLM optimization techniques - Pallavi Shekhar (LinkedIn)](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/pallavi-shekhar_5-llm-optimization-techniques-lets-understand-activity-7442067281532325888-4aOS)
- [FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14135)
- [vLLM / PagedAttention paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180)
- [AWQ: Activation-aware Weight Quantization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.00978)
- [Databricks: LLM Inference Performance Engineering](https://www.databricks.com/blog/llm-inference-performance-engineering-best-practices)

<a id="q475"></a>
### 475. How do you select GPUs for LLM inference?

**Answer:**

Selection is driven by **memory capacity, memory bandwidth, compute, interconnect, ecosystem, and cost**.

**1. Memory capacity (does it fit?)**
- Weights: params x bytes (70B in FP16 = 140 GB; FP8 = 70 GB; INT4 = ~35 GB).
- Plus KV cache (grows with batch x context length) and activations/overhead (~10-20%).
- This decides GPU count and whether quantisation is needed.

**2. Memory bandwidth (decode speed)**
Decode is bandwidth-bound: tokens/s per sequence is roughly bandwidth / bytes read per token (weights + KV). Roughly: A100 80GB ~2 TB/s, H100 SXM ~3.35 TB/s, H200 ~4.8 TB/s, L40S ~0.86 TB/s, consumer RTX 4090 ~1 TB/s.

**3. Compute (prefill and large batches)**: FP8/FP16 TFLOPS matter for long prompts, high concurrency, and multimodal encoders. H100/H200/B200 have FP8 (Blackwell adds FP4) tensor cores; A100 lacks FP8.

**4. Interconnect**: multi-GPU tensor parallelism needs NVLink/NVSwitch; PCIe-only boxes (L40S, 4090) scale poorly for TP and are best for models fitting on one GPU or with pipeline parallelism.

**5. Software/ecosystem**: CUDA + TensorRT-LLM/vLLM most mature; AMD MI300X (192 GB HBM, ROCm) is attractive for capacity; TPUs/Inferentia/Gaudi/LPUs need model/porting effort.

**6. Economics**: compare cost per million tokens at your target utilisation, not $/hour. Consider spot/reserved, availability, power, and rack density.

**Rules of thumb**
- Small models (<=13B) and cost-sensitive: L4/L40S/A10 or a single A100/H100.
- 70B class: 1x H200/MI300X (quantised) or 2-4x H100/A100 with TP.
- 400B+/MoE: 8x H100/H200/B200 nodes with NVLink, possibly multi-node.
- Always benchmark your model, context lengths and concurrency on candidates.

**Sources:**
- [How does a GPU work for Deep Learning? - Outcome School](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/how-does-a-gpu-work-for-deep-learning)
- [Transformer Inference Arithmetic (kipply)](https://kipp.ly/transformer-inference-arithmetic/)
- [NVIDIA H100 Tensor Core GPU](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/h100/)
- [LLM Inference Performance Engineering (Databricks)](https://www.databricks.com/blog/llm-inference-performance-engineering-best-practices)

<a id="q476"></a>
### 476. How does a GPU work for Deep Learning?

**Answer:**

A **GPU** is a massively parallel processor: thousands of simple cores optimised for throughput, in contrast to a CPU's few complex cores optimised for latency. Deep learning is dominated by matrix multiplications and elementwise ops, which parallelise perfectly.

**Architecture (NVIDIA view)**
- **Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs)**: each has CUDA cores (FP32/INT), **Tensor Cores** (specialised matrix-multiply-accumulate units for FP16/BF16/FP8/INT8, giving order-of-magnitude more matmul throughput), registers, shared memory/L1.
- **Execution model**: a kernel launches a grid of thread blocks; each block runs on an SM in **warps** of 32 threads executing in lockstep (SIMT). Massive multithreading hides memory latency.
- **Memory hierarchy**: registers -> shared memory/L1 (fast, tiny) -> L2 -> **HBM** global memory (large, ~2-5 TB/s on data-centre parts) -> host memory via PCIe/NVLink. Performance is often limited by memory bandwidth, not FLOPs.

**How training/inference uses it**
- Layers become GEMMs; frameworks (PyTorch) dispatch to cuBLAS/cuDNN/CUTLASS or fused kernels (FlashAttention, Triton) tuned for tensor cores.
- **Mixed precision** (BF16/FP16/FP8 with FP32 accumulators) doubles/quadruples throughput and halves memory.
- **Arithmetic intensity** (FLOPs per byte) decides whether an op is compute-bound (large matmuls, prefill, training) or memory-bound (decode, layernorm, softmax, elementwise). Kernel fusion reduces round-trips to HBM.
- Multi-GPU: NVLink/NVSwitch inside a node, InfiniBand/RoCE across nodes, NCCL collectives (all-reduce, all-gather) for data/tensor parallelism.

**Practical tips**: keep GPUs fed (data loaders, async copies), use large enough batches, avoid host-device sync, profile with Nsight/PyTorch profiler, watch memory fragmentation and OOMs.

**Sources:**
- [How does a GPU work for Deep Learning? - Outcome School](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/how-does-a-gpu-work-for-deep-learning)
- [NVIDIA Deep Learning Performance guide (GPU background)](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/performance/dl-performance-gpu-background/index.html)
- [Mixed Precision Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.03740)
- [FlashAttention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14135)

<a id="q477"></a>
### 477. How does a Google TPU work?

**Answer:**

A **Tensor Processing Unit** is Google's custom ASIC for neural-network workloads, built around a large **systolic array**.

**Core design**
- **Matrix Multiply Unit (MXU)**: a systolic array (e.g. 128x128 multiply-accumulate cells on recent generations). Weights are loaded into the array and activations stream through; each cell multiplies and passes partial sums to neighbours, so data is reused many times without repeated memory reads. This gives very high efficiency for matmul.
- **Vector and scalar units** handle activations, softmax, normalisation, control.
- **On-chip memory** (unified buffer/vector memory) plus **HBM**; compiler-controlled scratchpads rather than hardware caches.
- Reduced/mixed precision: BF16 (Google's Brain Float, invented for TPUs) with FP32 accumulation, INT8 for inference; newer generations add FP8.
- **Interconnect**: chips link with dedicated high-speed inter-chip interconnect (ICI) in 2D/3D torus topologies, organised into **pods** (thousands of chips) and reconfigurable slices, with optical circuit switching in later generations. This makes large-scale training with collective ops efficient.

**Programming model**
- **XLA** compiler ahead-of-time compiles JAX / TensorFlow / PyTorch-XLA graphs into fused TPU programs; static shapes are strongly preferred (dynamic shapes cause recompiles).
- Parallelism expressed via sharding annotations (GSPMD / `jax.sharding`).

**Versus GPUs**
- TPUs: less flexibility, excellent perf/watt and scaling on large, regular workloads, tightly integrated with Google Cloud, strong for training and serving Gemini-class models.
- GPUs: broader software ecosystem (CUDA), dynamic workloads, easier custom kernels, wider availability.

**Trade-offs**: ecosystem lock-in to GCP/XLA, and less community tooling for cutting-edge serving features than the CUDA stack (though vLLM TPU support is growing).

**Sources:**
- [How does a Google TPU work? - Outcome School](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/how-does-a-google-tpu-work)
- [In-Datacenter Performance Analysis of a Tensor Processing Unit](https://arxiv.org/abs/1704.04760)
- [Google Cloud TPU documentation](https://cloud.google.com/tpu/docs/intro-to-tpu)
- [JAX documentation](https://docs.jax.dev/en/latest/)

<a id="q478"></a>
### 478. How does an LPU work?

**Answer:**

An **LPU (Language Processing Unit)** is Groq's inference-oriented accelerator, designed for the sequential, memory-bound nature of LLM decoding.

**Key ideas**
- **Deterministic, software-scheduled execution**: instead of dynamic hardware scheduling, caches and speculation, the compiler statically schedules every instruction and data movement down to the clock cycle. Execution time is predictable, giving very low and consistent latency (no tail jitter from contention).
- **Large on-chip SRAM as primary weight memory** (hundreds of MB per chip) rather than off-chip HBM. SRAM bandwidth is far higher than HBM, which removes the memory-bandwidth bottleneck that limits decode tokens/s on GPUs.
- **Tensor-streaming architecture**: data flows through functional slices in a pipeline (like a conveyor/assembly line); the compiler coordinates matrix, vector and switch units.
- **Scale-out via chip-to-chip networking**: since each chip holds few weights in SRAM, a model is sharded across many chips (hundreds for a 70B model) connected by a deterministic, compiler-scheduled network, effectively pipelining/tensor-parallelising a model.

**Results and trade-offs**
- Very high single-stream tokens/s and low TTFT: attractive for real-time agents, voice, and interactive use.
- Capacity limits: SRAM is small, so serving a large model needs many chips (rack-scale), which affects cost per token and floor cost for low traffic; less flexible for training or arbitrary new architectures; it is an inference-only, proprietary stack accessed mainly via GroqCloud.
- Throughput-per-dollar depends on utilisation and batching strategy, and claims should be checked against workload-specific benchmarks.

**When to consider**: latency-critical applications where tokens/s per user matters more than cost per token at low utilisation.

**Sources:**
- [How does an LPU work? - Outcome School](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/how-does-an-lpu-work)
- [Groq: LPU inference engine](https://groq.com/)

<a id="q479"></a>
### 479. Estimate the GPU memory needed to serve a 70B model (weights, KV cache, activations). Does it fit on a single 80 GB GPU?

**Answer:**

**Weights**: params x bytes per param.
- FP16/BF16: 70e9 x 2 = **140 GB**
- FP8/INT8: **70 GB**
- INT4: **~35 GB** (about 37-40 GB with scales/zero-points)

**KV cache** per token = 2 (K and V) x layers x kv_heads x head_dim x bytes.
Llama-2/3-70B: 80 layers, GQA with 8 KV heads, head_dim 128, FP16:
2 x 80 x 8 x 128 x 2 B = 327,680 B ~ **0.31 MB/token** (about 0.3 GB per 1k tokens).
- One 8k-token sequence: ~2.5 GB. 32 concurrent 8k sequences: ~80 GB.
- Without GQA (64 KV heads) it would be 8x larger, about 2.5 MB/token.
- FP8 KV cache halves this.

**Activations**: during inference these are small compared to weights/KV (transient per-layer tensors, roughly hundreds of MB to a few GB depending on batch and prefill chunk size). Add CUDA context, framework and fragmentation overhead: ~5-10 GB. Reserve headroom (vLLM `gpu_memory_utilization` ~0.9).

**Does it fit one 80 GB GPU?**
| Config | Weights | Room for KV | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| FP16 | 140 GB | none | No; needs 2x80 GB minimum (tight), realistically 4x for KV/batch, or TP=2 with short contexts |
| FP8 | 70 GB | ~0-5 GB after overhead | Barely loads; almost no KV; impractical |
| INT4 (AWQ/GPTQ) | ~35-40 GB | ~30-35 GB | Yes; ~100k tokens of KV total at FP16 (e.g. several concurrent 8k requests) |

**Conclusion**: not in FP16 or realistically FP8 on one 80 GB card; INT4 fits with modest concurrency. On an H200 (141 GB) or MI300X (192 GB), FP8 fits comfortably. Multi-GPU tensor parallelism (2-4 x 80 GB) is the standard production setup for FP16/FP8.

**Sources:**
- [Transformer Inference Arithmetic (kipply)](https://kipp.ly/transformer-inference-arithmetic/)
- [Llama 2: Open Foundation and Fine-Tuned Chat Models (architecture with GQA)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.09288)
- [GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13245)
- [vLLM documentation](https://docs.vllm.ai/)

<a id="q480"></a>
### 480. Do the roofline math: how many tokens/sec can one H100 produce for a 70B model at batch size 1?

**Answer:**

**Roofline idea**: attainable performance = min(peak compute, memory bandwidth x arithmetic intensity). Decode at batch size 1 has very low arithmetic intensity (~1-2 FLOPs per byte), so it is **memory-bandwidth-bound**: each generated token requires reading all weights from HBM once.

**Numbers (H100 SXM)**: HBM3 bandwidth ~3.35 TB/s; dense FP16/BF16 ~990 TFLOPS, FP8 ~1,980 TFLOPS (spec-sheet peaks with sparsity excluded).

**Compute check**: FLOPs per token ~ 2 x 70e9 = 140 GFLOPs. At ~990 TFLOPS that would allow ~7,000 tokens/s, so compute is not the limit at batch 1.

**Memory bound**: tokens/s ~ bandwidth / bytes per token.
- FP16: 140 GB per token -> 3.35e12 / 1.4e11 ~ **24 tokens/s** (a 140 GB model does not fit in one 80 GB H100 anyway; this is the per-token bound on aggregate bandwidth for TP).
- FP8: 70 GB -> ~48 tokens/s ceiling, but 70 GB barely fits on 80 GB (no KV room).
- INT4: ~35 GB -> ~**95 tokens/s** ceiling.
Real-world efficiency is ~60-80% of peak bandwidth, so expect roughly 60-75 tok/s for INT4 in practice; add KV-cache reads (small at short context).

**Ridge point**: H100 FP16 ridge = 990e12 / 3.35e12 ~ **300 FLOPs/byte**. Batch 1 sits far left (memory-bound). Batching amortises the weight read: at batch B, intensity ~ B FLOPs/byte for 2-byte weights, so compute-bound around B ~ 150-300. Throughput therefore scales almost linearly with batch until then, which is why **continuous batching** massively boosts tokens/s per GPU at little latency cost.

**Interview takeaways**: decode speed is set by bandwidth and bytes/param (hence quantisation and speculative decoding help), TP over N GPUs gives up to N x aggregate bandwidth minus communication overhead, and prefill is compute-bound.

**Sources:**
- [Transformer Inference Arithmetic (kipply)](https://kipp.ly/transformer-inference-arithmetic/)
- [NVIDIA H100 Tensor Core GPU specifications](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/h100/)
- [LLM Inference Performance Engineering (Databricks)](https://www.databricks.com/blog/llm-inference-performance-engineering-best-practices)
- [Roofline: An Insightful Visual Performance Model (Williams et al.)](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~kubitron/cs252/handouts/papers/RooflineVyNoYellow.pdf)

<a id="q481"></a>
### 481. What is model parallelism vs data parallelism in distributed training?

**Answer:**

**Data parallelism (DP)**: every GPU holds a **full copy** of the model; each processes a different slice of the batch; gradients are **all-reduced** (averaged) so replicas stay in sync.
- Pros: simple, scales throughput almost linearly, no model changes (PyTorch DDP).
- Cons: model + gradients + optimiser states must fit on each GPU (Adam: ~16 bytes/param in mixed precision); all-reduce bandwidth grows with model size.

**Model parallelism (MP)**: the **model is split** across devices because it does not fit or to speed up single-batch compute.
- **Tensor (intra-layer) parallelism**: split weight matrices within a layer (Megatron-LM); needs all-reduce per layer, so needs fast NVLink.
- **Pipeline parallelism**: split layers into stages on different GPUs, micro-batches flow through (GPipe, 1F1B); cost is pipeline bubbles.
- **Expert parallelism** for MoE; **sequence/context parallelism** for long sequences.

**Sharded data parallelism (ZeRO/FSDP)** is a hybrid: data-parallel compute but parameters/gradients/optimiser states are sharded, gathered just-in-time.

**Comparison**
| | Data parallel | Model parallel |
|---|---|---|
| Memory per GPU | Full model | 1/N of model |
| Communication | Gradient all-reduce per step | Activations per layer/stage |
| Complexity | Low | High |
| Use when | Model fits | Model too large |

**3D parallelism** (DP x TP x PP), used for frontier-scale training: TP within a node, PP across nodes, DP (or FSDP) across replicas.

**Practical guidance**: start with DDP; if memory-bound, switch to FSDP/ZeRO; add TP for very large layers, PP when crossing slower interconnects; tune micro-batch count to reduce bubbles; overlap communication with computation.

**Sources:**
- [Megatron-LM: Training Multi-Billion Parameter Language Models Using Model Parallelism](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.08053)
- [ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.02054)
- [Efficient Large-Scale Language Model Training on GPU Clusters (3D parallelism)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04473)
- [PyTorch Distributed Data Parallel documentation](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/notes/ddp.html)

---

<a id="q482"></a>
### 482. What is tensor parallelism, and how does it help serve large models?

**Answer:**

**Tensor parallelism (TP)** splits individual layers' weight matrices across N GPUs so each GPU stores and computes a shard, and the partial results are combined with collective communication (Megatron-LM style).

**How it works in a Transformer block**
- **MLP**: first linear W1 is split by **columns** (each GPU computes a slice of the hidden activation, no communication needed since GeLU/SwiGLU is elementwise); second linear W2 split by **rows**, each GPU produces a partial sum, followed by an **all-reduce** to combine.
- **Attention**: heads are divided across GPUs (each GPU owns a subset of Q/K/V heads and its KV cache); the output projection is row-parallel with an all-reduce.
- So each block needs ~2 all-reduces (forward). With GQA, KV heads must be divisible by TP degree (or replicated).

**Benefits for serving**
- **Fits models larger than one GPU** (weights and KV cache both sharded).
- **Lower per-token latency**: each token's weight reads are spread over N GPUs' bandwidth, so decode approaches N x faster (minus communication).
- More KV-cache room per GPU, allowing larger batches.

**Costs and limits**
- All-reduce every layer means latency-sensitive collectives: needs **NVLink/NVSwitch**; scaling across nodes over InfiniBand is poor. Typical TP degree = 2, 4, 8 within a node.
- Diminishing returns: communication share grows as N grows, and small models see little benefit.
- Requires head/dimension divisibility.

**In practice**: `vllm serve model --tensor-parallel-size 4`; combine with pipeline parallelism across nodes (TP inside, PP across) and expert parallelism for MoE. For throughput at fixed model size, multiple replicas with lower TP degree are often more cost-efficient than one big TP group.

**Sources:**
- [Megatron-LM paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.08053)
- [vLLM: Distributed inference and serving](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/serving/parallelism_scaling.html)
- [Hugging Face: Tensor parallelism in Transformers](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/perf_train_gpu_many)
- [Efficient Large-Scale Language Model Training on GPU Clusters](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04473)

<a id="q483"></a>
### 483. What is pipeline parallelism?

**Answer:**

**Pipeline parallelism (PP)** partitions a model **by layers** into sequential **stages**, each on a different GPU (e.g. layers 1-20 on GPU0, 21-40 on GPU1, ...). Activations pass from stage to stage; in training, gradients flow backward.

**The bubble problem**: naively, only one stage is active at a time, so GPUs idle. Fix: split each batch into **micro-batches** and stream them through the pipeline so stages overlap.
- **GPipe**: all forward micro-batches, then all backward; bubble fraction ~ (p - 1) / (m + p - 1) for p stages and m micro-batches, so use m >> p. Needs activation recomputation (checkpointing) to control memory.
- **1F1B (PipeDream-Flush)**: interleave one forward with one backward per stage, reducing activation memory.
- **Interleaved schedules** (virtual stages per GPU) shrink the bubble further at the cost of more communication.

**Communication**: only activations at stage boundaries are sent (point-to-point), far less than TP's per-layer all-reduces, so PP tolerates slower interconnects (cross-node InfiniBand).

**Trade-offs**
- Pros: fits huge models across nodes, low communication volume, memory split across stages.
- Cons: pipeline bubbles, load imbalance if stages differ in cost, more complex scheduling, added per-request latency in inference (a token traverses all stages), so it improves throughput/capacity more than latency.

**Inference usage**: PP across nodes when a model does not fit in one node's aggregate memory (e.g. very large MoE), with continuous batching keeping stages busy; TP within nodes.

**3D parallelism**: TP within node + PP across nodes + DP/FSDP across replicas.

**Sources:**
- [GPipe: Efficient Training of Giant Neural Networks using Pipeline Parallelism](https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.06965)
- [PipeDream: Generalized Pipeline Parallelism for DNN Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.03377)
- [Efficient Large-Scale Language Model Training on GPU Clusters](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04473)
- [PyTorch pipeline parallelism documentation](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/distributed.pipelining.html)

---

<a id="q484"></a>
### 484. How does continuous batching improve LLM inference throughput?

**Answer:**

**Problem with static batching**: requests in a batch finish at different lengths, but the batch runs until the longest completes; short sequences leave idle "bubbles" (padding/wasted slots) and new requests wait for the whole batch to end. GPU utilisation and throughput suffer, and latency is poor.

**Continuous (in-flight / iteration-level) batching**, introduced in the Orca paper, schedules at the granularity of a **single decode iteration**:
- After every token-generation step, the scheduler removes finished sequences and **immediately admits waiting requests** into the freed slots.
- The batch composition changes every iteration; sequences at different positions run together (ragged batching via attention kernels that handle variable lengths, enabled by PagedAttention-style KV management).
- Prefill of a new request can be interleaved (or **chunked** into pieces) with ongoing decodes, so long prompts do not stall others.

**Why throughput rises**
- Decode is memory-bandwidth-bound: reading weights once serves many sequences, so larger effective batches give near-linear throughput gains until compute-bound.
- No idle slots waiting on stragglers -> much higher GPU utilisation; reports typically show several-fold (up to ~10-20x in some comparisons) throughput improvement over naive static batching.
- Lower queueing delay, better TTFT under load.

**Tuning knobs (vLLM)**: `max_num_seqs`, `max_num_batched_tokens`, chunked prefill, scheduling policy (FCFS/priority), preemption (swap or recompute) when KV memory runs out.

**Trade-offs**: larger batches raise per-token latency slightly (TPOT); memory (KV cache) becomes the limiting resource; prefill-decode interference needs chunked prefill or disaggregation. Balance throughput vs latency SLOs.

**Sources:**
- [Continuous Batching in LLMs - Outcome School](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/continuous-batching-in-llms)
- [Orca: A Distributed Serving System for Transformer-Based Generative Models (OSDI 2022)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi22/presentation/yu)
- [vLLM / PagedAttention paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180)
- [Sarathi-Serve: Taming Throughput-Latency Tradeoff in LLM Inference (chunked prefill)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.02310)

<a id="q485"></a>
### 485. What is speculative decoding, and how does it speed up inference?

**Answer:**

**Idea**: decoding is memory-bound, so verifying several tokens in one forward pass costs about the same as generating one. Use a cheap **draft** mechanism to propose k tokens, then have the large **target** model verify them all in a single parallel pass, accepting the longest correct prefix.

**Algorithm (Leviathan et al. / Chen et al.)**
1. Draft model q proposes tokens x1..xk autoregressively (cheap).
2. Target model p runs one forward pass over the prefix + k drafts, producing p(x_i | ...) for each position.
3. **Rejection sampling**: accept x_i with probability min(1, p(x_i)/q(x_i)); at the first rejection, resample from the normalised residual max(0, p - q) and stop. If all accepted, sample one extra bonus token from the target.
4. Repeat.

This guarantees the output distribution is **exactly identical** to sampling from the target alone (lossless). Under greedy decoding, acceptance is simply "draft token equals target argmax".

**Speedup**: expected accepted tokens per target pass ~ (1 - alpha^(k+1)) / (1 - alpha), where alpha is the acceptance rate. Practical speedups ~1.5-3x on predictable text (code, extraction, summarisation), lower on high-entropy creative text.

**Draft options**: a small model from the same family (needs shared tokenizer), Medusa heads, EAGLE, n-gram/prompt lookup, self-speculation (layer skipping).

**Trade-offs and tips**
- Extra memory for the draft; gains shrink at large batch sizes as the GPU becomes compute-bound (best for low-latency, low-concurrency serving).
- Tune k (typically 3-8) and choose a draft with high alpha (distilled from the target improves acceptance).
- Tree-based verification (multiple candidates) raises acceptance.
- Supported by vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, SGLang, llama.cpp.

**Sources:**
- [Speculative Decoding - Outcome School](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/speculative-decoding)
- [Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.17192)
- [Accelerating Large Language Model Decoding with Speculative Sampling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.01318)
- [vLLM speculative decoding docs](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/features/spec_decode.html)

---

<a id="q486"></a>
### 486. How does Medusa (multi-head speculative decoding) work?

**Answer:**

**Medusa** removes the need for a separate draft model. It adds several extra lightweight **decoding heads** on top of the target LLM's last hidden state; head i predicts the token at position t+i+1 (the original LM head predicts t+1).

**Mechanism**
1. Each Medusa head is a small MLP (one or two residual layers) followed by an output projection initialised from the LM head. K heads (typically 3-5) each output top candidates for their future position.
2. **Candidate generation**: combining top-k tokens from each head gives many candidate continuations, organised as a **tree**, not just one sequence.
3. **Tree attention**: candidates are verified in a single forward pass of the base model using a custom attention mask so each node attends only to its ancestors.
4. **Acceptance**: choose the longest candidate path consistent with the base model. Medusa-1 uses greedy match; a **typical acceptance** scheme accepts tokens whose probability under the base model exceeds a threshold, which permits sampling with temperature and increases accepted length (it is not strictly lossless like classic rejection sampling).
5. The accepted tokens advance the sequence; repeat.

**Training**
- **Medusa-1**: base model frozen, only heads trained (cheap, lossless w.r.t. base quality), often via self-distillation on the model's own outputs.
- **Medusa-2**: heads and base fine-tuned jointly for higher speed (~2.3-3.6x reported), needs care (e.g. self-distillation, LoRA) to preserve quality.

**Pros/cons**: no second model, easy deployment, small extra memory, ~2x typical speedups. Cons: heads predict independently from the same hidden state (no dependence on intermediate draft tokens), so acceptance is lower than in EAGLE; requires training per base model; gains diminish at high batch sizes.

**Sources:**
- [Medusa - Multi-Head Speculative Decoding - Outcome School](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/decoding-medusa)
- [Medusa: Simple LLM Inference Acceleration Framework with Multiple Decoding Heads](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.10774)
- [Medusa GitHub repository](https://github.com/FasterDecoding/Medusa)

---

<a id="q487"></a>
### 487. How does EAGLE (feature-level speculative decoding) work?

**Answer:**

**EAGLE** (Extrapolation Algorithm for Greater Language-model Efficiency) drafts at the **feature level** (the second-to-top-layer hidden states) rather than the token level.

**Key insight**: autoregression over features (hidden states before the LM head) is more regular and predictable than over tokens, but feature prediction is uncertain because of sampling randomness in the token path. EAGLE resolves this by feeding the draft model **both the previous features and the token sequence advanced by one step** (the actually sampled token), removing that uncertainty.

**Mechanism**
1. **Draft model** = a tiny autoregression head: an embedding layer + FC layer to fuse [feature_t, embedding of token_{t+1}], plus a single Transformer decoder layer; it reuses the target's LM head to convert predicted features into token distributions. It is only ~1 layer, so cheap.
2. It autoregressively predicts next features and tokens for several steps, building a **draft tree** (top-k branching, as in Medusa).
3. **Verification**: the target model verifies the whole tree in one pass with tree attention; standard speculative sampling rules are used, so **output distribution is preserved** (lossless).
4. Accepted tokens (and their true features) continue the process.

**Training**: the draft head is trained on a fixed dataset (e.g. ShareGPT) with a regression loss on features + classification loss on tokens; the base model is frozen and training takes hours on a few GPUs.

**Results**: reported ~2.7-3.5x speedup on Llama-2-chat-70B versus vanilla decoding in the paper, and typically better than Medusa and standard speculative decoding because of higher acceptance length. EAGLE-2 adds dynamic (context-aware) draft trees; EAGLE-3 moves to token prediction with multi-layer feature fusion.

**Trade-offs**: needs a trained drafter per target model; gains fall with large batch sizes; supported in vLLM/SGLang/TensorRT-LLM.

**Sources:**
- [EAGLE - Feature-Level Speculative Decoding - Outcome School](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/decoding-eagle)
- [EAGLE: Speculative Sampling Requires Rethinking Feature Uncertainty](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.15077)
- [EAGLE-2: Faster Inference with Dynamic Draft Trees](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.16858)
- [EAGLE GitHub repository](https://github.com/SafeAILab/EAGLE)

---

<a id="q488"></a>
### 488. What is N-gram Speculation in LLMs, and how does it speed up generation?

**Answer:**

**N-gram speculation** (a.k.a. prompt lookup decoding) is speculative decoding with **no draft model**: draft tokens are obtained by string matching against text already in the context.

**Mechanism**
1. Take the last n tokens generated (the n-gram, e.g. n = 2-4).
2. Search the prompt (and previously generated text) for earlier occurrences of the same n-gram.
3. If found, propose the k tokens that followed it as draft candidates.
4. The target model verifies all k in one forward pass (same accept-longest-matching-prefix logic; with greedy decoding it is exactly lossless, and with sampling standard rejection rules apply).
5. If no match, fall back to normal decoding for that step at negligible overhead.

**Why it works**: many LLM tasks copy from the context: summarisation, RAG answers quoting documents, code editing/refactoring, extraction, translation of repeated phrases, multi-turn chat repeating entities. There the next tokens are literally in the prompt, so acceptance is high.

**Benefits**
- Zero training, no extra memory, no extra model to deploy; works with any model; trivial to enable (vLLM `speculative_config` with `ngram` method, HF `prompt_lookup_num_tokens`).
- Speedups of ~1.5-2.5x on input-grounded tasks; sometimes more for code edits.

**Limitations**
- Little or no gain for open-ended generation with little overlap with the context; small CPU overhead for matching.
- Acceptance rate is lower than learned drafters (EAGLE, Medusa) in general workloads.
- Gains shrink at high batch sizes.

**Tuning**: choose max/min n-gram sizes and number of speculative tokens (num_speculative_tokens ~3-5); measure acceptance rate on real traffic; consider combining with learned drafters.

**Sources:**
- [N-gram Speculation in LLMs - Outcome School](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/n-gram-speculation-in-llms)
- [Prompt Lookup Decoding (GitHub)](https://github.com/apoorvumang/prompt-lookup-decoding)
- [Inference with Reference: Lossless Acceleration of LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.04487)
- [vLLM speculative decoding docs](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/features/spec_decode.html)

<a id="q489"></a>
### 489. What is KV cache, and how do you manage memory for it?

**Answer:**

**KV cache**: in autoregressive decoding, each new token's attention needs the Keys and Values of all previous tokens. Recomputing them every step would be O(n^2) per token; instead they are computed once and **cached** per layer and head, so each step processes only the new token and reads the cache.

**Size**: per token = 2 x layers x kv_heads x head_dim x bytes. Llama-3-70B (GQA, 8 KV heads, FP16) ~ 0.3 MB/token; a 128k context for one sequence ~ 40 GB. The cache grows linearly with batch x sequence length and often becomes the limiting resource (more than weights) at high concurrency or long context.

**Memory-management techniques**
- **PagedAttention (vLLM)**: split cache into fixed-size blocks (e.g. 16 tokens) allocated on demand via a block table, eliminating fragmentation and over-reservation (previous systems wasted 60-80%); enables sharing blocks across sequences (beam search, parallel sampling, **prefix caching**) with copy-on-write.
- **Architecture reductions**: MQA/GQA (fewer KV heads), MLA (DeepSeek's latent compression), sliding-window/local attention layers.
- **Quantisation**: FP8/INT8/INT4 KV cache (halves or quarters memory; check long-context quality).
- **Eviction/compression**: StreamingLLM (attention sinks + recent window), H2O (heavy-hitter oracle), SnapKV; lossy, task-dependent.
- **Prefix/prompt caching** across requests for shared system prompts and RAG context (radix trees in SGLang).
- **Offloading**: swap cold KV to CPU/NVMe (LMCache), with recompute vs swap on preemption.
- **Scheduling**: admission control, max sequences, chunked prefill, preemption policies; disaggregated prefill/decode with KV transfer.
- **Capacity planning**: reserve fraction (`gpu_memory_utilization`), cap `max_model_len`.

**Pitfalls**: OOM under long-context bursts, fragmentation, and cache-thrashing with low-hit-rate prefix caches.

**Sources:**
- [What is KV Cache in LLMs? - Outcome School](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/kv-cache-in-llms)
- [Efficient Memory Management for LLM Serving with PagedAttention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180)
- [Efficient Streaming Language Models with Attention Sinks (StreamingLLM)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.17453)
- [H2O: Heavy-Hitter Oracle for Efficient Generative Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.14048)
- [GQA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13245)

<a id="q490"></a>
### 490. What is Paged Attention?

**Answer:**

**PagedAttention** (vLLM, SOSP 2023) applies OS virtual-memory paging to the KV cache.

**Problem**: older servers pre-allocated one contiguous KV buffer per request sized for the maximum output length. This caused **internal fragmentation** (reserved but unused), **external fragmentation**, and no sharing, wasting an estimated 60-80% of KV memory, which limited batch size and therefore throughput.

**Mechanism**
- KV cache is divided into fixed-size **blocks** (e.g. 16 tokens) stored in non-contiguous physical GPU memory.
- Each sequence has a **block table** mapping logical block indices to physical blocks (like a page table). Blocks are allocated on demand as tokens are generated; when a sequence finishes, its blocks return to a free pool.
- The attention kernel is modified to gather K/V through the block table, computing attention over non-contiguous blocks.
- **Sharing with copy-on-write**: sequences with the same prefix (parallel sampling, beam search, shared system prompt) point to the same physical blocks with reference counts; a block is copied only when a sequence diverges. This underlies **automatic prefix caching**.
- **Preemption**: when memory runs out, blocks of lower-priority sequences can be swapped to CPU or recomputed.

**Benefits**: near-zero waste (<4% reported), much larger effective batch sizes, so roughly 2-4x higher throughput than prior systems (FasterTransformer, Orca) at similar latency in the paper, plus memory savings for complex decoding.

**Costs**: slight kernel overhead from indirection, block-size tuning (small blocks reduce waste but hurt kernel efficiency), added scheduler complexity.

**Related**: continuous batching benefits greatly from paged memory; SGLang's RadixAttention and TensorRT-LLM's paged KV cache use similar ideas.

**Sources:**
- [Paged Attention in LLMs - Outcome School](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/paged-attention-in-llms)
- [Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180)
- [vLLM documentation](https://docs.vllm.ai/)
- [SGLang: Efficient Execution of Structured Language Model Programs (RadixAttention)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.07104)

<a id="q491"></a>
### 491. How does GGUF work?

**Answer:**

**GGUF** (GPT-Generated Unified Format) is the single-file binary format used by **llama.cpp/ggml** to store LLMs for efficient local inference, succeeding the older GGML/GGJT formats.

**Structure**
- **Header**: magic number "GGUF", version, tensor count, metadata key-value count.
- **Metadata key-value store**: architecture (`general.architecture`), hyperparameters (context length, layers, heads, RoPE settings), **tokenizer** (vocab, merges, special tokens, chat template), quantisation version, licence and authorship. Extensible without breaking compatibility.
- **Tensor info**: name, dimensions, quantisation type, offset for each tensor.
- **Tensor data**: aligned blocks, laid out for **memory-mapping (mmap)**, so the OS lazily loads weights, giving fast start-up and letting multiple processes share pages.

**Why it is convenient**: everything needed (weights, tokenizer, config, template) is in one self-contained file, so no separate config/tokenizer files or version mismatch.

**Quantisation types**: block-wise schemes; weights are split into blocks (e.g. 32 or 256 values) with per-block scale (and min).
- Legacy: Q4_0, Q4_1, Q5_0, Q8_0.
- **K-quants** (Q2_K ... Q6_K): super-blocks with quantised scales; variants S/M/L mix bit-widths across tensors, keeping sensitive tensors (attention v, output) at higher precision.
- **I-quants** (IQ2/IQ3/IQ4): importance-matrix-guided lower-bit quantisation; imatrix calibration data improves quality at low bits.
- Rule of thumb: Q4_K_M is a common size/quality sweet spot (~4.5-5 bits/weight); Q8_0 nearly lossless; below 3 bits quality drops noticeably.

**Runtime**: llama.cpp dequantises on the fly in optimised kernels (AVX/NEON, Metal, CUDA, Vulkan), supports CPU/GPU layer offloading (`-ngl`), so models run on laptops, phones and Raspberry Pis; used by Ollama and LM Studio.

**Trade-offs**: excellent for local/edge and single-user inference; less suited to high-throughput multi-tenant GPU serving than vLLM/TensorRT-LLM.

**Sources:**
- [How does GGUF work? - Outcome School](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/how-does-gguf-work)
- [GGUF format specification (ggml)](https://github.com/ggml-org/ggml/blob/master/docs/gguf.md)
- [llama.cpp repository](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp)
- [Hugging Face: GGUF documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/gguf)

<a id="q492"></a>
### 492. How do you optimize inference for edge and mobile deployment?

**Answer:**

**Constraints**: limited RAM (a few GB), memory bandwidth, battery/thermal limits, no big GPU, intermittent connectivity, and privacy/latency requirements that motivate on-device inference.

**Optimisation stack**
1. **Choose the right model**: small language models (1-4B: Llama 3.2 1B/3B, Phi-3/4-mini, Gemma 2B, Qwen 0.5-3B) or distilled models; task-specific fine-tuning to reach quality at small size.
2. **Quantise aggressively**: INT8, then 4-bit (GGUF Q4_K_M, AWQ/GPTQ, MLC/ExecuTorch 4-bit group-wise); 4-bit cuts memory ~4x vs FP16 (a 3B model becomes ~2 GB). Use calibration (imatrix/AWQ) and keep embeddings/output layers at higher precision. Quantisation-aware training if quality drops.
3. **Reduce KV/memory**: GQA models, KV-cache quantisation, limit context length, sliding-window attention; mmap weights.
4. **Efficient runtime and hardware**: llama.cpp (CPU/Metal/Vulkan), MLC-LLM, ExecuTorch, ONNX Runtime, TensorFlow Lite/LiteRT, Core ML, Qualcomm QNN/Hexagon NPU, Apple Neural Engine; use NPU/GPU delegates, NEON/AVX kernels, operator fusion.
5. **Decoding tricks**: speculative decoding with tiny draft, n-gram lookup, shorter outputs, prompt caching of static prefixes, constrained decoding.
6. **Pruning/distillation/sparsity** where hardware supports it.
7. **System design**: hybrid edge-cloud (route hard queries to the cloud), lazy model loading, background download, model updates via delta/OTA, thermal-aware throttling, battery budgets.

**Metrics**: model size, peak RAM, TTFT and tokens/s on target devices, energy per token, quality vs FP16 baseline on your tasks.

**Pitfalls**: benchmarking on desktops rather than real devices, forgetting thermal throttling, quality regressions in low-bit quantisation (test long context and multilingual), OS memory-kill of large mmaps.

**Sources:**
- [How does llama.cpp run LLMs on everyday hardware? - Outcome School](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/how-does-llama-cpp-run-llms-on-everyday-hardware)
- [How does Model Quantization work? - Outcome School](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/how-does-model-quantization-work)
- [llama.cpp repository](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp)
- [ExecuTorch documentation](https://pytorch.org/executorch/)
- [MLC LLM documentation](https://llm.mlc.ai/docs/)

<a id="q493"></a>
### 493. What is model quantization (INT8, INT4, FP16, BF16), and how does it affect quality?

**Answer:**

**Quantisation** stores weights (and optionally activations/KV cache) in lower-precision numeric formats, reducing memory and bandwidth and increasing speed.

**Formats**
| Format | Bits | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| FP32 | 32 | Training master weights/accumulators |
| FP16 | 16 | 5-bit exponent, 10-bit mantissa; limited range, may need loss scaling |
| BF16 | 16 | 8-bit exponent (FP32 range), 7-bit mantissa; standard for training/serving, no loss scaling |
| FP8 (E4M3/E5M2) | 8 | Hopper/Blackwell tensor cores; ~2x throughput vs FP16 |
| INT8 | 8 | Integer with scale (and zero-point) |
| INT4 / FP4 | 4 | ~4x smaller than FP16; needs group-wise scales |

**Basic scheme**: q = round(x / s) + z; dequantise x ~ s (q - z). Scale s per tensor, per channel, or per **group** (e.g. 64-128 weights) - finer granularity means better accuracy, more overhead.

**Approaches**
- **PTQ (post-training)**: no retraining. Weight-only (GPTQ, AWQ, GGUF K-quants) and weight+activation (SmoothQuant, FP8, LLM.int8 with outlier handling).
- **QAT**: simulate quantisation during training for best low-bit quality; QLoRA fine-tunes on 4-bit NF4 base.

**Effect on quality**
- BF16/FP16: essentially lossless. FP8/INT8: typically negligible loss (<~1% on benchmarks).
- 4-bit weight-only with good methods: small degradation (often 1-3% on benchmarks), larger on reasoning, long-context, code, multilingual, and small models.
- <=3-bit: noticeable drops unless using advanced methods.
- **Activation outliers** in LLMs make activation quantisation harder than weight-only.

**Speed benefit**: decode is bandwidth-bound, so weight-only INT4 gives up to ~3-4x decode speedup; compute-bound prefill benefits from FP8/INT8 matmuls.

**Practice**: start with FP8/INT8, evaluate on your own tasks, use AWQ/GPTQ 4-bit for memory-constrained cases, keep sensitive layers in higher precision, compare perplexity plus downstream evals.

**Sources:**
- [How does Model Quantization work? - Outcome School](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/how-does-model-quantization-work)
- [AI Engineering Explained: LLM, RAG, MCP, Agent, Fine-Tuning, Quantization - video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lnfWvX66FUk)
- [LLM.int8(): 8-bit Matrix Multiplication for Transformers at Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.07339)
- [GPTQ: Accurate Post-Training Quantization for Generative Pre-trained Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.17323)
- [AWQ: Activation-aware Weight Quantization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.00978)
