<a id="q526"></a>
### 526. Write code to detect prompt injection attempts in user inputs.

**Answer:**

There is no perfect detector: prompt injection is an inherent weakness of instruction-following models, so detection is one layer of defence-in-depth. Layers: heuristics, a classifier, an LLM-based screen, and (most important) architectural controls.

```python
import re, unicodedata

PATTERNS = [
    r"ignore (all |any )?(previous|prior|above) (instructions|prompts)",
    r"disregard .{0,40}(system|previous) (prompt|instructions)",
    r"you are now (?:in )?(dan|developer mode|jailbroken)",
    r"reveal .{0,30}(system prompt|hidden instructions)",
    r"(print|repeat|output) .{0,30}(your|the) (instructions|system prompt)",
    r"</?(system|assistant)>|\[/?INST\]|<\|im_start\|>",
]
RX = [re.compile(p, re.I) for p in PATTERNS]

def normalise(text):
    t = unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", text)
    return "".join(c for c in t if unicodedata.category(c) not in ("Cf",))   # strip zero-width chars

def heuristic_score(text):
    t = normalise(text)
    return sum(bool(rx.search(t)) for rx in RX)

def detect(text, clf=None, llm_judge=None):
    if heuristic_score(text) >= 1:
        return {"blocked": True, "reason": "pattern"}
    if clf and clf(text) > 0.8:                       # e.g. fine-tuned DeBERTa / Prompt Guard model
        return {"blocked": True, "reason": "classifier"}
    if llm_judge and llm_judge(text):                 # cheap LLM with strict JSON verdict
        return {"blocked": True, "reason": "llm"}
    return {"blocked": False}
```

**Limits and better defences**
- Regex is trivially bypassed (paraphrase, translation, base64, typos). Use as a cheap first filter and for logging.
- **Indirect injection** (instructions hidden in web pages, emails, documents, tool outputs) is the bigger risk in RAG and agents. Scan retrieved content too.
- **Architectural controls:** least-privilege tools, human confirmation for side effects, separate untrusted content with delimiters and tell the model to treat it as data, no secrets in prompts, output filtering (block markdown image exfiltration), sandboxing, and not combining private data + untrusted content + external communication in one agent.
- Red-team regularly with attack suites and track attack success rate and false positives.

**Sources:**
- [Prompt Injection in LLMs (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/prompt-injection-in-llms)
- [Not what you've signed up for: Indirect Prompt Injection (Greshake et al.)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.12173)
- [OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications](https://owasp.org/www-project-top-10-for-large-language-model-applications/)
- [Anthropic: Mitigate jailbreaks and prompt injections](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/mitigate-jailbreaks)

### 527. Implement an LLM output guardrails system that checks for off-topic responses and PII leakage.

**Answer:**

Structure guardrails as a pipeline of independent validators run on the model output (and inputs), each returning pass/fail plus an action: block, redact, regenerate, or escalate.

```python
import re
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Result:
    ok: bool
    text: str
    reasons: list

PII = {
    "email": re.compile(r"\b[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.-]+\b"),
    "phone": re.compile(r"\b(?:\+?\d{1,3}[ -]?)?(?:\(?\d{2,4}\)?[ -]?)?\d{3}[ -]?\d{3,4}\b"),
    "ssn":   re.compile(r"\b\d{3}-\d{2}-\d{4}\b"),
    "card":  re.compile(r"\b(?:\d[ -]?){13,16}\b"),
}

def luhn(s):
    d = [int(c) for c in re.sub(r"\D", "", s)][::-1]
    return bool(d) and (sum(d[0::2]) + sum(sum(divmod(2 * x, 10)) for x in d[1::2])) % 10 == 0

def pii_guard(text):
    reasons = []
    for name, rx in PII.items():
        for m in rx.finditer(text):
            if name == "card" and not luhn(m.group()): continue
            reasons.append(name); text = text.replace(m.group(), f"[{name.upper()}_REDACTED]")
    return Result(True, text, reasons)          # redact, do not block

def topic_guard(text, question, embed, topic_centroids, th=0.35):
    a = embed(text); a = a / (a @ a) ** 0.5
    best = max(float(a @ c) for c in topic_centroids)
    return Result(best >= th, text, [] if best >= th else ["off_topic"])

def run_guardrails(question, output, embed, centroids, llm_judge=None):
    r = pii_guard(output)
    t = topic_guard(r.text, question, embed, centroids)
    if not t.ok and llm_judge and llm_judge(question, r.text):   # second-stage LLM check
        t = Result(True, r.text, [])
    if not t.ok:
        return Result(False, "I can only help with questions about our product.", t.reasons)
    return Result(True, r.text, r.reasons)
```

**Design notes**
- Prefer proven PII tooling (Microsoft Presidio, cloud DLP) with NER plus regex plus checksums; regex alone gives false positives/negatives.
- Off-topic detection: embedding similarity to allowed-topic centroids, a small classifier, or an LLM judge; cascade cheap to expensive to control latency.
- Frameworks: NVIDIA NeMo Guardrails, Guardrails AI, Llama Guard for safety classification.
- Guard both input and output; stream carefully (buffer or check chunks); log violations; measure false-positive rate because over-blocking hurts UX.

**Sources:**
- [How do LLM guardrails work? (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/how-do-llm-guardrails-work)
- [Microsoft Presidio](https://microsoft.github.io/presidio/)
- [NVIDIA NeMo Guardrails](https://github.com/NVIDIA/NeMo-Guardrails)
- [Llama Guard](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.06674)

<a id="q528"></a>
### 528. Build a multi-agent system where agents have different roles and collaborate on a task.

**Answer:**

Common patterns: **orchestrator-worker** (a planner delegates to specialists), **pipeline** (researcher, writer, reviewer), and **debate/critic loops**. Each agent is an LLM with its own system prompt, tools, and context; a coordinator routes messages and enforces budgets.

```python
def make_agent(name, system, tools=()):
    def run(task, context=""):
        return agent_loop(system=system, tools=tools,
                          user=f"{task}\n\nContext:\n{context}", max_steps=6)
    run.name = name
    return run

researcher = make_agent("researcher", "Find facts using search. Return bullet findings with source URLs.", tools=[web_search])
writer     = make_agent("writer",     "Write a clear 300-word brief using ONLY the provided findings.")
reviewer   = make_agent("reviewer",   'Check the draft against the findings. Return JSON {"approved": bool, "issues": [..]}.')

def orchestrate(goal, max_rounds=3):
    plan = llm_json("Break this goal into research questions (max 3): " + goal)
    findings = "\n".join(researcher(q) for q in plan["questions"])   # could run in parallel
    draft = writer(goal, findings)
    for _ in range(max_rounds):
        verdict = llm_json_parse(reviewer(draft, findings))
        if verdict["approved"]:
            return draft
        draft = writer(f"Revise to fix: {verdict['issues']}\n\n{draft}", findings)
    return draft
```

**Design considerations**
- **Structured hand-offs** (JSON, typed messages) beat free chat between agents; pass summaries, not entire transcripts.
- **Parallelise** independent sub-tasks; the orchestrator synthesises.
- **Guardrails:** step and cost budgets, termination conditions, and loop detection; unbounded agent chatter is a classic failure.
- **Tool scoping:** give each role only the tools it needs.
- **Observability:** trace every agent call; multi-agent bugs are hard without traces.
- **When not to:** a single agent with good tools is often cheaper and more reliable; multi-agent helps with parallelisable research, context isolation, and specialised prompts. Costs (tokens) multiply.
- Frameworks: LangGraph, AutoGen, CrewAI, OpenAI Agents SDK.

**Sources:**
- [Multi-Agent Systems (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/multi-agent-systems)
- [Anthropic: How we built our multi-agent research system](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system)

- [MetaGPT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.00352)

<a id="q529"></a>
### 529. Implement scaled dot-product attention with a causal mask from scratch (NumPy or PyTorch).

**Answer:**

Formula: `Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d_k) + M) V`, where `M` is `0` for allowed positions and `-inf` above the diagonal (future tokens). The `1/sqrt(d_k)` scaling keeps dot-product variance near 1 so softmax does not saturate (which would kill gradients).

```python
import torch, math

def causal_attention(q, k, v, attn_mask=None):
    """q, k, v: (batch, heads, seq, d_k). Returns (batch, heads, seq, d_k)."""
    d_k = q.size(-1)
    scores = q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) / math.sqrt(d_k)           # (B, H, T, T)
    T = scores.size(-1)
    causal = torch.triu(torch.ones(T, T, dtype=torch.bool, device=q.device), diagonal=1)
    scores = scores.masked_fill(causal, float("-inf"))           # block future positions
    if attn_mask is not None:                                    # e.g. padding mask (B,1,1,T), True = masked
        scores = scores.masked_fill(attn_mask, float("-inf"))
    weights = torch.softmax(scores, dim=-1)
    return weights @ v, weights
```

NumPy version of the core:

```python
import numpy as np
def attn_np(Q, K, V):
    T, d = Q.shape
    S = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(d)
    S = np.where(np.triu(np.ones((T, T), bool), 1), -np.inf, S)
    S = S - S.max(-1, keepdims=True)                             # numerical stability
    W = np.exp(S); W /= W.sum(-1, keepdims=True)
    return W @ V
```

**Checks:** row `i` of `weights` has zeros for columns `> i`; rows sum to 1; output at position `i` is unchanged if you modify tokens after `i`.

**Notes**
- Use `-inf` (or a large negative number in fp16/bf16 carefully); a fully masked row gives NaN, which happens with padding masks.
- Compute softmax in float32 for stability.
- Memory is O(T^2); production code uses `F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=True)`, which dispatches to FlashAttention-style fused kernels.
- Causal masking is what makes decoder-only training parallel across positions while preserving autoregressive semantics.

**Sources:**
- [Math behind Attention - Q, K, and V (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/math-behind-attention-qkv)
- [Causal Masking in Attention (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/causal-masking-in-attention)
- [Attention Is All You Need](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762)
- [PyTorch scaled_dot_product_attention](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention.html)

<a id="q530"></a>
### 530. Implement multi-head attention, then convert it to grouped-query attention.

**Answer:**

**Multi-head attention (MHA):** project the input into `H` heads of size `d_head = d_model / H`, run attention per head in parallel, concatenate, and apply an output projection.

**Grouped-query attention (GQA):** keep `H` query heads but only `G` key/value heads (`G` divides `H`). Each group of `H/G` query heads shares one K/V head. `G = H` is MHA; `G = 1` is multi-query attention (MQA). The gain is a much smaller KV cache and lower memory bandwidth at decode time, with quality close to MHA.

```python
import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F

class GQA(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, n_heads, n_kv_heads=None):
        super().__init__()
        self.h = n_heads
        self.g = n_kv_heads or n_heads            # n_kv_heads == n_heads -> plain MHA
        assert d_model % n_heads == 0 and n_heads % self.g == 0
        self.dh = d_model // n_heads
        self.wq = nn.Linear(d_model, self.h * self.dh, bias=False)
        self.wk = nn.Linear(d_model, self.g * self.dh, bias=False)   # fewer KV projections
        self.wv = nn.Linear(d_model, self.g * self.dh, bias=False)
        self.wo = nn.Linear(self.h * self.dh, d_model, bias=False)

    def forward(self, x):
        B, T, _ = x.shape
        q = self.wq(x).view(B, T, self.h, self.dh).transpose(1, 2)   # (B, H, T, dh)
        k = self.wk(x).view(B, T, self.g, self.dh).transpose(1, 2)   # (B, G, T, dh)
        v = self.wv(x).view(B, T, self.g, self.dh).transpose(1, 2)
        rep = self.h // self.g
        k = k.repeat_interleave(rep, dim=1)                          # share each KV head across `rep` query heads
        v = v.repeat_interleave(rep, dim=1)
        out = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=True)
        return self.wo(out.transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, T, self.h * self.dh))
```

Usage: `GQA(4096, 32, 32)` is MHA; `GQA(4096, 32, 8)` is GQA with 4x smaller KV cache; `GQA(4096, 32, 1)` is MQA.

**KV cache size per token** = `2 * n_layers * n_kv_heads * d_head * bytes`. Going from 32 to 8 KV heads cuts it by 4x, allowing longer contexts and larger batches.

**Notes:** models trained with MHA can be "uptrained" into GQA by mean-pooling K/V head weights within each group and briefly continuing training. In an optimised implementation avoid the physical `repeat_interleave` (use broadcasting or kernels that index the KV head).

**Sources:**
- [Multi-Head Attention in Transformers (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/multi-head-attention-in-transformers)
- [Grouped Query Attention (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/grouped-query-attention)
- [GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13245)
- [Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head is All You Need (MQA)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.02150)

<a id="q531"></a>
### 531. Implement a KV cache and single-step decode for causal multi-head attention.

**Answer:**

During autoregressive generation, keys and values of past tokens never change. Caching them means each new token computes only its own `q, k, v`, appends `k, v` to the cache, and attends over the cached history. This reduces per-step attention compute from O(T^2) to O(T) (and total generation from O(T^3) to O(T^2)), at the cost of memory.

```python
import torch, torch.nn as nn, math

class CachedMHA(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, n_heads):
        super().__init__()
        self.h, self.dh = n_heads, d_model // n_heads
        self.qkv = nn.Linear(d_model, 3 * d_model, bias=False)
        self.o = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model, bias=False)

    def _split(self, x):
        B, T, _ = x.shape
        return x.view(B, T, self.h, self.dh).transpose(1, 2)          # (B, H, T, dh)

    def forward(self, x, cache=None):
        """x: (B, T_new, D). Prefill: T_new = prompt length, cache=None. Decode: T_new = 1."""
        q, k, v = (self._split(t) for t in self.qkv(x).chunk(3, dim=-1))
        if cache is not None:
            k = torch.cat([cache["k"], k], dim=2)                       # (B, H, T_past + T_new, dh)
            v = torch.cat([cache["v"], v], dim=2)
        new_cache = {"k": k, "v": v}
        T_new, T_all = q.size(2), k.size(2)
        scores = q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) / math.sqrt(self.dh)           # (B, H, T_new, T_all)
        # causal mask: new token i (absolute pos T_all - T_new + i) sees keys <= itself
        mask = torch.ones(T_new, T_all, dtype=torch.bool, device=x.device).tril(diagonal=T_all - T_new)
        scores = scores.masked_fill(~mask, float("-inf"))
        out = torch.softmax(scores, -1) @ v
        out = out.transpose(1, 2).reshape(x.size(0), T_new, -1)
        return self.o(out), new_cache

# usage
attn = CachedMHA(64, 4)
prompt = torch.randn(1, 10, 64)
y, cache = attn(prompt)                       # prefill
tok = torch.randn(1, 1, 64)
y1, cache = attn(tok, cache)                  # one decode step, cache grows to length 11
```

**Sanity test:** the output of prefill+decode must equal a full forward pass over all 11 tokens (`torch.allclose`).

**Notes**
- Positional encodings: with RoPE, rotate `k` using its absolute position before caching.
- Memory per token: `2 * layers * kv_heads * d_head * bytes` (which is why GQA/MQA help). Repeated `torch.cat` reallocates; production systems preallocate (static cache) or use paged allocation (PagedAttention/vLLM).
- Prefill is compute-bound; decode is memory-bandwidth-bound.

**Sources:**
- [What is KV Cache in LLMs? (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/kv-cache-in-llms)
- [Efficient Memory Management for LLM Serving with PagedAttention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180)
- [Efficiently Scaling Transformer Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.05102)
- [Hugging Face: KV cache strategies](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/kv_cache)

<a id="q532"></a>
### 532. Implement BPE (Byte Pair Encoding) training and encoding from scratch.

**Answer:**

BPE starts from a base vocabulary (bytes, so any text is representable) and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair of tokens into a new token until a target vocab size is reached. Encoding replays the learned merges, in the order learned, on new text.

```python
from collections import Counter

def get_pairs(ids):
    return Counter(zip(ids, ids[1:]))

def merge(ids, pair, new_id):
    out, i = [], 0
    while i < len(ids):
        if i < len(ids) - 1 and (ids[i], ids[i + 1]) == pair:
            out.append(new_id); i += 2
        else:
            out.append(ids[i]); i += 1
    return out

def train(text, vocab_size):
    ids = list(text.encode("utf-8"))                 # base vocab: 256 bytes
    merges = {}                                      # (a, b) -> new id, insertion order = priority
    for new_id in range(256, vocab_size):
        pairs = get_pairs(ids)
        if not pairs: break
        best = max(pairs, key=pairs.get)             # most frequent pair (ties: first seen)
        ids = merge(ids, best, new_id)
        merges[best] = new_id
    return merges

def build_vocab(merges):
    vocab = {i: bytes([i]) for i in range(256)}
    for (a, b), new_id in merges.items():
        vocab[new_id] = vocab[a] + vocab[b]
    return vocab

def encode(text, merges):
    ids = list(text.encode("utf-8"))
    while len(ids) >= 2:
        pairs = get_pairs(ids)
        best = min(pairs, key=lambda p: merges.get(p, float("inf")))   # earliest-learned merge present
        if best not in merges: break
        ids = merge(ids, best, merges[best])
    return ids

def decode(ids, vocab):
    return b"".join(vocab[i] for i in ids).decode("utf-8", errors="replace")

merges = train("low lower lowest newer newest wider", 280)
vocab = build_vocab(merges)
assert decode(encode("lowest wider", merges), vocab) == "lowest wider"
```

**Refinements used in real tokenizers**
- **Pre-tokenisation:** split text with a regex (words, digits, punctuation, whitespace) so merges never cross word boundaries; train on word-frequency counts instead of the raw stream (much faster).
- **Special tokens** (`<|endoftext|>`), and byte-level fallback so there is no unknown token (GPT-2 style).
- Efficiency: incremental pair-count updates and priority queues instead of recounting every iteration (O(n) per merge here).
- Related: WordPiece (likelihood-based merging), Unigram LM (SentencePiece).

**Sources:**
- [Byte Pair Encoding (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/bpe-in-llms)
- [Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units](https://arxiv.org/abs/1508.07909)
- [Andrej Karpathy: minbpe](https://github.com/karpathy/minbpe)
- [Hugging Face: Byte-Pair Encoding tokenization](https://huggingface.co/learn/llm-course/chapter6/5)

<a id="q533"></a>
### 533. Implement top-k, top-p, and temperature sampling over a logits vector.

**Answer:**

Order of operations (the common convention): apply **temperature** to logits, then **top-k** filter, then **top-p** filter, then softmax and sample.

- **Temperature `T`:** `softmax(logits / T)`. `T < 1` sharpens (more deterministic); `T > 1` flattens; `T -> 0` approaches greedy.
- **Top-k:** keep only the k highest-logit tokens.
- **Top-p (nucleus):** keep the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability is at least `p`; the set size adapts to how peaked the distribution is.

```python
import numpy as np

def sample(logits, temperature=1.0, top_k=0, top_p=1.0, rng=np.random.default_rng()):
    logits = np.asarray(logits, dtype=np.float64)
    if temperature == 0:
        return int(np.argmax(logits))                       # greedy
    logits = logits / temperature

    if top_k and top_k < logits.size:
        kth = np.partition(logits, -top_k)[-top_k]
        logits = np.where(logits < kth, -np.inf, logits)    # ties at the threshold are kept

    if top_p < 1.0:
        order = np.argsort(-logits)
        probs = softmax(logits[order])
        cum = np.cumsum(probs)
        cutoff = np.searchsorted(cum, top_p) + 1            # include the token that crosses p
        remove = order[cutoff:]
        logits[remove] = -np.inf

    probs = softmax(logits)
    return int(rng.choice(logits.size, p=probs))

def softmax(x):
    x = x - np.max(x)                                       # numerical stability
    e = np.exp(x)
    return e / e.sum()
```

**Details and pitfalls**
- Always include at least one token (the crossing token in top-p; `top_k >= 1`).
- Subtract the max before `exp` to avoid overflow.
- Typical settings: chat `T` around 0.7, `top_p` around 0.9-0.95; deterministic tasks `T = 0`. Tuning both temperature and top-p at once makes behaviour hard to reason about; change one.
- Related: min-p, repetition/frequency penalties (applied to logits before sampling), and beam search for non-sampling decoding. `T=0` is not perfectly deterministic on GPUs (floating-point non-associativity, batching).

**Sources:**
- [The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration (nucleus sampling)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.09751)
- [Hierarchical Neural Story Generation (top-k sampling)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.04833)
- [Hugging Face: Text generation strategies](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/generation_strategies)
- [Hugging Face: How to generate text](https://huggingface.co/blog/how-to-generate)

<a id="q534"></a>
### 534. Implement an LRU cache with O(1) get/put, then add per-entry TTL.

**Answer:**

**LRU:** a hash map for O(1) lookup plus a doubly linked list ordered by recency (head = most recent). Python's `OrderedDict` provides both (`move_to_end`, `popitem(last=False)`).

```python
from collections import OrderedDict
import time, threading

class LRUCache:
    def __init__(self, capacity, default_ttl=None, clock=time.monotonic):
        self.cap, self.ttl, self.clock = capacity, default_ttl, clock
        self.d = OrderedDict()                     # key -> (value, expires_at or None)
        self.lock = threading.Lock()

    def _expired(self, exp):
        return exp is not None and self.clock() >= exp

    def get(self, key, default=None):
        with self.lock:
            item = self.d.get(key)
            if item is None: return default
            value, exp = item
            if self._expired(exp):                 # lazy expiration on access
                del self.d[key]; return default
            self.d.move_to_end(key)                # mark most recently used
            return value

    def put(self, key, value, ttl=None):
        ttl = self.ttl if ttl is None else ttl
        exp = self.clock() + ttl if ttl is not None else None
        with self.lock:
            if key in self.d: self.d.move_to_end(key)
            self.d[key] = (value, exp)
            if len(self.d) > self.cap:
                self._evict()

    def _evict(self):
        # prefer purging expired entries before evicting live LRU ones
        for k in [k for k, (_, e) in self.d.items() if self._expired(e)][:8]:
            del self.d[k]
        while len(self.d) > self.cap:
            self.d.popitem(last=False)             # least recently used
```

**Complexity:** get/put O(1) amortised. The expired-scan above is bounded (sample of 8) but a bulk scan is O(n); for strict bounds keep a **min-heap of `(expires_at, key)`** with lazy deletion (validate that the heap entry matches the current expiry), giving O(log n) purges.

**Design notes**
- Use a monotonic clock (immune to wall-clock jumps) and inject it for deterministic tests.
- TTL and LRU are independent: an entry can be evicted before it expires.
- Decide whether `get` refreshes TTL (sliding expiration) or not (absolute); state it explicitly.
- For a from-scratch interview version, implement the doubly linked list with sentinel head/tail nodes and a dict `key -> node`.
- Thread safety: a lock (or sharded locks); `functools.lru_cache` covers simple function memoisation.

**Sources:**
- [Python functools.lru_cache](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functools.html#functools.lru_cache)
- [Python collections.OrderedDict](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.html#collections.OrderedDict)
- [Cache replacement policies (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cache_replacement_policies)
- [Anthropic: Prompt caching (cache TTL in practice)](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/prompt-caching)

<a id="q535"></a>
### 535. Implement a token-bucket rate limiter for an LLM API where cost scales with tokens, then make it distributed.

**Answer:**

**Token bucket:** a bucket holds up to `capacity` units and refills at `rate` units per second. A request costs units; if enough are available it proceeds, otherwise it waits or is rejected. It allows bursts up to `capacity` while enforcing the long-run average rate. For LLMs the unit is **tokens** (TPM limits), not requests, and the cost is only partly known up front: input tokens are known, output tokens are estimated (`max_tokens`) then **reconciled** after completion.

```python
import time, threading

class TokenBucket:
    def __init__(self, rate_per_sec, capacity, clock=time.monotonic):
        self.rate, self.cap, self.clock = rate_per_sec, capacity, clock
        self.tokens, self.ts = capacity, clock()
        self.lock = threading.Lock()

    def _refill(self):
        now = self.clock()
        self.tokens = min(self.cap, self.tokens + (now - self.ts) * self.rate)
        self.ts = now

    def try_acquire(self, cost):
        with self.lock:
            self._refill()
            if cost <= self.tokens:
                self.tokens -= cost; return True
            return False

    def wait_time(self, cost):
        with self.lock:
            self._refill()
            return max(0.0, (cost - self.tokens) / self.rate)

    def refund(self, amount):                      # reconcile: estimated - actual
        with self.lock:
            self.tokens = min(self.cap, self.tokens + amount)

def call_llm(bucket, prompt_tokens, max_tokens, do_call):
    est = prompt_tokens + max_tokens               # reserve worst case
    while not bucket.try_acquire(est):
        time.sleep(bucket.wait_time(est))
    resp = do_call()
    bucket.refund(est - resp.usage.total_tokens)   # give back unused
    return resp
```

Note: a request whose cost exceeds `capacity` can never be admitted; reject it or cap `max_tokens`.

**Distributed version:** keep state in Redis and refill+consume **atomically** with a Lua script (so concurrent workers cannot race).

```python
LUA = """
local key, rate, cap, now, cost = KEYS[1], tonumber(ARGV[1]), tonumber(ARGV[2]), tonumber(ARGV[3]), tonumber(ARGV[4])
local d = redis.call('HMGET', key, 'tokens', 'ts')
local tokens, ts = tonumber(d[1]) or cap, tonumber(d[2]) or now
tokens = math.min(cap, tokens + (now - ts) * rate)
local ok = 0
if tokens >= cost then tokens = tokens - cost; ok = 1 end
redis.call('HSET', key, 'tokens', tokens, 'ts', now)
redis.call('EXPIRE', key, math.ceil(cap / rate) * 2)
return ok
"""
# ok = r.eval(LUA, 1, f"rl:{tenant}", rate, cap, r.time()[0] + r.time()[1]/1e6, cost)
```

**Distributed concerns:** use Redis server time (not client clocks); one bucket per tenant/model/key; a two-level limit (RPM and TPM); Redis latency on the hot path (local pre-check or batched leases); failure mode (fail open vs closed); fairness and priority queues; honour upstream 429 and `Retry-After` headers; sharding by key.

**Sources:**
- [Token bucket (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Token_bucket)
- [Stripe: Scaling your API with rate limiters](https://stripe.com/blog/rate-limiters)
- [Redis: Lua scripting and EVAL](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/interact/programmability/eval-intro/)

<a id="q536"></a>
### 536. Write an async batch processor that runs an LLM call over 50,000 documents with a concurrency limit, retries with jitter, and error isolation.

**Answer:**

Requirements: bounded concurrency (do not create 50k tasks that all hit the API), per-item retries with jittered backoff, one failure must not kill the batch, and resumability (checkpointing) because a 50k run will be interrupted.

```python
import asyncio, random, json, os

async def process_all(docs, call_llm, concurrency=32, max_attempts=5, out_path="results.jsonl"):
    done = set()
    if os.path.exists(out_path):                                 # resume support
        with open(out_path) as f:
            done = {json.loads(l)["id"] for l in f}
    todo = [d for d in docs if d["id"] not in done]

    queue = asyncio.Queue(maxsize=concurrency * 4)
    write_lock = asyncio.Lock()
    stats = {"ok": 0, "failed": 0}

    async def handle(doc, out):
        for attempt in range(max_attempts):
            try:
                result = await asyncio.wait_for(call_llm(doc["text"]), timeout=60)
                rec = {"id": doc["id"], "ok": True, "result": result}
                stats["ok"] += 1
                break
            except (asyncio.TimeoutError, RetryableError) as e:
                if attempt == max_attempts - 1:
                    rec = {"id": doc["id"], "ok": False, "error": repr(e)}; stats["failed"] += 1
                else:
                    await asyncio.sleep(random.uniform(0, min(30, 0.5 * 2 ** attempt)))   # full jitter
            except Exception as e:                               # non-retryable: isolate, don't crash
                rec = {"id": doc["id"], "ok": False, "error": repr(e)}; stats["failed"] += 1
                break
        async with write_lock:
            out.write(json.dumps(rec) + "\n"); out.flush()

    async def worker(out):
        while True:
            doc = await queue.get()
            try:
                await handle(doc, out)
            finally:
                queue.task_done()

    with open(out_path, "a") as out:
        workers = [asyncio.create_task(worker(out)) for _ in range(concurrency)]
        for d in todo:
            await queue.put(d)                                   # backpressure via bounded queue
        await queue.join()
        for w in workers: w.cancel()
    return stats
```

**Why this design**
- A **fixed worker pool with a bounded queue** keeps memory flat and gives natural backpressure (alternatively `asyncio.Semaphore` + `gather`, but that creates all tasks up front).
- **Error isolation:** exceptions caught per item; failures recorded, not raised. Re-run only failed ids later (dead-letter file).
- **Jitter** prevents synchronised retry waves; pair with a global rate limiter (token bucket) and adapt concurrency down on 429s.
- **Idempotent output + checkpointing** (append JSONL keyed by id) makes the job resumable.
- **Cost control:** dedupe inputs, estimate tokens, and consider the provider's **Batch API** (asynchronous, typically discounted) when latency is not required.
- Track progress, throughput, error rate, and total spend; graceful shutdown on SIGINT.

**Sources:**
- [Python asyncio: Queues](https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio-queue.html)
- [AWS: Exponential Backoff and Jitter](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/architecture/exponential-backoff-and-jitter/)
- [OpenAI Batch API guide](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/batch)
- [Anthropic: Message Batches](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/batch-processing)

<a id="q537"></a>
### 537. Write a streaming SSE parser for LLM token streams that handles arbitrary chunk boundaries.

**Answer:**

SSE is a text protocol: events are separated by a blank line; each line is `field: value` (`data`, `event`, `id`, `retry`); lines starting with `:` are comments; multiple `data:` lines in one event are joined with `\n`. Network chunks can split anywhere, including mid-line, mid-event, in the middle of a multibyte UTF-8 character, or between `\r` and `\n`. So the parser must **buffer bytes, decode incrementally, and only emit complete events**.

```python
import codecs, json

class SSEParser:
    def __init__(self):
        self.decoder = codecs.getincrementaldecoder("utf-8")()   # safe across split multibyte chars
        self.buf = ""
        self.cr_pending = False
        self.event, self.data, self.last_id = "message", [], None

    def feed(self, chunk: bytes):
        text = self.decoder.decode(chunk)
        if self.cr_pending and text.startswith("\n"):             # \r | \n split across chunks
            text = text[1:]
        self.cr_pending = text.endswith("\r")
        self.buf += text.replace("\r\n", "\n").replace("\r", "\n")
        *lines, self.buf = self.buf.split("\n")                   # last piece may be incomplete
        for line in lines:
            ev = self._line(line)
            if ev: yield ev

    def _line(self, line):
        if line == "":                                            # dispatch event
            if not self.data:
                self.event = "message"; return None
            ev = {"event": self.event, "data": "\n".join(self.data), "id": self.last_id}
            self.event, self.data = "message", []
            return ev
        if line.startswith(":"):                                  # comment / keep-alive
            return None
        field, _, value = line.partition(":")
        value = value[1:] if value.startswith(" ") else value
        if field == "data": self.data.append(value)
        elif field == "event": self.event = value
        elif field == "id": self.last_id = value
        return None

# usage with an LLM stream
p = SSEParser()
for chunk in http_stream_bytes():                                # arbitrary boundaries
    for ev in p.feed(chunk):
        if ev["data"] == "[DONE]": break
        delta = json.loads(ev["data"])["choices"][0]["delta"].get("content", "")
        print(delta, end="", flush=True)
```

**Tests to write:** feed the same stream split at every byte offset (and random splits) and assert identical events; include CRLF, multi-line `data:`, comments, emoji split across chunks, a trailing partial event (should be discarded at EOF), and a `[DONE]` sentinel.

**Provider specifics:** OpenAI-style streams send `data: {json}` then `data: [DONE]`; Anthropic sends typed `event:` names (`content_block_delta`, `message_stop`). Tool-call arguments arrive as JSON string fragments that must be accumulated and parsed only once complete. Handle mid-stream `error` events and disconnects.

**Sources:**
- [How does Token Streaming work? (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/how-does-token-streaming-work)
- [WHATWG: Server-Sent Events specification](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/server-sent-events.html)
- [Anthropic: Streaming Messages](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/streaming)
- [OpenAI: Streaming responses](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/streaming-responses)

<a id="q538"></a>
### 538. Implement a minimal agent loop with tool dispatch, error handling, and a step budget.

**Answer:**

The loop: send messages plus tool schemas, inspect the response, if it contains tool calls execute them and append results, repeat until the model returns a final answer or a budget is exhausted.

```python
import json, time
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Budget:
    max_steps: int = 10
    max_seconds: float = 120
    max_tokens: int = 100_000

def agent_loop(llm, tools, messages, budget=Budget(), confirm=None):
    """llm(messages, tool_schemas) -> {'content': str|None, 'tool_calls': [{'id','name','args'}], 'usage': int}"""
    start, tokens = time.monotonic(), 0
    seen = {}                                                    # loop detection
    schemas = [t.schema for t in tools.values()]

    for step in range(budget.max_steps):
        if time.monotonic() - start > budget.max_seconds or tokens > budget.max_tokens:
            return {"status": "budget_exceeded", "messages": messages}
        resp = llm(messages, schemas)
        tokens += resp["usage"]
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": resp["content"], "tool_calls": resp["tool_calls"]})

        if not resp["tool_calls"]:
            return {"status": "done", "answer": resp["content"], "steps": step + 1}

        for call in resp["tool_calls"]:
            sig = (call["name"], json.dumps(call["args"], sort_keys=True))
            seen[sig] = seen.get(sig, 0) + 1
            if seen[sig] > 2:
                out = "ERROR: you already made this exact call repeatedly; try a different approach or answer."
            elif call["name"] not in tools:
                out = f"ERROR: unknown tool {call['name']}. Available: {list(tools)}"
            elif tools[call["name"]].needs_approval and confirm and not confirm(call):
                out = "ERROR: user denied this action."
            else:
                try:
                    out = str(tools[call["name"]].run(**call["args"]))[:8000]   # truncate huge outputs
                except TypeError as e:
                    out = f"ERROR: bad arguments: {e}"
                except Exception as e:
                    out = f"ERROR: {type(e).__name__}: {e}"
            messages.append({"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": call["id"], "content": out})

    return {"status": "max_steps", "messages": messages}
```

**What matters**
- **Errors become observations**, so the model can retry or change approach; only infrastructure failures abort.
- **Budgets** on steps, wall time, tokens/cost; on exhaustion, return a partial result or force a final "summarise what you have" call rather than failing silently.
- **Loop detection** (identical repeated calls) and truncation of oversized tool output.
- **Safety:** allow-listed tools, argument validation, human approval for destructive actions, sandboxed execution, and prompt-injection-aware handling of tool output.
- **Observability:** log each step (prompt, tool, latency, tokens) for debugging and evaluation.
- Every assistant tool call must get a matching tool result message.

**Sources:**
- [AI Agent Loop (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/ai-agent-loop)
- [Anthropic: Building effective agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents)
- [ReAct](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629)
- [Anthropic tool use documentation](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/tool-use)

## Behavioral and Scenario-Based Questions

<a id="q539"></a>
### 539. What is AI Engineering, and how does it differ from Machine Learning Engineering?

**Answer:**

**AI Engineering** is the discipline of building products and systems on top of pre-trained (foundation) models: choosing models, prompting, retrieval, tool use, fine-tuning when needed, evaluation, deployment, and monitoring. **ML Engineering** traditionally centres on building and training models (feature engineering, training pipelines, model architecture, MLOps for custom models).

| Dimension | ML Engineering | AI Engineering |
|---|---|---|
| Starting point | Data, then train a model | Existing foundation model (API or open weights) |
| Main levers | Features, architecture, hyperparameters | Prompts, context/RAG, tools, fine-tuning, orchestration |
| Data needs | Large labelled datasets | Small eval sets, documents, few examples |
| Iteration speed | Days to weeks per training cycle | Minutes to hours (prompt/pipeline changes) |
| Evaluation | Well-defined metrics on held-out labels | Open-ended outputs: LLM judges, human review, task rubrics |
| Failure modes | Overfitting, drift | Hallucination, prompt injection, non-determinism, cost/latency |
| Skills | Statistics, deep learning, feature pipelines | Software engineering, product sense, evals, infra, security |

**Overlap:** both need data quality, experiment tracking, monitoring, and deployment discipline. AI engineers often need ML knowledge (embeddings, fine-tuning, quantisation) but the centre of gravity is **software engineering around models**: reliability, evaluation, observability, cost management, guardrails.

**Interview tip:** stress that the AI engineer's leverage is evaluation and system design, since building a demo is easy but making it reliable, measurable, and affordable is the job. Mention the shift from "model-centric" to "application-centric" work.

**Sources:**
- [Chip Huyen: Building A Generative AI Platform](https://huyenchip.com/2024/07/25/genai-platform.html)
- [Chip Huyen: AI Engineering (O'Reilly)](https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/ai-engineering/9781098166298/)
- [Latent Space: The Rise of the AI Engineer](https://www.latent.space/p/ai-engineer)
- [Google: Rules of Machine Learning](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/guides/rules-of-ml)

<a id="q540"></a>
### 540. How do you decide whether a problem needs AI or a traditional software solution?

**Answer:**

Start from the problem and the cost of being wrong, not from the technology. Use the simplest solution that meets the requirement.

**Decision questions**
1. **Can the logic be written as explicit rules?** If yes (validation, calculations, routing by fixed criteria), use code: it is deterministic, testable, cheap, and explainable.
2. **Is the input unstructured or the rules too numerous/fuzzy?** Natural language, images, audio, messy documents, or "I know it when I see it" judgements favour AI.
3. **Is an imperfect answer acceptable?** Tasks where 90-95% accuracy with human review adds value fit AI; tasks needing 100% correctness (payments, compliance decisions) need deterministic logic or AI only as a suggestion layer.
4. **Is there a fallback and human-in-the-loop path?**
5. **Do latency, cost, and privacy budgets fit?** An LLM call costs cents and seconds versus microseconds for code.
6. **Can you evaluate it?** If you cannot define success and build a test set, you cannot manage an AI feature.
7. **Is the value large enough** to cover build, run, and maintenance costs (evals, monitoring, model upgrades)?

**Practical approach**
- Prototype a baseline (regex, rules, keyword search, classical ML) first; compare against the LLM on a small labelled set.
- Prefer **hybrid** designs: deterministic code for control flow and validation, AI for the fuzzy step (extraction, classification, summarisation).
- Prefer a small classifier or traditional ML when the task is narrow, high volume, and labelled data exists.

**Example:** "Extract invoice fields" is a good LLM/vision fit; "compute VAT on those fields" stays as code.

**Sources:**
- [Google: Rules of Machine Learning (Rule 1: don't be afraid to launch without ML)](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/guides/rules-of-ml)
- [Anthropic: Building effective agents (find the simplest solution)](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents)
- [Eugene Yan: Patterns for Building LLM-based Systems](https://eugeneyan.com/writing/llm-patterns/)
- [Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems](https://papers.nips.cc/paper/2015/hash/86df7dcfd896fcaf2674f757a2463eba-Abstract.html)

<a id="q541"></a>
### 541. How do you measure the ROI of an AI feature?

**Answer:**

ROI = (measured benefit - total cost) / total cost. The difficulty is attributing benefit and counting all costs.

**Benefits (pick metrics tied to the business goal)**
- Efficiency: time saved per task, tickets deflected, handling time, throughput per employee.
- Revenue: conversion, retention, upsell, engagement.
- Quality: error rate, CSAT/NPS, first-contact resolution.
- Risk: compliance findings avoided.

**Costs**
- Inference (tokens, GPUs), retrieval/vector infra, tooling and observability.
- Engineering and product time to build, plus ongoing evals, prompt/model upgrades, and on-call.
- Human review, data labelling, legal/security review.
- Failure costs: escalations, incorrect answers, incident handling.

**How to measure credibly**
1. Establish a **baseline** before launch (current handling time, cost per ticket).
2. Run an **A/B test or staged rollout** with a control group; avoid before/after comparisons confounded by seasonality.
3. Track **leading indicators** (acceptance rate of suggestions, edit distance, thumbs up/down) and **lagging business KPIs**.
4. Compute **unit economics**: cost per successful task, not cost per request. A cheaper model that fails more often may cost more overall.
5. Account for adoption: benefit = per-user gain x active usage; low adoption kills ROI.
6. Report ranges and assumptions; revisit as token prices and model quality change.

**Example:** a support copilot cuts average handling time by 20% for 50 agents; multiply by loaded hourly cost, subtract inference plus maintenance, and compare against a control group.

**Pitfalls:** vanity metrics (usage without outcomes), ignoring maintenance costs, and treating token cost as the whole cost.

**Sources:**
- [Chip Huyen: Building A Generative AI Platform](https://huyenchip.com/2024/07/25/genai-platform.html)
- [Anthropic: Define your success criteria](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/test-and-evaluate/define-success)
- [Eugene Yan: Patterns for Building LLM-based Systems](https://eugeneyan.com/writing/llm-patterns/)
- [Google: Rules of Machine Learning](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/guides/rules-of-ml)

<a id="q542"></a>
### 542. How do you handle hallucinations when they occur in a production AI system?

**Answer:**

Treat it as an incident-management and continuous-improvement problem with layers: contain, diagnose, fix, prevent.

**1. Contain (immediate)**
- Reproduce from logged trace (prompt, retrieved context, model version, parameters).
- If harmful, mitigate fast: feature flag, stricter refusal behaviour, disable the affected path, or route to a human.
- Communicate to affected users when the impact warrants it.

**2. Diagnose (find the root cause)**
- **Retrieval failure:** the right document was not retrieved, so the model guessed.
- **Context failure:** answer present but ignored (too long, poorly ordered, conflicting sources).
- **Knowledge gap:** no grounding at all, the model answered from parametric memory.
- **Prompt/instruction issue:** no permission to say "I don't know".
- **Generation issue:** sampling too hot, weak model for the task.

**3. Fix**
- Ground with RAG and require citations/quotes; instruct "answer only from the context, else say you don't know".
- Improve retrieval (chunking, hybrid search, reranking).
- Lower temperature, use a stronger model, or constrain output with structured formats.
- Add verification: groundedness check, citation validation, self-consistency, or tool-based verification (calculator, database query instead of free-text recall).
- Add abstention thresholds and human escalation for low confidence or high-stakes topics.

**4. Prevent**
- Add the failing case to a regression eval set; run evals in CI.
- Monitor online (groundedness scores on sampled traffic, user feedback, escalation rates).
- UX: show sources, communicate uncertainty, make verification easy.

**Key point:** you cannot reach zero hallucination; you design so errors are rare, detectable, low-impact, and recoverable.

**Sources:**
- [Anthropic: Reduce hallucinations](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-hallucinations)
- [Survey of Hallucination in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.05232)
- [SelfCheckGPT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.08896)
- [Seven Failure Points When Engineering a RAG System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.05856)

<a id="q543"></a>
### 543. How do you decide between using an LLM API vs self-hosting an open-source model?

**Answer:**

Start with an API to validate value, then revisit self-hosting when data shows a clear reason.

| Factor | API (hosted) | Self-host (open weights) |
|---|---|---|
| Time to market | Hours | Weeks (infra, serving, tuning) |
| Quality ceiling | Frontier models | Strong but usually a step behind the frontier; can be fine-tuned for a narrow task |
| Cost at low/variable volume | Pay per token, cheap | GPUs idle, expensive |
| Cost at high steady volume | Can be large | Often cheaper per token if utilisation is high |
| Data privacy / residency | Depends on contract (zero retention, regional endpoints) | Full control, on-prem/VPC |
| Latency control | Provider-dependent, shared | Tunable (batching, quantisation, speculative decoding) |
| Customisation | Prompting, limited fine-tuning | Full fine-tuning, LoRA, custom decoding |
| Operations | Provider handles scaling, uptime | You own serving, upgrades, monitoring, on-call |
| Vendor risk | Deprecations, price/policy changes | Model stays fixed and reproducible |

**Decision drivers**
- **Compliance:** regulated data that cannot leave your boundary points to self-hosting (or private cloud offerings from providers).
- **Scale and utilisation:** compute break-even using real traffic (tokens/day, peak-to-average ratio) and total cost including engineers and GPUs.
- **Task difficulty:** hard reasoning/agentic tasks usually need frontier APIs; narrow classification or extraction can run on a small tuned model.
- **Team capability** to operate GPU serving (vLLM, TGI) reliably.

**Common pragmatic pattern:** hybrid, with a router: small self-hosted model for simple/high-volume traffic and an API model for hard queries, with fallback across providers. Abstract the model behind an interface so migration is cheap, and keep an eval suite to compare candidates objectively.

**Sources:**
- [vLLM documentation](https://docs.vllm.ai/)
- [FrugalGPT: How to Use LLMs While Reducing Cost](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.05176)
- [Chip Huyen: Building A Generative AI Platform](https://huyenchip.com/2024/07/25/genai-platform.html)
- [LLM Routing (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/llm-routing)

<a id="q544"></a>
### 544. How do you manage stakeholder expectations for AI projects?

**Answer:**

The core issue is that AI is probabilistic and demos mislead: stakeholders see a perfect demo and assume production parity.

**Practices**
1. **Define success up front** in business terms with measurable thresholds (accuracy on an agreed test set, deflection rate, time saved) and agree what "good enough to launch" means.
2. **Educate early and concretely:** explain that outputs are probabilistic, show real failure examples, and give error rates instead of adjectives.
3. **Use staged delivery:** prototype, then internal pilot, then limited beta with humans in the loop, then wider rollout. Each stage has exit criteria.
4. **Share evaluation results regularly** using a stable eval set and a simple dashboard, so progress and regressions are visible and not anecdotal.
5. **Be honest about uncertainty:** provide ranges for timelines (research-like work is uncertain), and identify risks (data quality, hallucination, cost, security) at kickoff.
6. **Frame trade-offs as options:** quality vs latency vs cost vs risk, with a recommendation.
7. **Design the product around failure:** fallbacks, human review, confidence display, feedback buttons. Stakeholders accept imperfection when it is managed.
8. **Align on ownership and maintenance:** models and prompts need ongoing evaluation, budget, and model upgrades.
9. **Say no early** to use cases where AI is a poor fit.

**Sample line:** "On our 300-question test set the assistant answers 88% correctly, 7% abstains, and 5% wrong; for the wrong ones a human reviews before customers see them. Here is our plan to get wrong answers under 2%."

**Interviewers look for:** communication clarity, data-based framing, risk awareness, and pushing back constructively.

**Sources:**
- [Google: People + AI Guidebook](https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/)
- [Anthropic: Define your success criteria](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/test-and-evaluate/define-success)
- [Eugene Yan: Patterns for Building LLM-based Systems](https://eugeneyan.com/writing/llm-patterns/)
- [NIST AI Risk Management Framework](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework)

<a id="q545"></a>
### 545. Describe your approach to debugging a poor-performing RAG system.

**Answer:**

Debug RAG by **separating retrieval from generation** and measuring each stage, instead of tweaking prompts blindly.

**Step 1: build a diagnostic eval set.** 50-200 real questions with reference answers and, ideally, the gold source passages. Include hard and failing cases from logs.

**Step 2: classify each failure by stage**

| Symptom | Likely cause | Check |
|---|---|---|
| Right doc not in top-k | Retrieval failure | Recall@k, MRR on gold passages |
| Right doc retrieved but answer wrong | Generation/context issue | Is the evidence in the prompt? Is it ignored? |
| Answer contradicts sources | Hallucination, weak grounding prompt | Groundedness / faithfulness check |
| Answer correct but incomplete | k too small, chunk too small, multi-hop needed | Inspect context |
| Good answer for some users only | Metadata filter/ACL bug, stale index | Filter logs, index freshness |

**Step 3: fix retrieval first (usually the bottleneck)**
- Ingestion: parsing quality (tables, PDFs), chunk size/overlap, metadata, contextual headers.
- Embedding model fit for the domain/language; fine-tune if necessary.
- Hybrid search (BM25 + dense) for IDs, acronyms, rare terms.
- Query rewriting/expansion, HyDE, multi-query, decomposition for multi-hop.
- Reranker over a larger candidate pool.

**Step 4: fix generation**
- Order and trim context (lost-in-the-middle), dedupe, cite sources, allow "I don't know", lower temperature, stronger model if needed.

**Step 5: institutionalise**
- Trace every request (query, rewritten query, retrieved ids/scores, final prompt, answer).
- Automated evals (retrieval metrics + LLM-judged faithfulness/relevance, e.g. RAGAS) in CI; change one variable at a time; monitor production with user feedback.

**Outcome:** a ranked list of failure categories with measured impact, so the team fixes the largest contributor first.

**Sources:**
- [Seven Failure Points When Engineering a RAG System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.05856)
- [RAGAS](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.15217)
- [Lost in the Middle](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172)
- [Anthropic: Contextual Retrieval](https://www.anthropic.com/news/contextual-retrieval)

<a id="q546"></a>
### 546. How do you stay current with the rapidly evolving AI landscape?

**Answer:**

Interviewers want to see a **systematic, filtered, hands-on** habit, not a list of buzzwords.

**A sustainable system**
- **Primary sources (weekly):** arXiv (cs.CL, cs.LG) via curated feeds or Hugging Face Daily Papers; model release notes and docs from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Meta, Mistral; changelogs of the libraries I use (vLLM, LangChain/LangGraph, Hugging Face).
- **Curated commentary:** a few high-signal newsletters/blogs and engineering write-ups (for example Latent Space, Eugene Yan, Chip Huyen, Simon Willison); conference talks (NeurIPS, ICLR, AI Engineer Summit).
- **Hands-on:** rebuild or test new ideas in small experiments; keep a personal eval set to try new models on my own tasks within an hour of release; side projects and open-source contributions.
- **Community:** reading groups at work, internal demos, discussions with peers.
- **Depth over breadth:** learn fundamentals (attention, RL from feedback, retrieval, evaluation, systems) so new papers slot into an existing mental model.

**Filtering:** ask "Does this change a decision on my product?" Track a few themes deeply (for example agents, evals, inference efficiency), skim the rest, and ignore hype until reproduced. Prefer benchmarks I can run myself over leaderboard claims.

**Sharing:** summarise learnings for the team (short notes, lunch-and-learns); teaching cements understanding and spreads context.

**Concrete example to give:** "When a new long-context model was released, I ran it against our internal eval set, measured cost and latency, and wrote a one-page recommendation; we switched one workload and cut cost by X%."

**Sources:**
- [Latent Space podcast and newsletter](https://www.latent.space/)
- [Hugging Face Daily Papers](https://huggingface.co/papers)

- [Simon Willison's Weblog](https://simonwillison.net/)

<a id="q547"></a>
### 547. How do you balance innovation with reliability in AI systems?

**Answer:**

Innovation without reliability erodes trust; reliability without innovation loses the market. The balance comes from **process and architecture**, not from choosing one.

**Principles**
1. **Evals as the safety net:** a regression suite (golden set, adversarial cases, production samples) that gates every prompt, model, or pipeline change. Fast evals enable fast experimentation.
2. **Progressive delivery:** shadow mode, then canary, then A/B, then full rollout with feature flags and instant rollback.
3. **Tiered risk:** experiment aggressively in low-risk surfaces (internal tools, suggestions with human review); be conservative where errors are costly (money, health, legal).
4. **Pin and version everything:** model version, prompt version, index version, parameters; upgrade deliberately, not automatically.
5. **Design for failure:** timeouts, retries, fallbacks (cheaper model, cached answer, non-AI path), guardrails, rate limits, and human escalation.
6. **Observability:** tracing, quality metrics, cost, latency, drift dashboards, and alerts on quality SLOs, not just uptime.
7. **Simple by default:** prefer the simplest architecture that meets the need; add agents/complexity only when evals show a gain worth the maintenance cost.
8. **Time-boxed exploration:** spikes and prototypes in a sandbox with clear graduation criteria to production.

**Example:** trial a new model in shadow mode on 5% of traffic, compare LLM-judged quality, latency, and cost against the current model, then canary with automatic rollback on SLO breach.

**Sources:**
- [Anthropic: Building effective agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents)
- [Google SRE Book: Embracing risk and error budgets](https://sre.google/sre-book/embracing-risk/)
- [Hamel Husain: Your AI product needs evals](https://hamel.dev/blog/posts/evals/)
- [Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems](https://papers.nips.cc/paper/2015/hash/86df7dcfd896fcaf2674f757a2463eba-Abstract.html)

<a id="q548"></a>
### 548. Tell me about a challenging AI project you worked on. What was the problem? What approach did you take? What trade-offs did you make? What was the outcome?

**Answer:**

This is a personal question, so the answer must come from your real experience. Use **STAR** (Situation, Task, Action, Result) and add explicit trade-offs and learnings. Below is a sample structure with an illustrative example (adapt to your own work).

**Sample answer**
- **Situation:** Our support team handled about 20k tickets/month; agents spent much of their time searching a large, messy knowledge base. Leadership wanted an AI assistant for agents.
- **Task:** I owned the RAG pipeline and evaluation. Success criteria: at least 85% of answers judged correct by senior agents, p95 latency under 5 seconds, cost under a set budget per ticket.
- **Action:**
  - Built an eval set of 250 real tickets with agent-written reference answers before writing the system.
  - Baseline RAG scored about 60%; error analysis showed retrieval was the main failure (PDFs parsed badly, chunks split tables, acronym queries missed).
  - Fixed parsing and chunking, added hybrid BM25 + dense search and a reranker, added query rewriting, and grounded answers with citations plus an "I don't know" path.
  - Rolled out in shadow mode, then to a pilot group with a thumbs up/down and edit tracking.
- **Trade-offs:** reranker added roughly 300 ms latency but raised correctness substantially; chose a mid-size model with prompt caching instead of the largest model for cost; chose abstention over answering low-confidence questions, which reduced coverage slightly but increased trust.
- **Result:** correctness rose from about 60% to about 88% on the eval set; average handling time fell about 20% in the pilot; weekly regression evals caught two prompt changes that would have hurt quality.
- **Learnings:** evals first, fix retrieval before prompts, involve end users early.

**What interviewers look for:** a genuinely hard problem, clear ownership, measurable results, honest trade-offs and failures, and reflection. Do not fabricate numbers; use real ones or state approximate ranges. Be ready for deep follow-ups on any detail.

**Sources:**
- [Situation-Behavior-Impact and STAR method overview (Indeed career guide)](https://www.indeed.com/career-advice/interviewing/how-to-use-the-star-interview-response-technique)
- [Seven Failure Points When Engineering a RAG System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.05856)
- [Hamel Husain: Your AI product needs evals](https://hamel.dev/blog/posts/evals/)
- [Eugene Yan: Patterns for Building LLM-based Systems](https://eugeneyan.com/writing/llm-patterns/)

<a id="q549"></a>
### 549. How would you handle a situation where an AI model produces biased or harmful outputs in production?

**Answer:**

Treat it as a severity-graded incident with both an engineering and a governance response.

**1. Respond immediately**
- Triage severity (legal, safety, reputational, affected groups). Escalate to product, legal, security, and trust and safety as needed.
- **Contain:** feature flag off, tighten filters, switch to a safer model or prompt, or add a human review step. Preserve logs and evidence.
- Communicate transparently with stakeholders and, when required, affected users or regulators.

**2. Investigate root cause**
- Reproduce with the logged trace; determine whether the source is the base model, training/fine-tuning data, retrieved content, the prompt, missing guardrails, or an adversarial user (jailbreak).
- Measure scope: slice outputs by demographic, language, and topic to see how widespread and who is affected.

**3. Fix**
- Prompt and policy changes (explicit guidelines, examples), output classifiers/moderation (Llama Guard, provider moderation APIs), stricter retrieval sources.
- Model-level: switch or fine-tune with balanced data, preference tuning against the behaviour.
- Add refusal/escalation paths and human oversight for sensitive decisions.

**4. Prevent**
- Add cases to the eval and red-team suite; use bias benchmarks and counterfactual tests (swap names, genders, or dialects and compare outputs).
- Monitor fairness metrics and harmful-content rates online; set alert thresholds.
- Document in model/system cards and follow a review process before launch (impact assessment).
- Blameless post-mortem and update the launch checklist.

**Key point:** bias cannot be fully eliminated; you measure it, mitigate it, keep humans in high-stakes loops, and stay accountable.

**Sources:**
- [NIST AI Risk Management Framework](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework)
- [Llama Guard](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.06674)
- [Red Teaming Language Models with Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.03286)
- [Model Cards for Model Reporting](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.03993)

<a id="q550"></a>
### 550. How do you approach cost optimization for an AI system that's exceeding budget?

**Answer:**

**First measure, then optimise.** Instrument cost per request, per feature, per tenant, and per successful task; find the top spenders (usually a few features or long-context calls).

**Levers, roughly ordered by impact and effort**
1. **Reduce tokens:** shorten prompts, trim retrieved context (better retrieval, reranking, fewer chunks), cap `max_tokens`, request concise outputs, compress or summarise history.
2. **Prompt caching:** place stable content (system prompt, docs, tool definitions) first so cached prefixes are billed at a discount.
3. **Response and semantic caching** for repeated queries.
4. **Right-size the model:** route easy requests to small/cheap models and hard ones to strong models (routing, cascades); use smaller fine-tuned models for narrow tasks.
5. **Batch APIs** for non-interactive workloads (typically discounted).
6. **Avoid unnecessary calls:** deterministic code where possible, dedupe, early exits, and fewer agent steps (loop limits, cheaper planning).
7. **Self-host or use quantised models** if volume and utilisation justify it (vLLM, batching, speculative decoding).
8. **Product controls:** rate limits, quotas per tier, usage-based pricing.
9. **Fix waste:** retries that duplicate cost, runaway agent loops, streaming continuing after client disconnect.

**Guard quality:** every change is validated on the eval set (cost-quality frontier); track cost per successful task, not raw spend. Set budgets and alerts, and forecast with traffic growth.

**Example:** a support bot reduced cost about 50% by routing 70% of queries to a small model, enabling prompt caching, and cutting retrieved chunks from 10 to 5 after adding a reranker, with no measured quality drop.

**Sources:**
- [FrugalGPT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.05176)
- [Anthropic: Prompt caching](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/prompt-caching)
- [LLM Routing (Outcome School)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/llm-routing)
- [OpenAI: Batch API guide](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/batch)

<a id="q551"></a>
### 551. Describe a time when you had to choose between model accuracy and latency. How did you make the decision?

**Answer:**

Personal question: use a real example and STAR. Key is to show a **data-driven decision framework**, not a hunch.

**Sample answer (illustrative)**
- **Situation:** We built an autocomplete-style assistant inside an editor. The best model gave about 6 points higher quality on our eval set but had p95 latency of about 3.5 s; a smaller model was under 800 ms.
- **Task:** decide which to ship given user experience and cost constraints.
- **Action:**
  1. Defined what users actually needed: interactive suggestions lose value after roughly a second, so we set a p95 latency budget with product.
  2. Ran the eval set on candidate models and measured quality, TTFT, total latency, and cost.
  3. Ran a small user test and looked at acceptance rate; the slower model's suggestions were better but were accepted less because users had moved on.
  4. Explored ways to close the gap: streaming, prompt trimming, caching, speculative decoding, and a **hybrid**, with the small model for inline completions and the larger model on an explicit "improve" action.
- **Result:** shipped the hybrid design; acceptance rate increased about 15% compared to the slow model, cost dropped, and the large model was reserved for high-value moments.
- **Learning:** define quality and latency budgets from the user journey; measure end-to-end outcomes.

**Framework to cite:** latency budget from UX, quality floor from evals, cost, and options that avoid a binary choice (routing, streaming, distillation, quantisation, caching, async processing).

**Interviewers look for:** explicit metrics, stakeholder alignment, and creative alternatives.

**Sources:**
- [Efficient Memory Management for LLM Serving with PagedAttention (vLLM)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180)
- [Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.17192)
- [Anthropic: Reducing latency](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-latency)
- [FrugalGPT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.05176)

<a id="q552"></a>
### 552. How would you handle a situation where your AI system's quality degrades over time?

**Answer:**

Degradation is expected; the question is how quickly you detect and diagnose it.

**Detect**
- Continuous **online evaluation** on sampled production traffic (LLM-judge scores, groundedness, task success), plus user signals (thumbs down, regeneration rate, escalations, edits).
- A **fixed golden set** run on a schedule to separate real regressions from input shift.
- Alerts on quality SLOs, refusal rates, output length, latency, and cost anomalies.

**Diagnose: common causes**
- **Provider/model change:** silent updates behind an alias; behaviour of hosted models can change over time. Pin dated model versions.
- **Data drift:** user queries shift (new topics, languages, seasonality).
- **Knowledge drift:** stale or corrupted index, broken ingestion, changed document formats, deleted sources.
- **Prompt/pipeline changes:** an unrelated edit affecting behaviour; dependency upgrades; tokenizer or embedding model changes.
- **Upstream tools/APIs** changing schemas or returning errors.
- **Feedback loops** and adversarial use.

**Bisect systematically:** compare traces from good and bad periods, replay old queries through the old and new configuration, and check versions of model, prompt, index, and tools.

**Fix**
- Roll back to the last-known-good configuration; then repair (refresh the index, update prompts, add examples, re-tune retrieval, fine-tune on new data, update the eval set).
- Add the failure cases to regression tests.

**Prevent**
- Version and pin everything, canary deployments, scheduled re-evaluation, index freshness monitoring, and a documented runbook with owners.

**Sources:**
- [How is ChatGPT's behavior changing over time?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.09009)
- [Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems](https://papers.nips.cc/paper/2015/hash/86df7dcfd896fcaf2674f757a2463eba-Abstract.html)
- [Google: Rules of Machine Learning](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/guides/rules-of-ml)
- [Langfuse: LLM observability and evaluation](https://langfuse.com/docs)

<a id="q553"></a>
### 553. How do you communicate AI limitations to non-technical stakeholders?

**Answer:**

Aim for accurate mental models, using plain language, concrete examples, and numbers.

**Techniques**
- **Analogies:** "a very well-read new hire who works fast but sometimes states things confidently without checking; it needs sources and review."
- **Show, do not tell:** demonstrate real failure cases (wrong facts, sensitivity to phrasing, refusal to say unknown) next to successes.
- **Use numbers:** "on our test set it is right about 90% of the time, so 1 in 10 answers needs correction; here is how we catch those."
- **Explain in business terms:** what a failure costs (wrong refund, compliance risk) and what mitigation exists (human review, citations, guardrails).
- **Set boundaries:** what it is good at (drafting, summarising, extracting, search) vs poor at (exact arithmetic, guaranteed facts, up-to-date information without tools, tasks requiring accountability).
- **Cover key limitations briefly:** hallucination, non-determinism, knowledge cutoff, data privacy, bias, cost and latency.
- **Pair every limitation with a mitigation and a decision:** avoid a list of scary caveats.
- **Avoid jargon:** say "makes things up" or "fabricates plausible-sounding answers" before "hallucination"; "cannot cite where it learned this" rather than "parametric memory".
- **Provide a one-page summary** and revisit as capabilities and results evolve; keep an FAQ.
- **Design UX to reinforce it:** sources, disclaimers where they matter, easy feedback and correction.

**Tone:** confident and calm, neither hype nor doom; invite questions and align on acceptable risk.

**Sources:**
- [Google: People + AI Guidebook (setting expectations)](https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/)
- [Anthropic: Reduce hallucinations](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-hallucinations)
- [NIST AI Risk Management Framework](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework)
- [Survey of Hallucination in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.05232)

<a id="q554"></a>
### 554. How would you approach building an AI feature with limited labeled data?

**Answer:**

Start with what foundation models give you for free and add labels only where they matter most.

**1. Clarify the task and success metric;** create a small but high-quality **eval set** first (100-500 examples). This is non-negotiable even with little data.

**2. Zero/few-shot with a strong LLM:** careful instructions, structured output, and 3-10 well-chosen examples (dynamic few-shot: retrieve similar examples per query). This is often enough.

**3. Improve with retrieval and tools:** RAG for knowledge, tools for computation.

**4. Get more labels cheaply**
- **Active learning:** label the examples where the model is uncertain or where errors concentrate.
- **LLM-assisted labelling / weak supervision:** use a strong model to pre-label, humans verify a sample (measure agreement).
- **Synthetic data:** generate varied examples (with diversity controls and human validation) to augment.
- Programmatic labelling functions (Snorkel-style) and heuristics.
- Use production feedback (accept/reject, edits) as labels.

**5. Fine-tune only if needed:** parameter-efficient methods (LoRA), or distil a strong LLM into a small task model once you have hundreds to thousands of examples; small encoders with SetFit work for classification with few examples.

**6. Transfer learning and data augmentation** where applicable (paraphrase, back-translation).

**7. Reduce risk:** human-in-the-loop, confidence thresholds, and abstention while data accumulates; ship early to collect real data (data flywheel).

**Pitfalls:** evaluating on synthetic data generated by the same model being evaluated, leakage between few-shot examples and test set, and label noise.

**Sources:**
- [Language Models are Few-Shot Learners](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.14165)
- [Snorkel: Rapid Training Data Creation with Weak Supervision](https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.10160)
- [SetFit: Efficient Few-Shot Learning Without Prompts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.11055)
- [LoRA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685)

<a id="q555"></a>
### 555. Describe your experience working with cross-functional teams on AI projects.

**Answer:**

Personal question: use real experience, structured as STAR, emphasising **collaboration mechanics**. Here is a sample structure.

**Sample answer (illustrative)**
- **Situation:** I led the engineering of a document-intelligence feature involving product, design, data/ML, legal, security, customer support, and domain experts.
- **Task:** deliver a reliable feature while aligning very different priorities and vocabularies.
- **Action:**
  - **Shared goals and metrics:** agreed with product on success criteria and an eval set; a weekly dashboard made progress visible to everyone.
  - **Domain experts as labelers and judges:** they wrote reference answers and reviewed failures; I turned their feedback into eval cases so it persisted.
  - **Design:** worked with designers on UX for uncertainty (citations, confidence, edit and feedback controls) since model behaviour shapes the interface.
  - **Security/legal:** early review of data flows, PII handling, vendor terms, and prompt-injection risks to avoid late blockers.
  - **Translation:** explained probabilistic behaviour with examples; used demos and error analysis sessions instead of slides.
  - **Process:** clear ownership (RACI), short feedback loops, written decision records, joint triage of quality issues.
- **Result:** launched on schedule with measurable quality targets met; support team adopted the feedback loop, cutting time to fix recurring issues.
- **Lessons:** involve non-engineers early, make evaluation shared, and document trade-offs.

**Interviewers look for:** empathy, communication, conflict handling (for example, a PM pushing for ship date vs quality), and evidence of influence without authority. Include one disagreement and how you resolved it with data.

<a id="q556"></a>
### 556. Where do you see AI engineering heading in the next 3-5 years?

**Answer:**

There is no single right answer; interviewers want a reasoned, grounded view with acknowledged uncertainty. Themes I would argue (as projections, not certainties):

- **Agents move into real workflows:** longer-horizon, tool-using systems (coding, research, operations). The differentiators become reliability, permissions, sandboxing, and human oversight, not just model capability.
- **Evaluation and observability become core disciplines:** eval-driven development, trace analysis, online evaluation, and regression testing become standard, like unit tests and monitoring.
- **Context engineering over prompt tricks:** managing memory, retrieval, tool definitions, and long contexts efficiently; standard protocols for tool integration (for example MCP) reduce glue code.
- **Cost and latency keep falling:** smaller, faster, and better models; more routing, distillation, on-device and edge inference; commoditisation of base capability shifts value to data, workflow integration, and UX.
- **Multimodal by default:** text, image, audio, and video handled in a single system; voice interfaces mature.
- **Security and governance mature:** prompt injection and data exfiltration defences, audit trails, regulation (for example the EU AI Act), and compliance tooling.
- **Roles converge:** AI engineering blends software engineering, product, and evaluation; AI-assisted development changes how engineers work, raising the bar on system design and judgement.
- **Open vs closed:** continued strong open-weight models make hybrid and self-hosted options practical.

**Advice for the answer:** connect trends to what you are doing to prepare (learning agents/evals, building projects), and acknowledge that predictions are uncertain and change quickly.

**Sources:**
- [Anthropic: Building effective agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents)
- [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/)
- [EU AI Act overview](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/)
- [Latent Space: The Rise of the AI Engineer](https://www.latent.space/p/ai-engineer)
