<a id="q557"></a>
### 557. Why are you interested in this AI engineering role?

**Answer:**

Personalise this with the actual company and role. A strong answer links **your background**, **the problem space**, and **the company's specifics**, in about 60-90 seconds.

**Structure**
1. **Hook:** what draws you to the field: turning fast-moving model capabilities into dependable products.
2. **Fit:** two or three specific experiences that match (for example, built a RAG system with an eval suite, cut inference cost, shipped agents with guardrails). Give one measurable result.
3. **Company/role specifics:** show research: the product, users, technical challenges (scale, domain, data), values, or recent launches. Explain why *this* problem interests you rather than praising the company generically.
4. **Growth and contribution:** what you want to learn and what you will bring (evaluation rigour, cross-functional communication, ownership).
5. **Close:** tie back to the impact you want to have.

**Sample (adapt)**
"I enjoy the part of AI work where a demo becomes something people rely on: evals, retrieval quality, cost and latency, safety. In my last role I built a RAG assistant, set up the evaluation pipeline, and improved answer correctness from about 60% to about 88% while halving cost per query. What excites me about this role is your focus on [specific domain], where correctness and trust matter and where the data and workflow problems are hard. I want to work on [specific challenge] with a team that treats evaluation as a first-class practice, and I think my experience shipping and monitoring LLM systems can help."

**Pitfalls:** generic enthusiasm, focusing only on compensation or prestige, criticising your current employer, and saying you like "AI" without specifics.

<a id="q558"></a>
### 558. Your PM wants to ship an AI feature with a 15% hallucination rate on edge cases. How do you communicate the risk?

**Answer:**

Do not say "no". Make the risk **concrete, quantified, and decision-ready**, and offer a path to ship safely.

**1. Clarify the number.** 15% of what? Edge cases only or overall? What share of traffic are edge cases? Overall expected error = share_of_edge_cases x 15% (for example 10% edge cases x 15% = 1.5% of requests, which at 100k requests/month is about 1,500 wrong answers). Check the confidence interval and how the test set was built.

**2. Translate to impact.** What happens when it is wrong: mild annoyance, wrong refund, legal or safety exposure, reputational damage? Show 3-5 real examples of failures, ranked by severity.

**3. Present options with trade-offs (not a veto)**
- Ship to a limited beta or internal users first, with feedback capture.
- Ship with mitigations: citations, abstention on low confidence, human-in-the-loop for high-risk categories, disclaimers, restrict scope (exclude the edge categories or route them to a human or non-AI flow).
- Delay two weeks to reduce the rate (targeted retrieval fixes, guardrails, model change) with a measurable target.
- Ship fully as is (state clearly the risk being accepted and who owns it).

**4. Define launch criteria and monitoring:** thresholds (for example under 3% on high-severity categories), online groundedness sampling, kill switch, rollback plan, and an owner for incident response.

**5. Put it in writing** and align on who accepts the residual risk.

**Sample line:** "On edge cases we are wrong 15% of the time, which we estimate is about 1.5% of all traffic. The worst failures involve billing. I recommend a limited launch that routes billing edge cases to human review, with a target to cut the rate below 5% in three weeks."

**Interviewers look for:** quantification, stakeholder empathy, offering alternatives, and shared ownership.

**Sources:**
- [Google: People + AI Guidebook](https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/)
- [Anthropic: Reduce hallucinations](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-hallucinations)
- [NIST AI Risk Management Framework](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework)
- [Google SRE Book: Embracing risk](https://sre.google/sre-book/embracing-risk/)

<a id="q559"></a>
### 559. A non-technical executive asks why your AI feature cannot be 100% accurate. How do you explain LLM limitations?

**Answer:**

Give a short, jargon-free explanation, an analogy, and a path forward focused on business risk.

**Core explanation (30 seconds)**
"The model does not look facts up like a database. It learned patterns from huge amounts of text and generates the most plausible next words. That makes it flexible and able to handle messy requests, but it also means it can produce something that sounds right and is wrong. The same flexibility that lets it understand a question phrased a thousand ways is why we cannot guarantee a perfect answer every time."

**Analogy:** an excellent, fast new employee who has read a huge library. They will handle most tasks well, but occasionally misremember and say it confidently. You reduce mistakes with reference materials (retrieval), checklists (guardrails), and review for important decisions, but you never reach literally zero.

**Reasons in plain terms**
- It generates rather than retrieves, so it can invent details.
- It does not know what it does not know; confidence is not reliable evidence of correctness.
- Language is ambiguous; different people may want different answers.
- Its knowledge is frozen at training time and may miss company-specific or recent facts.
- Outputs can vary between runs.

**What we do about it**
- Ground answers in our documents and show sources.
- Measure accuracy on a test set (for example 92% on a representative sample), and track it continuously.
- Automatic checks and human review where errors are costly.
- Use deterministic code for anything that must be exact (calculations, compliance rules).
- Let the system say "I don't know."

**Reframe:** "The right question is what accuracy we need for this use case, what an error costs, and what safeguards make the residual risk acceptable. Humans are not 100% accurate either; our target is better than the current process with a safety net."

**Sources:**
- [Survey of Hallucination in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.05232)
- [Anthropic: Reduce hallucinations](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-hallucinations)
- [Google: People + AI Guidebook](https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/)
- [NIST AI Risk Management Framework](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework)

<a id="q560"></a>
### 560. You need to choose between a complex agentic system that scores 15% better on benchmarks, or a simpler RAG pipeline that is easier to maintain. How do you decide?

**Answer:**

Treat it as a cost-benefit decision using your own evidence, not headline benchmark numbers.

**1. Interrogate the 15%**
- Which benchmark? Does it reflect **your** tasks and users? Re-run both candidates on your eval set, including edge cases.
- Is 15% relative or absolute, and does it matter for the business metric? Check confidence intervals and variance across runs (agents are more variable).
- Where do the gains come from: a few hard query types (multi-step, cross-document) or across the board?

**2. Count total cost of ownership**
- Inference: agents typically use many more LLM calls and tokens, and add latency (multi-step) and variance in latency.
- Reliability: more failure modes (loops, tool errors, compounding errors), harder to debug, and harder to test deterministically.
- Security surface: more tools means more prompt-injection and permission risk.
- Maintenance: prompts, tools, orchestration, and model upgrades; on-call burden and team skills.
- Observability and evaluation effort.

**3. Weigh the value of the gain**
- If the 15% concentrates on high-value, hard queries, consider a **hybrid**: simple RAG by default, escalate to an agentic path only for complex queries (routing).
- If most queries are simple lookups, the simple pipeline wins.

**4. Decide with criteria:** quality floor and target, latency (p95), cost per successful task, reliability SLOs, team capacity, risk level. A weighted scorecard makes the trade-off explicit.

**5. Reduce regret:** start with RAG (baseline, faster to ship), build eval and tracing, then add agentic capabilities incrementally where evals show measurable gains; keep the architecture modular so components can be swapped.

**Principle:** use the simplest system that meets the requirements; add complexity only when measured gains justify the operational cost.

**Sources:**
- [Anthropic: Building effective agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents)
- [Anthropic: How we built our multi-agent research system](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system)
- [ReAct](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629)
- [Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401)
